title: APOBEC3 antagonism fully explains HIV-1 Vif essentiality in THP-1 cells under interferon and differentiation conditions.
SENTRA: Privacy-Preserving Training in Outsourced Cloud Environments
abstract: Training machine learning models in untrusted clouds requires strong guarantees of confidentiality, integrity, and correctness, while remaining scalable and resilient to node churn. These challenges are further amplified in emerging agentic AI systems, where autonomous and distributed learning components require trustworthy coordination and secure state management across heterogeneous cloud environments. Existing Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) lack scalability and remain vulnerable to side-channel attacks for large workloads, while pure secure multi-party computation (MPC) approaches incur prohibitive overhead in practice. SENTRA (Secure ENclave-based TRaining Architecture) addresses these challenges through a hybrid architecture that combines TEEs, secret sharing, and communication-efficient MPC with system-level mechanisms that secure the entire training lifecycle. SENTRA introduces a scalable collective attestation protocol that verifies all participating enclaves and enforces hardware exclusivity before any node may store or process secret shares. Training data and model parameters are stored as secret shares in a versioned enclave-backed key–value store (KVS), providing rollback resistance and consistent state under the stated threat model. SENTRA further supports dynamic, fault-tolerant membership management, rollback resistance, and recovery from node failures. Evaluation of a prototype implementation shows that SENTRA achieves up to 8.89 samples/s throughput in software-only mode. In hardware-enclave mode, SENTRA provides memory-isolated confidentiality, fault-tolerant membership management, rollback resistance under the stated threat model, and recovery from node failures in approximately 8 seconds.
journal: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

title: Ghost Approvals: Approval-Provenance Failure in Agentic AI Frameworks
abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly execute actions for users, including transfers, deployments, account changes, and data release. Human approval gates are meant to prevent these actions from running until a reviewer has inspected the proposed action and issued a decision. Because approval can arrive after a delay, frameworks often persist workflow state and resume later. The resume path therefore becomes a security boundary: it must distinguish evidence that a human approved from approval-shaped values stored in mutable state. We define Approval-Provenance Failure as a condition in which a workflow resume path treats mutable approval-relevant state as evidence that a trusted human approval path produced a decision. Our adversary can write approval-relevant workflow state, but cannot use the approval path, change the model, modify tool code, invoke the tool directly, write the business database, mint a valid approval artifact, or access the approval issuer key. We evaluate 18 agent frameworks with human approval, interruption, or pause-resume behavior. Thirteen are exposed, three are resistant, and two are non-applicable. In exposed cases, state-only approval forgery causes gated action execution after a negative control blocks ordinary resume. The failure also forges the evidence of human oversight itself: across 500 paired audit traces, genuine and forged records are statistically indistinguishable, with exact-match rate 1.0 and AUC 0.5 under the tested native audit-field projection, while provenance evidence separates them with AUC 1.0. Finally, we evaluate a provenance-bound approval artifact that authenticates the decision with a MAC or digital signature and is verified at resume time. The full artifact check blocks 13 adversarial variants on five representative targets with microsecond-scale verification cost.
journal: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

title: LEASH: Zero-Trust Containment for AI Agent Swarms
abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly spawn sub-agent swarms that carry derived credentials to APIs, databases, and production infrastructure. When an operator kills a misbehaving orchestrator, its descendants keep exercising valid credentials for minutes to hours, since every deployed revocation mechanism needs network connectivity to a central authority, unavailable precisely when the network is degraded or adversarial. This paper presents LEASH - Liveness-Enforced Authorization for Swarm Hierarchies, which applies the zero-trust principle of continuous verification to a delegation hierarchy without a reachable authority. A parent emits a signed, epoch-indexed liveness beacon every Δh seconds, where Δh is the beacon interval, and each child staples a fresh beacon into every authentication proof, and the enforcement point checks freshness using only cached public keys and a local clock. Revocation happens by omission: when beacons stop, all descendants fail closed within a bounded zombie window Wz ≤ Wmax + Δh + ϵ , where Wmax is the maximum beacon age and ϵ is the clock skew. Immediate-parent verification at O(1) and full-chain verification at O(d), where d is the hierarchy depth, extend this bound against compromised intermediates. We evaluate LEASH with real GPT-4o-mini agent swarms: 0.71% tool-call overhead, cascading revocation across a 49-agent four-level hierarchy within bound, and 295 × less credential-theft exposure versus OAuth 2.0. Under prompt injection that bypasses application-layer guardrails, LEASH denies every post-revocation tool call, since enforcement sits below the LLM.
journal: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security

title: Emergence-Driven Security of LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are no longer limited to text generators, but they can also plan, call tools, delegate tasks to other agents, act within external environments, and change states in response to their actions. In Anthropic’s recent report on an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign involving Claude Code, individual subtasks appeared legitimate when evaluated in isolation but became malicious when combined into an autonomous attack sequence. Consequently, the security of such complex LLM-based agentic systems may fail even when each component appears secure in isolation. This position and open-problem paper argues that LLM agent security should be studied as emergence-driven security: the analysis of security properties that arise from the interactions among agents and its components over time. We define emergence-driven security and provide a conceptual taxonomy to classify emergent security-related phenomena in LLM agents, covering both beneficial and harmful forms of emergence. Based on these insights, we propose EASE, an Emergence-Aware Security Evaluation framework that provides a systematic process for assessing how interactions among agents combine over time to produce harmful or beneficial system-level security outcomes. Finally, we conclude by outlining open problems for studying emergent behavior in LLM agents in the context of security. The paper is intended to provide a foundation for examining how the emerging capabilities and operational needs of LLM agents may shape security evaluations that go beyond static, model-level testing.

A Novel Hardware-Aware Multi-Objective Evolutionary Neural Architecture for Crop-Disease Classification on Edge Devices
abstract: Crop disease detection plays a pivotal role in improving yields and quality, thereby supporting the efficient utilization of agricultural resources. Conventional detection methods suffer from limited scalability, subjective detection, and reduced reliability under varying environmental conditions. Machine learning and deep learning-based approaches have demonstrated their strong capabilities for efficient crop disease classification from versatile field and plant images. However, non-scalable architectures of these existing models consume large amounts of parameters, computational overhead, memory, and high latency. To address the aforementioned challenge, this research paper proposes hardware-aware, multi-objective, evolutionary search-based neural architectures for efficient crop detection on low-power edge devices. The proposed framework utilizes an EfficientNet-Lite model as the main component, whose parameters are optimized by the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) to achieve high classification performance, low inference latency, and limited computational parameters. In the proposed optimization, the framework predicts the performance of learning networks and estimates their execution time on the target edge hardware without testing each model directly. It then identifies a set of efficient architectures with varying accuracy, latency, and energy trade-offs, enabling the selection of the most suitable model based on the target device's requirements. Extensive Experimentation is carried out using PlantVillage datasets, and performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, latency, and computational parameters are calculated. Results illustrates the suggested framework has achieved the accuracy of 0.98, precision of 0.9734, recall of 0.973 with latency and parameters on different edge architectures. Compared with EfficientNet-B0 and MobileNetV3, it is [A]× faster and [B]× smaller, with accuracy within [C]%. These results show that hardware-aware evolutionary search can produce compact and accurate models for real-time plant disease monitoring in the field

title: Fail-Closed Authorization for Tool-Using AI Agents: A Capability Contract and Case Study
abstract: For tool-using LLM agents the decisive question is whether a concrete tool call is authorized before it executes. We describe the Agent Security Contract (ASC), a deny-by-default, pre-execution gate for agent and MCP tool calls. An ASC policy pins a SHA-256 digest of the approved tool catalog, declares per-agent tool allowlists with argument constraints, marks high-impact tools that require out-of-band approval, and bounds call rates; each decision (ALLOW, BLOCK, REQUIRE_APPROVAL) is emitted as an integrity-checked (unkeyed) JSON evidence envelope, and every error path we enumerate and test resolves to BLOCK. We evaluate the open-source implementation on static, recorded tool-call traces only; no live agent is run. Bypasses of the v0.1.0 demo policy found in review were fixed in v0.2.0; on a 60-case adversarial probe, allowed attacks fall from 32 to 1 (a policy gap), at the cost of 3 new benign over-blocks. On the author-constructed 66-scenario v0.2.1 corpus, designed around these checks, ASC returns the expected verdict in 66/66 cases; tool-name RBAC (Python and OPA/Rego) admits 30 of its 33 attacks by construction, and mutation testing shows the corpus exercises few policy constraints (8 of 62 single-constraint mutants killed). As a held-out check we replay 132 AgentDojo v1.2 ground-truth traces under policies frozen beforehand. With tool-level approval policies, 25 of 26 non-empty attack traces but also 60 of 97 benign tasks are held for approval. v0.2.0's strict-argument rule makes these unadapted policies block 94 of 97 benign tasks. Policies derived mechanically from AgentDojo's tool signatures first hit v0.2.0's lack of optional arguments (31 benign blocks); with v0.2.1 they reproduce the tool-level verdicts on all 132 traces, with no blocks and no newly admitted attack, so type-only declarations add no protection here. Median in-process latency is about 38 us per trace.

title: Cotransplantation With Human AAT-MSCs Enhances Human Islet Graft Survival in Humanized Mice by Modulating B- and T-Cell Responses.
Autonomous drilling and blasting operations in open-pit mining: automation of the process cycle, drilling accuracy and management of blast fragmentation of rocks
abstract: Drilling and blasting is a basic stage of open-pit mining that governs the particle-size distribution in the muck pile and, consequently, the costs of excavation, haulage and processing. Blasting accounts for 20–35% of the mining cost and up to 90% of the rock breaking by volume. Manual operations cause drilling inaccuracy, excessive consumption of explosives, an increased oversize yield, higher seismicity and risks to personnel. The paper systematizes directions of drilling and blasting robotization across the following five process stages: drilling, pattern and charge design, charging, initiation and fragmentation diagnostics. It also introduces a unified five-level automation-maturity scale, i.e. manual → mechanized → automated → robotic → autonomous operations. An integral robotization efficiency index is proposed, with process weights normalized by their contribution to the effects. Fragmentation forecast is made using the Kuznetsov–Rammler model and the Swebrec function. The median fragment size shifts from 420 to 350 mm and the oversize yield drops from 7.8 to 2.9% for a model block (250 mm hole diameter). Industry effects of automation are generalized including a 50–75% reduction in the hole deviation, a 40–65% drop in oversize, a 5–12% decrease in the specific explosive consumption, a 10–20% gain in the drilling productivity and a 15–30% reduction in seismicity. In the typical and target scenarios the integral index equals 56% and 88%. Implementation barriers and a roadmap for drilling and blasting robotization within the process-control system and the digital twin of the pit are outlined.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Classical Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Crop Type Classification From Sentinel-2 Ndvi Time Series
abstract: Accurate crop type classification from satellite imagery underpins food security monitoring, subsidy verification, and precision agriculture. The objective of this study is to establish which classification paradigm – classical machine learning or deep learning – provides higher accuracy and better cross-domain transferability for crop type mapping from Sentinel-2 NDVI time series, focusing on the underrepresented conditions of Ukrainian agriculture. Nine classifiers – six classical (Random Forest, SVM, XGBoost, LightGBM, KNN, Gradient Boosting) and three deep-learning-based (Temporal CNN, Bidirectional LSTM, Transformer encoder) – are evaluated on the multi-country AgriSen-COG benchmark and independently tested on a Ukrainian farm dataset (Krynychanska community, Dnipro region; four crops, 2025 season, 38,867 samples). Performance is assessed through overall accuracy (OA), balanced accuracy, weighted/ macro F1, Cohen’s kappa, Matthews correlation coefficient, ROC AUC, and per-class F1. The scientific novelty lies in: (a) the first unified nine-model comparison under identical protocols on a standardized European benchmark with simultaneous cross-domain transfer evaluation on independent Ukrainian field data; (b) quantification of the domain gap between Western-European benchmark and Ukrainian agricultural conditions for both classical and deep learning methods. Results show that deep learning models outperform classical classifiers on the benchmark, with TempCNN achieving the highest OA (0.839) – 3.2 % above the best classical model (XGBoost, 0.813). Upon cross-domain transfer, accuracy degrades substantially across all models (mean ΔOA = -56.4 %), yet deep learning retains a relative advantage: DL models lose on average 52.1 % vs. 58.5 % for classical ML, and TempCNN transfers best (OA = 0.441, +34.9 % relative to the best classical transfer). Per-class analysis reveals that only maize transfers reliably (F1 ≥ 0.82), while rapeseed and sunflower require domain adaptation. Conclusions. The practical significance of the results consists in providing evidence-based guidelines for selecting classification methods in operational crop monitoring systems, demonstrating that TempCNN is the preferred model for both in-domain accuracy and cross-domain robustness, and confirming that domain adaptation is essential before deploying benchmark-trained classifiers in Ukrainian agriculture.

title: Integrated Scheduling of Wind Power and Pumped Hydroelectric Storage Based on an MILP Model
abstract: In this article, we develop a tractable mixed-integer linear programming framework for the annual scheduling of a hybrid offshore wind and pumped hydroelectric energy storage system. The proposed formulation uses McCormick envelopes to relax the non-convex hydraulic power relations while embedding generation dispatch within a direct current optimal power flow model. In particular, we incorporate a cumulative storage incentive into the objective function to capture the trade-off between net electricity-market revenue and intra-horizon water availability, examining its weighting multiplier through a systematic sensitivity analysis. We illustrate the performance of the proposed formulation applied to (i) a modified PJM five-bus benchmark and (ii) an IEEE 30-bus network hosting two hybrid installations, driven by historical wind profiles from Tamaulipas and locational marginal prices from the Mexican wholesale electricity market. Moreover, we assess the selected binary operating-mode sequences ex post by re-optimizing the continuous dispatch under the exact bilinear hydraulic equations. The numerical results demonstrate that coordinated dispatch enhances energy arbitrage and dynamic grid interaction. In the five-bus case, the reference cumulative storage incentive raises the average upper-reservoir elevation relative to scheduling without the incentive, but both schedules end at the minimum operating level. Thus, the incentive improves water availability within the annual horizon without preventing terminal depletion or guaranteeing long-term water reserves.

title: Climatic Controls of Interannual Variability in Forest Land Surface Phenology Across Poland
abstract: Understanding how consistently forest phenology responds from year to year is important for characterizing vegetation responses to climatic variability, yet most studies have focused on long-term phenological trends. Here, we assessed the spatial patterns and environmental controls of detrended interannual variability in the start (SOS) and end (EOS) of the growing season across Polish forests during 2003–2025. SOS and EOS were derived from MODIS NDVI time series, while climatic controls were evaluated using variable-specific preseason windows. Generalized additive models were used to relate phenological variability to long-term climatic conditions, interannual climate variability, aridity, and topography. SOS and EOS variability showed distinct spatial patterns and contrasting climatic sensitivities. SOS was most strongly associated with temperature during the 30-day preseason, whereas EOS showed weaker and more variable climatic relationships. The relevant preseason periods differed among climatic variables and between SOS and EOS. Environmental relationships were predominantly nonlinear, with important effects of temperature, precipitation, soil moisture, solar radiation, aridity, and elevation. The models explained 35.2% and 51.6% of the deviance in SOS and EOS variability, respectively. These findings demonstrate that interannual variability provides complementary information to long-term phenological trends and that SOS and EOS respond differently to climatic and environmental conditions.

title: Orientation-Aware Feature Flow Network for Oriented Object Detection in Remote Sensing Images
abstract: Remote sensing oriented object detection faces the challenge of maintaining consistent rotational geometric information throughout feature representation, cross-scale propagation, and bounding-box localization. To address this issue, this paper proposes a direction–scale collaborative optimization method for oriented object detection. A frozen DINOv3 encoder is adopted as the semantic feature source to enhance target discrimination in complex backgrounds through global semantic modeling and dense feature representation. Rotation-Oriented Space-to-Depth Convolution (ROSPD) is introduced to preserve fine-grained spatial structures and local directional-response cues during downsampling. In addition, a Rotation-Aware Residual Fusion (RARF) module estimates local axial agreement between adjacent feature levels and uses it to condition residual multi-scale fusion. A ProbIoU–NWD joint loss with deterministic target-size-adaptive weighting is further constructed: it emphasizes NWD supervision for small objects and gradually returns to ProbIoU as target size increases, thereby improving localization stability under low-overlap conditions. Experiments on DIOR-R and DOTA-v1.5 demonstrate that the proposed method effectively improves the detection and localization performance of multi-scale oriented objects in complex remote sensing scenes.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Credit Card Approval Prediction Using Class Imbalance Handling Methods in the PyCaret AutoML Framework
abstract: Credit card approval processes are often performed manually, leading to inefficiencies, higher operational costs, and inconsistent decision-making. This study comparatively evaluates several machine learning models under different class imbalance handling strategies to predict credit card approval using the PyCaret AutoML framework. Two experimental scenarios were conducted on a dataset of 25,128 credit card applications, namely PyCaret's built-in SMOTE-based imbalance handling and random undersampling. In the SMOTE-based scenario, the Random Forest model achieved high accuracy, but its recall for the minority class was only 36.11%. In contrast, random undersampling produced more balanced performance, with the Gradient Boosting model achieving 100% recall. These findings indicate that class imbalance handling plays a critical role in credit card approval prediction, and that random undersampling provides more reliable minority-class detection than PyCaret's built-in SMOTE approach for the evaluated dataset.
journal: Jurnal JTIK (Jurnal Teknologi Informasi dan Komunikasi)

title: The AI Era's Lines of Code? A Case Study on What an Engineer's Token Spend Measures
abstract: Organizations use engineers' token spend to monitor AI adoption, set budgets, and measure productivity, but the metric's relationship with engineering output is unclear. We link five weeks of token usage in coding agents to the commits of 404 engineers at JetBrains, and analyze a company survey of 412 employees. We find that token spend varied mostly between engineers, and which engineers spent the most stayed largely the same over the five weeks. Among weeks with similar commit counts, the 90th percentile of spend was 39 to 240 times the 10th. Within an engineer, doubling spend was associated with about 10% more commits. Available work metrics explained 38% of the variation in spend between engineers and 13% of the week-to-week variation within an engineer. In the survey, respondents in technical roles reported in nearly nine of ten agent evaluations using agents for tasks beyond coding, such as analysis, research, and planning. Token spend therefore measures how much engineers use agents across many kinds of work and not the outcome and value of that work. We recommend using token spend at most for resource accounting, and evaluating agent-assisted work with evidence about tasks and outcomes.

title: Living constitutions: Participatory alignment for sovereign foundation models
abstract: In Constitutional AI, a plain-text "constitution" encodes values and gets incorporated into a model via post-training. However, the procedure for creating such a constitution poses significant challenges: who contributes, who decides which norms are included, and to what extent must the process be participatory or democratic? These challenges can be paralyzing. Yet, we argue that taking action is essential: without a deliberate constitution, sovereign models would risk misalignment or default to norms set by frontier model providers. We propose treating the development of a constitution as an evolving, participatory process akin to citizen science, iteratively drafted, tested, and refined. We therefore formulate five desirable principles: iterative, modular, justifiable, positional, and legitimate. We further argue that such a document must remain responsive not only over time but across the people it governs, and propose that provisions be marked as settled, contested, or underdetermined, so that durable disagreement is recorded in the constitution rather than resolved away. Empirically, we show via agent-based modelling that proposed process for maintaining living constitutions is robust against 50% bad actors among citizens - assuming a share of 75% participants with good intent in the deliberative body. This indicates that the proposed process tolerates a substantial share of adversarial participants.

title: Prompt2Echo (P2Echo): Text-Prompted Multi-View Echocardiography Segmentation with One Model
abstract: Automated segmentation in multi-view echocardiography is essential for comprehensive cardiac assessment, yet remains challenging due to substantial anatomical and appearance variability across standard acoustic windows. In this paper, we present P2Echo, a unified framework capable of segmenting diverse cardiac structures across multiple standard echocardiographic views using a single model controlled by structured view-aware text prompts. Unlike recent foundation model adaptations that rely on implicit latent priors, P2Echo explicitly conditions the segmentation process via a novel Dynamic Image-Text Alignment (DyITA) module. DyITA integrates a differentiable routing mechanism and token differential operators to dynamically modulate decoder features according to the requested view and target structure. This allows the network to adaptively switch its processing pathways for different views without architectural changes. Extensive experiments on a large-scale internal dataset (seen during training) and held-out evaluation on three external datasets demonstrate that P2Echo matches or exceeds both view-specific specialists and state-of-the-art universal models at a fraction of their computational cost, offering an efficient, controllable solution for multi-plane cardiac analysis. Code is available at: https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/P2Echo.

title: Minimum Synthesis Time for Single-Deletion Correcting Codes of Prescribed Size
abstract: DNA is a promising medium for data storage, but the high cost of DNA synthesis remains a major obstacle to its widespread deployment. In the reference-based synthesis model, synthesis time is measured by the length of the reference sequence. Previous studies have analyzed code sizes under synthesis-time constraints and constructed cost-constrained codes, including codes that correct deletions. In this paper, we study the minimum synthesis time for codes of prescribed size, considering both unrestricted codes and single-deletion correcting codes. We establish finite-length lower bounds valid for arbitrary reference sequences and upper bounds using existing $q$-ary differential VT codes. For fixed $q\geq3$, $A>0$, and $R\in(0,1)$, we determine the minimum synthesis time up to an $O(1)$ term when the code size is $M_n=\lfloor Aq^{Rn}\rfloor$. The corresponding redundancy is $(1-R)n\log_2q-\log_2A+o(1)$ bits. In particular, for these code sizes, the minimum synthesis time for single-deletion correcting codes exceeds that for unrestricted codes by a term proportional to $\ln n$, and we determine its coefficient. We also derive upper and lower bounds for code sizes $\lfloor q^n/(nq^{s_n})\rfloor$, where $s_n\to\infty$ and $s_n=o(n)$. These sizes correspond to redundancy $\log_2 n+s_n\log_2q+o(1)$ bits. For code sizes $\lfloor q^n/(nq^c)\rfloor$ with fixed constant $c$, the redundancy is $\log_2 n+c\log_2q+o(1)$ bits. We give conditions under which single-deletion correcting codes exist or do not exist for all sufficiently large $n$, together with bounds on the minimum synthesis time. These results show how code size and the single-deletion correcting constraint affect synthesis time and provide theoretical guidance for the construction of cost-constrained codes.

title: Double-quantum enhanced coherent control and magnetic sensing of spin defects in hexagonal boron nitride
abstract: The negatively charged boron vacancy ($V_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a promising spin defect for quantum sensing in two-dimensional material systems. Previous hBN experiments have mainly exploited the two spin-triplet ground-state single-quantum transitions separately. Here we implement a double-quantum driving scheme based on simultaneous resonant microwave excitation of both ground-state single-quantum transitions, establishing coherent control of the $Δm_s=2$ manifold in a $V_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$ ensemble. We compare the resulting double-quantum response with the corresponding single-quantum protocol under identical experimental conditions. The double-quantum protocol enhances the optical readout contrast and yields a 2.6-fold signal-to-noise improvement in AC magnetometry. We further use the double-quantum relaxation channel as a differential probe of electric-field and strain noise, showing that the present data are compatible with correlated-surface or volume-distributed fluctuations, while short-range uncorrelated surface-noise models are disfavored within the assumptions of our analysis. These results establish double-quantum coherent control and frequency-resolved AC magnetometry in hBN spin ensembles, and identify the sample-dependent measurements needed to determine the microscopic origin of the dominant relaxation channels.

title: Deep Personalization: Continuous Context Observation for Local Proactive Agents
abstract: As AI agents become increasingly capable, users must still recognize when and how to ask for help, leaving many opportunities for useful support unrealized. Proactive agents hold the promise to close this gap, but effective proactivity requires understanding users' real-time activities and personalizing intervention timing so that assistance is offered when it is likely to be helpful rather than disruptive. We introduce deep personalization, a closed-loop process that connects continuous context observation with continual agent adaptation: an agent observes user activity, selectively retains long-term context, and adapts intervention decisions from implicit feedback. We initiate deep personalization in Coco, a proactive desktop agent, by having a separate Observer Agent that monitors desktop activity, maintains compact long-term user modeling context, and learns when assistance is desirable from implicit signals such as engagement, dismissal, explicit requests, and repeated work patterns. We further develop efficient on-device strategies to enable the Observer Agent to run on local AI compute platforms without streaming raw activity data off-device. For evaluation at scale without collecting sensitive real-user activity, we introduce a data-synthesis pipeline that transforms existing computer-use trajectories into OSWorld-Persona, a benchmark with persona-conditioned intervention labels. On OSWorld-Persona, deep personalization improves macro F1 across three model backbones from 0.12-0.19 under direct prompting to 0.35-0.48 after adaptation, a 2.4-3.0x relative gain. In a week-long user study, we observe that Coco improves its macro-averaged F1 score from 0.199 to 0.515. These results suggest that on-device deep personalization can make proactive agents more timely and increasingly aligned with each user's everyday work.

title: Fragment-Free Constraint Programming for the Preemptive Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem
abstract: This article addresses the preemptive flexible job shop scheduling problem with makespan minimization (FJm | pmtn | C_max). We propose an exact constraint programming approach that completely avoids representing the processing fragments of an operation. Operations are placed in flexible time windows, where Horn's workload condition guarantees feasible preemptive scheduling, and Jackson's preemptive earliest-deadline-first rule reconstructs exact processing segments post-optimization in O(n log n) time per machine. To manage undecided machine assignments, we extend the PreemptiveNoOverlap global constraint to optional intervals within IBM ILOG CP Optimizer, performing overload checking and preemptive edge-finding in O(n log n) time while eliminating infeasible machine alternatives. The CP model is warm-started using a multi-round MILP assignment relaxation with Carlier's head-tail bounds and a window-based greedy heuristic. Extensive computational experiments on 276 pFJSSP benchmark instances and 78 pJSSP instances demonstrate that the proposed method significantly advances the state of the art. Within a 600~s time limit, it improves the upper bounds of the previously published logic-based Benders decomposition by 3.6% on average, increases the number of proven optimal pFJSSP instances from 102 to 180, and closes 74 instances for the first time (including the entire Barnes family). On the pJSSP under identical hardware conditions, it proves 67 of 78 instances optimal (compared to 51 by the baseline solver Mistral) and closes 9 of the 11 long-standing open problems.

title: Differentially Private Statistical Inference for Rankings from Pairwise Comparisons
abstract: Reliable inference for rankings of large language models based on human pairwise comparisons must preserve the privacy of individual preference records. To meet this need, we develop methods for score and rank inference under the Bradley-Terry model with edge differential privacy. For an objective-perturbed estimator, a new leave-one-out analysis establishes finite-sample bounds on Euclidean and entrywise estimation errors. For sufficiently dense comparison graphs, the error bounds extend to smaller privacy budgets, including regimes in which its privacy term dominates its statistical term. A uniform asymptotic expansion yields asymptotically valid confidence intervals for individual scores and pairwise score differences. To improve finite-sample performance, we account for both regularization bias and privacy-induced randomness by combining a plug-in ridge-bias correction with Gaussian-Laplace calibration. We further establish a bootstrap procedure for simultaneous rank inference, providing asymptotically valid confidence sets for individual ranks and tests of top-$K$ membership. When the comparison probability is public and known, all proposed inferential procedures require no additional privacy budget. We evaluate finite-sample performance through simulations and apply the proposed methods to rank large language models for creative writing.

title: Route-Time Conflict Maps for Cooperative End-to-End Autonomous Driving
abstract: Existing cooperative end-to-end driving works at Class A (status-sharing) of the SAE J3216 classes of cooperative driving automation (CDA): vehicles exchange what they perceive, not what they intend, so each plans alone when to go, which limits cooperation and leads to deadlock when both vehicles yield or to collisions when both go. We present When2Go, a cooperative end-to-end driving system that learns when to go by sharing intent under CDA Class B or higher. Each vehicle broadcasts its LiDAR detections with forecast motion as instance tokens, together with its plan and intended trajectory. The receiver draws the fused detections, forecasts and partner plans into a route-time conflict map, the occupancy along its route over the planning horizon, on which a planner scores candidate speed profiles. Where two intended trajectories conflict, an order gate, a precedence network distilled from a right-of-way rule, decides who goes first; both vehicles evaluate it on the same messages and so reach the same order. When2Go imitates the rule-based expert of V2Xverse, which sees the simulator's ground truth; stops that When2Go cannot observe within its 2 s planning horizon are relabelled, so that it does not learn to wait without an observable cause. For our runs only, the benchmarks' PID controller steers by When2Go's waypoints instead of the route, and its forced push of long-waiting vehicles is off. With one model, When2Go sets the state of the art on three closed-loop CARLA benchmarks: 97.8 and 90.7 driving score on InterDrive without and with traffic (best published 90.1 and 78.9), 70.0 on the public V2Xverse protocol (best of sixteen rerun methods 59.1) and 88.2 on MDrive (best rerun 85.1), with 95.0% of its vehicles collision-free (87.7%).

title: Mobile AI Factory: Building Specialized Language Models for Your Mobile Device
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) running on mobile devices can keep user data private and work without connectivity. But they perform well only when fine-tuned for the target task and sized for the target device, a process that today requires repeated expert tuning. We present {\it Mobile AI Factory}, an agentic system that builds a fine-tuned, quantized SLM for a given task and phone. Given a task specification and a target phone, an orchestrator LLM chooses whether to tune hyperparameters, mine real data, or generate synthetic examples, while fixed rules roll back changes that hurt accuracy. The factory searches from small to large models across base models and quantizations, adapts its accuracy goal as it searches, and uses real measurements of the target phone across inference engines and backends. We evaluate Mobile AI Factory on ten tasks and four Android phones. On an unseen testset, its on-device models outperform two five-shot frontier models on five tasks, by up to 0.34, and match them on three more. Its search comes within 0.03 of exhaustively training all 27 model variants on an entity extraction task, while using 19$\times$ less GPU time. Phone measurements also matter: the best configuration changes across phones. Without phone measurements, Claude Opus 5.5, given the full hardware and model specifications, misses the app's requirements in 25\% of easy and moderate cases and in 60\% of hard ones. Code is available at: https://github.com/evanly-gh/SLM_Factory.

title: Distribution Shift Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery using Machine Learning Models
abstract: Remote sensing imagery acquired by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) supports wide range of applications; however, deploying machine learning (ML) models on resource-constrained aerial platforms introduces challenges beyond predictive accuracy, particularly when deployment data differ from the distributions observed during training. Such shifts are common in remote sensing due to geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual variations. A practical solution is to equip deployed models with mechanisms that detect emerging distribution shifts and support subsequent responsive actions. This paper presents an empirical case study of three open-source detection tools: (i) Alibi-Detect; (ii) NannyML; and (iii) PyTorch-OOD. Using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts, we evaluate both detection effectiveness and computational latency of these tools. Our results reveal differences in detection behavior and processing cost across methods and implementations, highlighting trade-offs between detection capability and response-time. These findings motivate further work toward lightweight, and latency-aware monitoring mechanisms for resource-constrained systems.

title: Parallel Broyden Methods for Efficiently Evaluating Nonlinear State Space Models
abstract: Nonlinear state space models are typically evaluated sequentially, limiting their ability to exploit modern parallel hardware. Recent work has shown that state space models can be evaluated in parallel by reformulating evaluation as a root-finding problem, which can be solved with a parallel form of Newton's method. However, exact Newton methods require expensive multiplication of dense Jacobian matrices, and quasi-Newton methods based on diagonal approximations, while more scalable, are often slow to converge because they neglect interactions across state dimensions. We introduce a novel quasi-Newton approach based on Broyden's method, which captures coupling terms with diagonal-plus-low-rank approximations to blocks of the Jacobian. We construct the approximations from trajectory secants, avoiding automatic differentiation while retaining the favorable scaling of diagonal approximations and remaining compatible with parallel scan through rank compression. We prove finite-step recovery of the exact trajectory under the compressed scan, and show that convergence is tracked by the compression error and by the block approximation error along the current trajectory error, rather than in spectral norm. Empirically, we show that our method is advantageous when interactions are approximately low rank or when Jacobian evaluation is expensive: on low-rank RNNs, parallel MCMC algorithms, and denoising diffusion models, it converges in fewer iterations than other quasi-Newton methods and is the fastest parallel method when Jacobian evaluation is expensive or state dimensions are large.

title: EJAI: Judgment-Preserving Civic AI for Data Center Environmental Justice
abstract: Communities in the United States and around the world are contesting data centers, the physical infrastructure of AI. These disputes pose environmental justice issues: residents must weigh unevenly distributed burdens using evidence scattered across metrics, corporate claims, policy documents, and public testimony. A formative study with 10 users showed that dashboards and single-agent AI can settle questions before people examine that evidence. Here we present EJAI, a source-grounded system that links an interactive map, retrieved evidence, missing-data statements, and two stakeholder personas that allow people to inspect evidence and form their own policy recommendations. In a small functional benchmark of 21 queries, retrieved evidence supported 98.4% of factual claims and the system acknowledged missing evidence in 32 of 33 cases. Persona alignment carried a grounding cost: the Corporate Executive omitted some evidence that conflicted with its assigned priorities. In a within-subjects study, 15 participants acting as residents prepared for a simulated town hall. Some checked cited AI claims while treating map metrics as official, some made conditional recommendations with safeguards such as water-use disclosure, and some found the personas simplified or biased. Our results suggest that civic AI can support preparation for public reasoning when it makes evidence, gaps, and disagreement open to inspection, and that corpus imbalance and two-sided personas remain open justice concerns.

title: GEMOR-GS: Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM
abstract: Photorealistic and metrically consistent world representations are a primary requirement for LiDAR--inertial--visual SLAM systems that serve robots over continuous operation. 3D Gaussian splatting makes such representations attainable by supplying an explicit, renderable, and queryable scene model. We present GEMOR-GS (Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM) to make the Gaussian map geometrically accurate, globally refined, and re-enterable, providing a better appearance for robot perception and decision-making. To improve the 3DGS map, the LiDAR--camera extrinsic is first estimated offline by direct-method alignment over dedicated calibration segments and reused by all following online and offline processes. Under the calibrated geometry, keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters are refined alternately under a gated differentiable-rendering and LiDAR--projection objective. The final global reconstruction is then rebuilt from the refined keyframe schema with all online constraints lifted. For the robot SLAM lifecycle, the method recovers the pose from the 3DGS map after tracking loss through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP coarse localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement. Experiments on one self-collected and five public sequences quantify each element: the offline reconstruction wins all paired keyframes against the online map by 14.3--19.9 dB, improves PSNR by approximately 9 dB over Gaussian-LIC2, and achieves 86--100% held-out relocalization success tied to extrinsic quality. The results show that GEMOR-GS improves the geometric accuracy, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability of the 3DGS map, serving as a dependable robot world model for SLAM and downstream tasks.

title: Discovering Structurally Plausible and Interpretable Cognitive Models with Large Language Models
abstract: Computational cognitive modeling has traditionally relied on manual model construction, which is a time-intensive process that requires substantial domain expertise. Although recent LLM-based approaches have begun to automate model generation, they often prioritize predictive accuracy at the expense of structural plausibility and parameter identifiability. We introduce DisCo, an LLM-guided framework that discovers interpretable symbolic cognitive models through evolutionary search with two structural components: a Validator that filters structurally invalid models, and a Cleaner that promotes parameter identifiability by removing redundant parameters. Across three behavioral tasks, DisCo consistently discovers models that achieve performance competitive with task-specific baselines. Ablation analyses show that the Validator is important for recovering psychologically meaningful structure. Without this component, models tend to violate behavioral constraints and show less consistent associations with external cognitive measures. These results suggest that LLM-driven model discovery, when coupled with appropriate structural constraints, can yield cognitively plausible models that go beyond predictive fit.

title: Earth Embeddings in Environmental Remote Sensing
abstract: Earth observations from satellite platforms have profoundly transformed research and applications across numerous domains. However, uneven observation coverage and frequent data gaps continue to limit their ability to capture Earth's surface dynamics. Moreover, processing multi-modal Earth observations requires substantial computational resources and sophisticated data harmonization frameworks, which may not be readily accessible to many remote sensing practitioners. Earth embeddings have emerged as promising solutions to these challenges. As general-purpose representations converted from multi-source Earth observations, Earth embeddings can support a wide range of downstream tasks with no requirement of task-specific feature design and preprocessing. In this study, we first introduce the theoretical foundations of Earth embeddings. Then, we review several representative Earth embedding products. We next examine the applications of Earth embeddings across six major domains of environmental remote sensing. Finally, we systematically assess the performance of Earth embeddings in four downstream tasks, including hyperspectral image classification, individual tree crown segmentation, crop yield prediction, and aboveground biomass mapping. Our review and case studies suggest that, despite several advantages over conventional Earth observation data, current Earth embeddings do not always outperform remote sensing imagery or hand-crafted features. Earth embeddings should not be viewed as a direct replacement for conventional EO data, but rather as representations that provide stable information across space and time. Remote sensing practitioners may consider evaluating Earth embeddings' suitability for specific tasks and using them strategically, rather than assuming superior performance by default.

title: When to Start Denoising? Adaptive Denoising Entry for Generative Video Compression
abstract: Generative video compression offers a promising solution for compressing and reconstructing videos under extremely low bitrate constraints, among which the diffusion-based solutions still achieve the best performance by providing the powerful generative latent prior. However, their effectiveness critically depends on when the compressed latent is introduced into the diffusion process, which directly governs the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and perceptual realism. To address this limitation, we identify denoising start-timestep selection as a key factor governing this trade-off and formulate it as a geometric optimization problem. Based on this formulation, we propose a novel adaptive diffusion entry method for generative video compression (ADE-GVC), the first timestep-aware generative video compression framework, featuring a lightweight predictor that estimates an adaptive denoising start point from the compressed latent. A temporal adapter further extracts compression-aware conditions and injects them into a pretrained video diffusion model, enabling the reconstruction of videos with both high fidelity and realism. More importantly, we observe a strong quantitative relationship between the predicted timesteps and the distortion between the original and compressed latents, providing empirical support for our optimization formulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ADE-GVC achieves the state-of-the-art performance on perceptual metrics and substantially improves reconstruction realism over existing generative video compression methods. Notably, our ADE-GVC achieves an average bitrate savings of 40.99\% (on DISTS) and 95.24\% (on PSNR) compared to the latest open-source baseline GLC-Video.

title: Multifidelity Operator Inference for Non-intrusive Model Reduction under Data Scarcity
abstract: Many-query analyses, in which a computational model is repeatedly evaluated, play an important role in uncertainty quantification and optimization for engineering design. However, many-query analyses can be prohibitively expensive when considering high-fidelity numerical models, especially those governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). Surrogate modeling replaces costly simulations with cheap approximations, enabling practical uncertainty quantification and design workflows. Machine learning (ML) approaches to surrogate modeling have gained significant traction in the development of surrogate models due to their non-intrusive nature; they do not require access to the underlying simulation code. The Operator Inference (OpInf) approach, in particular, fits reduced operators to state and corresponding time derivative data. However, high-fidelity training data is scarce due to limited computational budgets, and OpInf models trained on such scarce data often exhibit high variance, a critical liability in high-risk engineering design. We propose Multifidelity Operator Inference (MF-OpInf), which reduces this variance by supplementing scarce high-fidelity snapshots with abundant low-fidelity data drawn from coarser discretizations of the same problem. MF-OpInf handles data across varying fidelity levels by utilizing a multifidelity linear regression framework to estimate the reduced operators. Numerical experiments on model PDE problems demonstrate that MF-OpInf predicts PDE solution fields with higher accuracy compared to the high-fidelity-only OpInf with the same computational budget.

title: Tri-Stack-PIM: A Heterogeneous Multi-Die 3D-Integrated Processing-in-Memory Architecture for Efficient LLM Inference
abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference during autoregressive decoding is fundamentally memory-bandwidth-bound. Existing three-dimensional (3D) stacked processing-in-memory (PIM) architectures alleviate the off-chip bandwidth wall, yet remain constrained by several limitations: physical layer (PHY), controllers, and direct memory access (DMA) engines compete with arithmetic units for advanced-node base-die area; hybrid-bonding keep-out zones fragment the base-die floorplan and impede physical design; compute tiles built in a dynamic random access memory (DRAM) process are restricted to low logic density, capping achievable throughput; and nonlinear operations offloaded to the host reintroduce a communication bottleneck. We present Tri-Stack-PIM, a heterogeneous three-die architecture that resolves these tensions by dedicating a top DRAM die to storage, a middle buffer die on a mature process node to PHYs, DMA engines, and near-memory compute units, and a bottom base die on an advanced node exclusively to single-instruction-multiple-data (SIMD) multiply-accumulate (MAC) arrays. We further introduce a Unified Buffer-Aware Ready-based (UBAR) hardware out-of-order micro-operation scheduler that enforces cross-die dependency correctness at runtime while maximizing issue-slot utilization through a multi-term priority function, recovering up to 90% of the cycles that an in-order policy would forfeit. A joint architecture-dataflow co-exploration identifies Pareto-optimal configurations that reduce the energy-delay product (EDP) by 33-66x over naive parameter selection. Evaluated across multi-head, grouped-query, and multi-query attention (MHA, GQA, MQA) mechanisms with batch sizes 1-32, Tri-Stack-PIM achieves geometric-mean speedups of 4.95x, 2.57x, and 1.68x across all three attention mechanisms and batch sizes over a graphics processing unit (GPU) baseline, AttAcc, and H2-LLM, respectively.

title: MouldIt: Data Efficiency of Multi-Task Temporal Representation Learning in Injection Moulding
abstract: Smart industrial solutions that can address multiple tasks require models that understand the underlying processes. We examine representation learning for modeling the injection moulding process as an example of such solutions. We consider its data efficiency and multi-modal benefit compared to classical machine learning alternatives. To this end, we synthesize a process-informed dataset based on a real reference cycle of an Erlanger Träger part. We then introduce MouldIt, a temporal convolution and attention based variational autoencoder that reconstructs in-mould signals, while classifying parts as acceptable or as one of our synthetic failure modes. We evaluate MouldIt on two tasks, known-class classification and unknown-class detection, across nine dataset sizes in single-modal and multi-modal settings. We compare it with an accept-all baseline and the classical methods k-nearest neighbors, logistic regression, random forests, and principal component analysis, which we adapt to support both tasks. MouldIt outperforms classical methods across both tasks from 4000 cycles in the single-modal setting and from 2000 cycles in the multi-modal setting. It achieves part sorting losses of 6.0 $\pm$ 0.7% and 1.0 $\pm$ 0.3% in the single-modal and multi-modal settings respectively, ranking first across all baselines and a combination of principal component analysis and random forests.

title: DrugCoding: A Scientific Programming Agent for Drug Discovery
abstract: Drug discovery involves multiple interconnected research stages, including molecular design, property prediction, and virtual screening. These processes are characterized by complex workflows, interdependent computational tasks, and diverse specialized tools, placing substantial demands on the coordination of scientific models and computational resources. However, existing large language model (LLM)-based scientific agents still face challenges in autonomous planning of complex tasks, adaptive selection of specialized models, and reliable execution of multi-stage scientific computations, limiting their effectiveness in automating complex drug discovery workflows. To address these challenges, we propose DrugCoding, a scientific programming agent system that integrates scientific task planning, adaptive model routing, multi-agent collaboration, and programmatic tool execution. DrugCoding enables autonomous task planning and dynamic model adaptation for complex research objectives. It can flexibly invoke specialized scientific models, autonomously generate and execute code according to task requirements, and leverage multi-agent collaboration to support efficient execution and reliable validation of complex scientific tasks. To evaluate DrugCoding's performance in scientific tool invocation and multi-stage task execution, we conduct multi-turn tool-calling experiments across diverse language models and scientific tool interfaces. Experimental results demonstrate that DrugCoding achieves an average session-level Pass@1 of 97.35% on the full benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline, Codex, by 9.24%. On the challenging subset, DrugCoding achieves 97.92%, exceeding the strongest baseline.

title: EgoHMP: Achieving Precise Human Motion Prediction in 3D Scenes via Egocentric Cues
abstract: The complex interactive dependencies between human behavior and 3D scenes make accurately predicting human intent a major challenge for human motion prediction (HMP). While recent studies use human gaze to infer intent, gaze signals suffer from ambiguity, drift, and a reliance on eye-tracking hardware. Research in cognitive science indicates that egocentric views inherently encode potential interactions, while head motion serves as a crucial precursor in motion planning. Motivated by this, we propose EgoHMP, a novel framework that uses egocentric views and head motions as robust carriers of interaction intent. By translating this intent into an envisioning of future interactions, EgoHMP achieves precise HMP in 3D scenes. EgoHMP first employs a vision-motion alignment encoder to align the visual and motion feature spaces. Based on these aligned features, an egocentric intent predictor with a modality-aware modulation mechanism adaptively suppresses invalid interaction cues to predict an accurate interaction probability map. Furthermore, to enhance the stability and realism of the generated motions, we propose a contact-aware motion decoder. Specifically, inspired by the human cognitive process of planning trajectories prior to action execution, we first predict a global trajectory to serve as a self-prompt, effectively mitigating the optimization conflict in diffusion models. Subsequently, we introduce a multi-stage denoiser, which relieves motion artifacts by incorporating human contact modeling through a multi-stage optimization strategy. Finally, a GCN-based motion decoder is employed to synthesize physically plausible and semantically consistent motions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EgoHMP achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: Efficient control of multi-agent robust MDPs through tensor trees
abstract: This paper introduces a tensor-based framework for controller synthesis of stochastic multi-agent systems under temporal logic specifications that couple the agents, such as one agent reaching its goal only after another agent has reached its own. The agents are modeled as robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs), whose transition probabilities are only known to lie in an ambiguity set, for instance due to abstraction errors, learned models, or uncertain parameters. We show that the decoupled nature of the ambiguity sets allows one to decompose the computation of a lower bound on the satisfaction probabilities into per-agent factors, so that only the per-agent ambiguity sets need to be stored. This leads to improved memory complexity compared to monolithic approaches. We compare our approach with state-of-the-art approaches based on approximate simulation relations and with interval MDP abstractions. On a four-agent ordered reach-avoid benchmark, our approach certifies a lower bound twice as high as the simulation relation- based approach with 20 times less memory, and needs about 200 times less memory than the interval MDP abstraction, even at a resolution with about a million times more joint cells.

title: Priority-Aware Firm and Flexible Capacity Quantification for Large-Load Interconnection
abstract: We study how to unlock existing transmission capacity to accelerate large-load interconnection under differentiated quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. We establish an efficient framework to quantify firm and flexible hosting capacities and assess marginal values of grid upgrades. Specifically, we define multiple flexible capacity tiers with differentiated QoS limits and design a two-layer priority rule to allocate curtailment among tiers. We then formulate a mixed-integer chance-constrained model to jointly quantify firm and flexible capacities under QoS and priority constraints. To improve computational efficiency, we derive an equivalent aggregate formulation that eliminates individual curtailment variables and priority binaries without changing the feasible capacity set. Numerical results show the computational advantage of aggregation. Multi-tier flexible capacity increases total admitted capacity by 45.0\% over the firm-only hosting capacity.

title: BypassGym: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents' Endpoint Defense Evasion Capabilities
abstract: Artificial intelligence agents increasingly automate cybersecurity tasks, including offensive operations. Frequent attacks across the web make endpoint detection and response (EDR) a critical defense, but whether AI agents can evade it remains unclear. Benchmarks evaluate the offensive capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents in areas such as penetration testing and vulnerability discovery. One important capability that these benchmarks do not address is defense evasion, specifically whether an agent can develop a program that executes a payload without being blocked or terminated by a deployed EDR. We introduce BypassGym, to our knowledge the first benchmark to systematically evaluate this capability on real endpoints. Given command-and-control (C2) shellcode, an agent must generate and compile a loader that executes the payload without being blocked or terminated. A supplementary evasion knowledge skill provides domain knowledge and supports comparisons with and without this input. BypassGym is built on Proxmox VE(PVE), so the evaluation environment runs real Windows systems and EDR products inside virtual machines and returns structured detection feedback to the agent. We evaluate 5 lightweight model backends against 6 EDR products and 3 payloads, and find that even these simple models generate successful submissions, with DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash reaching 17/18 successful runs and Bitdefender allowing only 5 of 15 runs to pass. These results provide a systematic measurement of current AI agents' endpoint defense evasion capabilities and identify areas for defenders to investigate.

title: On Private Knowledge Retrieval and Private Inference for secure multi-agent systems
abstract: Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems. In real multi-agent systems, agents need to deal with malicious agents some of which can exploit security vulnerabilities to do harm. A memory poisoning attack is an example of exploiting a vulnerability to modify agents knowledge and, thus, affect its behavior. In an agent, there are different types of memory systems (semantic, episodic, and short-term) which have their own characteristics and for which different memory poisoning attacks may be developed. In this paper we focus on semantic memory, we discuss its attack, and mitigation strategies. We introduce private knowledge retrieval and private inference. We propose a signature system in the knowledge base to prevent from undesired manipulation. This should avoid memory poisoning attacks by introducing security by design in the construction of the semantic memory. In our architecture, an agent contains a local Prolog-like inference system (i.e., using Horn clauses to represent knowledge) which accesses an external knowledge base to get the required knowledge. This externally signed knowledge base is accessed privately. We provide different implementations in Python using different privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy (IT-PIR).

title: Agentic AI Meets Formal Verification in the Era of Agentic Hardware Development
abstract: As AI agents become increasingly capable of generating and optimizing hardware circuits, ensuring the correctness of AI-generated designs becomes more important. Meanwhile, advances in AI lower the barriers to developing and applying formal methods, creating new opportunities to automate and improve hardware verification. This invited paper presents an overview of the methodologies and applications of hardware formal methods in the AI era. First, we examine how agentic AI advances hardware formal methods across three levels: specification, proof construction, and reasoning engines. Second, we discuss how formal methods support reliable AI-driven hardware development through RTL generation, debugging, and correctness-preserving optimization. We review representative research alongside our recent contributions, highlighting key technical advances and insights from experimental results. Finally, we discuss future research opportunities toward proof-native hardware development, where formal reasoning could become an integral part of autonomous hardware design.

title: Toward Autonomous RTL and Synthesis Optimization: Benchmarking and Self-Improving Agents
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents are creating new opportunities for hardware design optimization. This paper examines three connected directions toward autonomous RTL and synthesis optimization: (1) Realistic benchmarking. We discuss reference-based and open-ended RTL optimization benchmarks that evaluate optimization opportunities under realistic EDA workflows. (2) Tool-grounded RTL optimization. We present Dr. RTL, a multi-agent framework that automates critical-path analysis, RTL rewriting, and implementation-level evaluation, while continuously improving through reusable optimization skills. Evaluated on 20 real-world RTL designs, Dr.~RTL achieves average WNS/TNS improvements of 21\%/17\% with a 6\% area reduction over commercial synthesis. (3) Design-specific synthesis optimization. We explore agent-driven synthesis script tuning and the discovery of executable synthesis algorithms across intermediate representations, technology-independent optimization, and technology mapping. Finally, we envision AI-native design automation that jointly explores architectural, RTL, and EDA algorithm design spaces, guided by verification constraints and implementation feedback.

title: Continuous-Time Modeling of Destination-Constrained Dynamic Systems via Doob's $h$-Transform
abstract: Existing work on modeling destination-constrained dynamic systems has mainly focused on discrete-time formulations with linear destination constraints or Gaussian destination distributions. Since practical systems are more naturally modeled in continuous time and often subject to nonlinear/non-Gaussian constraints/distributions, this paper proposes a unified measure-transformation framework for continuous-time modeling of systems subject to deterministic or distributional constraints on a nonlinear function of the terminal state. The framework starts from an unconstrained Itô stochastic differential equation, typically derived from physical laws to describe the system's forward evolution without destination information, and takes its induced path measure as unconstrained measure. Doob's $h$-transform is employed to transform this measure into a constrained path measure incorporating destination information through an injected drift. The resulting system is proved to satisfy the constraints while preserving the laws of the unconstrained state process conditioned on the destination information. The transition density is derived, and the path measure of the distributionally constrained system is proved to uniquely minimize Kullback--Leibler divergence from the unconstrained path measure among those satisfying the same distributional constraint. Its injected drift is further shown to converge pointwise to that of the deterministically constrained system as the destination distribution shrinks to the prespecified value. For linear time-varying unconstrained systems, a simplified form of the constrained systems is derived in terms of the conditional expectation of the terminal state, leading to the development of trajectory-generation algorithms. Numerical simulations evaluate the proposed framework under both types of destination constraints.

title: Linear stability of viscous stratified shear flows with arbitrary equations of state
abstract: A mathematical framework is developed to analyse the linear stability of viscous stratified flows with arbitrary equations of state. The model accommodates equations of state of the form $p=Φ(T,ρ)$ or $ρ=φ(T)$, together with a set of governing dimensionless parameters. Density stratification is unrestricted, allowing for the study of non-Boussinesq effects. A low-Mach-number approximation is employed to filter out acoustic phenomena. The framework is applied to two viscous stratified configurations of plane Couette flow: a triple-layer density profile supporting the Taylor--Caulfield instability (TCI), and a differentially heated supercritical fluid exhibiting a distinct instability mechanism. Following validation against reference studies, we present new results showing that non-Boussinesq effects weaken the viscous TCI, whilst viscosity can further destabilise the supercritical fluid instability, in contrast to the stabilising influence of buoyancy.

title: Harnessing collaborative networks for nonparametric quantile learning
abstract: Data are increasingly distributed across networked agents that must learn collaboratively without exchanging raw observations or relying on central coordination. Existing decentralized methods largely focus on finite-dimensional models with smooth and strongly convex objectives, leaving nonparametric distributional learning over networks underexplored. We study decentralized nonparametric quantile regression in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. The standard kernel estimator is poorly suited to this setting: the check loss is nonsmooth, while its representer theorem formulation requires a global, data-dependent basis whose dimension grows with the total sample size. We reformulate the estimator using convolution smoothing and shared random features, yielding a differentiable objective with a common, data-independent parameterization of substantially lower dimension. We develop a gradient-adjusted alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm that replaces costly local minimization with network-corrected gradient updates, together with a communication-enhanced variant that selectively transmits updates. We establish nonasymptotic error bounds for the smoothed full-kernel and random-feature estimators, showing that the latter attains the full-kernel rate with suitable bandwidth and feature dimension. We also show both algorithms converge linearly to the random-feature consensus estimator. Simulations and a real data application demonstrate competitive predictive accuracy with substantial computational and communication savings.

title: Detection of local recombination and mutation hotspots in bacterial genomes using neural posterior estimation
abstract: Motivation: Recombination and mutation rates in bacteria vary along the genome, and regions of elevated rate (hotspots) often reflect selection on specific genes. Detecting them is difficult because the two processes leave overlapping signals in sequence data, clonal relationships act as a confounder, and inference must scale to whole genomes. Existing methods assume a constant mutation rate and/or rely on a small set of summary statistics. Results: We present a simulation-based framework that infers gene-specific recombination and mutation rates under a well-specified model of bacterial recombination. Neural posterior estimation (NPE) is trained on simulations conditioned on a fixed clonal genealogy, using a wide range of summary statistics. Gene length is also used as both a parameter and an observed statistic, so that the model learns about its effect on other statistics and thus becomes applicable across different gene lengths. To identify hotspots, we introduce a circular posterior-propagated Difference-of-Gaussians detector that contrasts local and regional smoothers of the posterior log rates, carrying NPE uncertainty into hotspot probabilities. On simulated data, the method recovers the true rates, with credible intervals that narrow as gene length increases. We also apply the new methodology to three real datasets in Bacillus cereus, Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli to showcase its usefulness in a range of situations. Availability and implementation: The Python implementation is freely available from https://github.com/haochu-liu/bacnpe.

title: RF3DGS: Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting with Self-Priors
abstract: 3D reflection removal is crucial in applications demanding high-fidelity visualization, such as museum exhibitions. In this work, we propose Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting (RF3DGS), a novel method for superior reflection removal. RF3DGS exclusively leverages a widely-adopted photometric prior for reflection removal: that the minimum pixel intensity across multi-view images corresponding to the same 3D point strongly correlates with reflection-free information. However, generalizing this principle to a 3D Gaussian Splatting within a multi-view context is non-trivial. To address this, RF3DGS first optimizes a vanilla 3DGS model using a geometric prior to estimate a coarse, reflection-free depth map for each view. Leveraging these depth maps and photometric prior, a 3D warping process aggregates reflection-free information from auxiliary views to construct a clean transmission pseudo-label for a given reference view. This pseudo-label provides a robust self-supervised signal for optimization. We further introduce an Adaptive Twin Rendering (ATR) loss to synergistically utilize this pseudo-label while preserving high-frequency details from the original, reflection-degraded images. By adeptly fusing these internal 3D self-priors with the ATR loss, RF3DGS demonstrates state-of-the-art reflection removal performance across both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we establish the first 3D reflection removal benchmark, based on the Unity rendering engine, for rigorous quantitative evaluation.
