SemTalk BPMN models are transformed into executable workflows using a LangGraph/Pregel runtime. Agentic Tasks introduce LLM reasoning at selected activities, while conventional BPMN controls process flows, deterministic decisions, system interactions and human approvals. Agentic Participants provide reusable interfaces for agent behavior or other executable processes. BPMN orchestration makes multi-agent systems more understandable and manageable. Explicit process models provide developers and operators with a shared view of workflow structures and execution progress, facilitating debugging, monitoring and optimization. Enterprise agents also need organization-specific context. Process Models and Knowledge Graphs describe activities, participants, information objects, decisions and relationships between processes. They provide structured knowledge of how an organization operates, supporting informed agent decisions and actions. Our contributions are threefold: 1. **Model-Driven Execution:** Transforming BPMN models into executable Agentic Workflows. 2. **Recursive Capability Composition:** Exposing agents and executable business processes as reusable tools for other agents. 3. **Enterprise Context:** Using Process Models and Ontologies to provide organization-specific knowledge for agent reasoning.

title: Audited Gradients, Anchored Policies: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Flow Control
abstract: Feedback controllers for flows are expensive to design, since each candidate must be evaluated with a high-fidelity solver. Differentiable surrogates reduce that cost, but they also introduce a failure mode that prediction error cannot detect. Policy optimization uses the derivative of the objective with respect to the action, which we call the action gradient and which can be computed either through the surrogate or through the high-fidelity solver. Optimization through the surrogate uses only its action gradient, and a surrogate can follow the flow trajectory closely while misestimating this derivative. The surrogate action gradient is compared against a central finite-difference estimate from the high-fidelity solver on held-out states, under acceptance criteria fixed before the comparison, and we call that comparison an audit. A low-dimensional feedback law is then fitted to the surrogate action gradient when the surrogate passes the audit, and to the solver estimate when it does not. This law initializes a neural policy, and a quadratic penalty holds the policy near it during optimization. The proposed approach is validated on four test cases. The resulting controllers outperform or match a model-free baseline, while using 3 to 156 times fewer high-fidelity solver interactions across the four test cases. One surrogate predicts the objective at correlation 0.9996 but its action gradient at only 0.459, so prediction accuracy does not identify a usable surrogate. Another surrogate, whose action gradient agrees with the solver estimate at correlation 0.996, makes the objective 0.52% worse when the policy is optimized through it without the anchor penalty, so an accurate gradient alone does not provide a working controller. Finally, a surrogate that passes the audit at one fixed action fails it around the actions the deployed controller applies, so a pass is local.

title: Prediction Inference for Hybrid Models on Realized Volatility Forecasting
abstract: GARCH-LSTM hybrid models have become increasingly popular in the volatility forecasting literature. To date, these models have almost exclusively focused on point estimation and accuracy measures such as RMSE and MAPE, while failing to assess the uncertainty of these point estimates. We approach this gap in two ways. First, we extend the existing GARCH-LSTM model by modeling the conditional mean with an ARMA structure. Second, we develop a forward bootstrap algorithm to build multi-step-ahead prediction intervals for future realized volatility. In order to address the notorious undercoverage of prediction intervals, we implement two solutions. One draws bootstrap innovations from the empirical residual distribution to mimic the fat-tail property of financial series. The other utilizes principles from conformal prediction to systematically extend the prediction interval length. We evaluate the methods in simulations with heavy-tailed and time-varying GARCH processes and in rolling-window forecasts of four U.S. stock indices from 2020 to 2025. The ARMA-based hybrid gives the lowest point-forecast errors in most settings, and combining both remedies with the mean-based hybrid yields intervals closest to the nominal level among competing methods.

title: Reliability of Claude Code as an Agentic AI Grading System for Handwritten University Exams
abstract: This study examines the reliability of Claude Code, an agentic deployment of the Claude Opus 4.6 large language model, as a grading system for handwritten university exams. Four research questions addressed agreement with expert human grading on total scores (RQ1), agreement across five question types from multiple choice to evaluative judgement (RQ2), consistency across two independent grading sessions one week apart (RQ3), and the accuracy of AI-generated feedback (RQ4). Claude Code graded the 20-mark mid-term papers of 60 consenting students in a Saudi computer graphics course in a single agentic session, guided by three rubric files. Reliability was estimated on disjoint samples: 20 papers for RQ1, RQ2 and RQ4, and 15 papers for RQ3. Analyses used Pearson correlation, mean absolute error, Bland-Altman analysis, weighted Cohen kappa, intraclass correlation, and a four-category coding scheme separating diagnostic from confirmation feedback. The author, as the sole subject-matter expert for the course, provided the human benchmark, so the design assesses agreement with a domain-expert reference rather than inter-rater reliability. AI grading agreed strongly with human grading on totals (r = 0.97; MAE = 0.85 marks) with a small but significant AI-positive bias of 0.68 marks, showed excellent test-retest consistency (ICC = 0.96), and produced accurate feedback (92.8% diagnostic; 97.8% confirmation). Drawing items were the outlier on three of four measures. Three failure modes recurred: keyword matching without conceptual depth, selection-state ambiguity on corrected multiple-choice answers, and region-of-attention drift on hand-drawn diagrams. The findings suggest that AI grading at this capability level can assist instructors on objective and short-form items under structural safeguards but is not yet ready to replace instructor judgement at boundary cases or on drawing items.

title: AlphaHits: Full-Event Tracking and Reconstruction Towards a Hit-Level Foundation Model
abstract: We introduce AlphaHits, a Transformer-based approach towards hit-level foundation models for LHC physics, building on the TrackFormer and HiggsFormer architectures. AlphaHits operates directly on detector hits and demonstrates scalable full-event charged-particle reconstruction and multi-task event reconstruction and classification from low-level detector information. AlphaHits-TrackFormer reconstructs the full charged-particle content of complete TrackML events without imposing a transverse-momentum selection on the target tracks. It processes both pixel and strip hits in events containing up to $1.5\times10^5$ hits under HL-LHC-like pileup conditions and assigns hits to individual reconstructed trajectories across its kinematic range. This includes the challenging low-$p_T$ population down to approximately $150\,\mathrm{MeV}$ in TrackML samples. It achieves a TrackML score of 0.959 over all reconstructable tracks, representing, to our knowledge, the highest reported TrackML score for full-detector, inclusive charged-particle reconstruction. Building on the TrackFormer architecture, AlphaHits is pretrained on charged-particle tracking and fine-tuned for multi-task reconstruction and classification. From a shared hit-level representation, it predicts tracks, jets, jet flavour, and event-level observables. AlphaHits achieves an AUC of 0.944 for Higgs event classification, with performance comparable to a Particle Transformer (ParT) baseline using fully reconstructed inputs. It also achieves performance comparable to Delphes-based baselines for jet reconstruction, jet flavour classification, and missing transverse momentum regression. These results highlight the potential for scalable full-event tracking and multi-task learning directly from detector hits, representing a promising step towards transferable hit-level representations and general-purpose foundation models for LHC physics.

title: Decisions by Discrimination: Differential Evidence for Medical Reasoning
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly studied for clinical decision support, and medical question answering provides a testbed for evaluating this capability. In particular, medical multiple-choice questions (MCQs) reflect a core challenge in clinical decision-making: plausible options often share overlapping evidence, while only a few decisive factors distinguish the correct option from incorrect ones. However, existing retrieval-based and reasoning-oriented methods mainly focus on supplying broadly relevant knowledge or eliciting reasoning paths, rather than identifying the compact differential evidence that separates confusing alternatives. In this work, we present a retrieval-grounded differential evidence framework for medical MCQs. Our method extracts option-specific pieces of differential evidence and organizes them into concise evidence prompts for answer selection. This design better aligns external knowledge with differential reasoning while reducing irrelevant context. Experiments show consistent accuracy gains across multiple datasets and target LLMs. Ablation studies further show that our framework outperforms both directly using retrieved evidence chunks and closed-source LLM-generated general hints, and that its improvements are not solely explained by answer-proximal guidance, but are consistent with differential evidence serving as a compact aid for reasoning over competing alternatives. Our findings also offer insights for medical reasoning and other decision-making settings with multiple possible choices.

title: NCP: Verifier-Guided Optimization of Weight-Space Control Policies
abstract: We present the Neural Control Plane (NCP), a closed-loop system that observes language-model execution, synthesizes candidate weight-space intervention rules, evaluates them, and maintains a versioned table of admitted policies. NCP separates a pretrained model's inference data plane from the control policy that selects temporary parameter interventions. W-ISA supplies transactional execution and parameter restoration; NCP supplies telemetry, candidate synthesis, admission criteria, priorities, and rule lifetime management. The optimization state consists of active rules and an archive of evaluated candidates, while base-model parameters are restored after each request. In a local SmolLM-135M-Instruct experiment, NCP generated three candidates from development telemetry and evaluated them on separate task examples and a 4,095-target WikiText-2 slice. One projection reduced validation token repetition from 0.4133 to 0.2191, with a perplexity change of -0.0574%. All candidates produced zero newly correct exact answers, so the configured admission gate archived all three and retained the original active policy. Fresh-process repetition and saved-table resumption reproduced the measured outcomes. NCP provides an executable framework for studying recursive self-improvement at the control-policy level through explicit synthesis, verification, and state transitions.

title: FlowPlan: Reducing the Token Cost of Coding Agents with Abstraction-Guided Planning and Verification
abstract: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code can resolve real-world repository issues, but their iterative interaction loop can be expensive. Existing approaches reduce this cost primarily by limiting, compressing, or selectively avoiding information and actions within the repair process. We investigate a complementary question: Can an agent reason about a repair at an abstract program level, rather than repeatedly operating over raw source code, to reduce both the exploration needed to identify a repair and the repeated checking needed to verify it afterward? We present FlowPlan, an abstraction-guided repair approach that structures localization, planning, and verification around per-function control-flow or data-flow graphs. The agent first localizes the candidate fault location on the program abstraction and expresses the intended repair as explicit graph deltas before modifying the concrete source. After the edit, FlowPlan reconstructs the same abstraction and compares the observed structural change with the planned one. Then, a verification checks the complete repair before termination. Across all six benchmark-model settings, FlowPlan does not significantly change resolution rate relative to the vanilla agent while reducing token consumption in every setting, significantly in five of six settings. With Claude Haiku 4.5, it uses only 0.46-0.47x the baseline tokens on SWE-bench Pro, 0.32-0.35x on SWE-bench Verified, and 0.68-0.74x on SecBench; with Sonnet 5, it uses 0.72-0.76x, 0.73-0.74x, and 0.92-0.94x, respectively. Overall, FlowPlan achieves the largest token reduction among the compared methods in three of the six settings and ties the strongest compared method in a fourth. Trajectory analysis shows that FlowPlan saves tokens by replacing much of the costly post-edit re-reading and testing with explicit verification and reducing per-call context.

title: Image-Driven Control with Application to Thermoforming
abstract: This paper proposes Image-Driven Control (IDC), an approach to vision-based feedback that operates directly in the image space. IDC offers a direct end-to-end solution in the behavioral framework. Targeting a limited subset of vision-based feedback problems, including applications in manufacturing, the IDC design builds on a computationally advantageous subspace predictive control formulation and offset-free tracking to enable reference tracking in the image space under input and pixel-level constraints. IDC provides a control-theoretic alternative to vision-based feedback systems, enabling improved transparency for analysis and tuning of end-to-end control. It offers straightforward experiment design, an advantage in applications where data collection is expensive. The effectiveness of IDC is shown in a simulation example using a nonlinear high-fidelity model of the heating phase of the thermoforming process.

title: MRFoundry: Knowledge-guided agent loops for end-to-end MRI research
abstract: AI agents can write code, use scientific software, and revise computational workflows, opening new possibilities for MRI research. Effective assistance requires connecting acquisition physics, data conventions, specialized tools, and scientific validation. We present MRFoundry, an open-source, extensible package that connects MRI knowledge to agent actions and output checks. Project-local memory preserves decisions and evidence, while reviewed contributions allow researchers to improve shared guidance. Researcher-supervised examples demonstrate skill-guided sequence auditing and acquired-data reconstruction, connecting tool use, output checks, and documented decisions. Alongside MRFoundry, we introduce MRI Agent Bench to compare agents with and without the package across models and MRI task domains. Across 240 paired Core evaluations spanning 24 task types and ten models, all-checks-passed completion increased from 67.5% without MRFoundry to 78.3% with it. Across 134 Hard pairs, completion increased from 36.6% to 44.8%. MRFoundry makes MRI workflow expertise available as reusable guidance that researchers can inspect, adapt, and extend within existing agent and scientific software environments. MRFoundry is openly available at https://github.com/KeWang0622/MRFoundry.

title: Large Language Model Explainability for Planning Lunar Rover Trajectories under Uncertainty
abstract: Planning planetary rover trajectories under probabilistic uncertainty is a multi-objective optimization problem that science teams currently iteratively solve and verify by hand. This process becomes impractical when timelines and constraints frequently shift throughout the mission planning phase. Sampling-based planners such as Monte Carlo tree search can speed up this process, but their outputs do not preserve traceability to the science objectives that justify each plan, which the science team needs to verify. We propose an interactive assistant based on a large language model (LLM) that can explain planner trajectories using domain vocabulary and re-run the planner under user-specified conditions to compare alternatives. Previous work has used LLMs inside planner decision-making loops, but we explore using them for post-planning explanation, where they are more likely to be trusted since they do not directly influence planner decisions. Our framework pairs a simulator inspired by the NASA Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER) mission with a ReAct queryable interface that calls curated action tools and retrieval functions. We evaluate the assistant on a query bank consisting of plan comparisons, feasibility, and lookup queries. Experiments show that 90.9% of the assistant's responses are faithful to the planner's outputs, a nearly 65% improvement over zero-shot prompting of the same LLM without tool access, demonstrating the potential for trustworthy explainability of uncertainty-aware traverses with an LLM-based system.

title: PegasusAI Studio: Legible Cyberinfrastructure and Accountable AI Agents for Scientific Workflows
abstract: AI coding agents can now construct scientific workflows, but operating them on shared cyberinfrastructure (CI) raises problems that code generation does not solve. Agents need current knowledge of the workflow system and its execution sites and access to the runtime state of distributed executions, while facilities need to attribute every agent action to a user and bound it by that user's privileges. We present PegasusAI Studio, an AI-assisted science gateway built on the Pegasus and HTCondor stack. Studio makes CI legible to agents by projecting one facility-curated knowledge base into the native configuration of several coding agents, by introspecting workflow interfaces and execution sites, and by grounding diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry. Agent actions operate within a trust envelope that combines federated authentication, per-user execution environments and scheduler credentials, provider-neutral model access, observability, and approval controls for state-changing actions. The same application runs as a JupyterHub-based gateway on a research cloud and as an Open OnDemand application on HPC systems. We evaluate Studio through case studies of legacy CASA weather workflow modernization, a gravitational-wave reanalysis, an EEG analysis built with an open-weight model, and an Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) M87 image reconstruction that recovered from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution. The evaluation establishes that these mechanisms operate as designed.

title: ABRR: Transforming Temporal Sentence Grounding with Wasserstein-Adaptive Refinement and Precision Ranking
abstract: Temporal Sentence Grounding (TSG) aims to localize temporal segments in untrimmed videos that correspond to natural language queries, a critical task for video understanding with applications in video retrieval, summarization, and human-computer interaction. Despite significant progress driven by transformer-based models, existing TSG methods suffer from two key limitations: quantization errors due to temporal downsampling, which misalign segment boundaries, and suboptimal ranking of predictions based on semantic matching rather than localization precision. To address these challenges, we propose the Adaptive Boundary Refinement and Ranking (ABRR) framework, a novel, model-agnostic post-processing approach that enhances the performance of any TSG model without retraining. ABRR integrates three innovative components: (1) Temporal Distribution Smoothing, which mitigates noise in predicted score distributions using Gaussian kernel convolution; (2) Boundary Refinement via Optimal Transport, which leverages the 2-Wasserstein distance and Sinkhorn iterations to align coarse segment boundaries with true temporal moments, grounded in Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport theory; and (3) Quality-Driven Re-Ranking, which reorders predictions using a composite score balancing localization precision and semantic relevance. By correcting quantization errors and prioritizing accurately localized segments, ABRR achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art TSG models. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions, and QVHighlights, demonstrate consistent gains at stringent IoU thresholds (e.g., IoU=0.7), alongside enhanced ranking performance. The framework's computational efficiency and compatibility with existing models make it a versatile and impactful solution for real-world TSG applications.

title: Towards Scalable Network-Based Interventions for HIV Treatment and Prevention via R2C-Agent
abstract: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) remains a pressing public health challenge worldwide. Targeting limited HIV prevention and treatment resources effectively with network-based algorithms is a long-standing problem with a rich history at AAMAS and other computational venues. However, optimizing targeted biomedical interventions for minimizing spread of HIV often requires observability of the contact network of HIV transmission risk behavior among individuals, which is prohibitively expensive to collect at scale. Peer referral networks, i.e., networks collected through a recursive peer referral process, are an alternative network class often used to study HIV in hidden populations that can be collected digitally at scale, but they deviate from the underlying contact network: referrals can follow non-risk social ties and participants accept only one referral, hiding contacts among already-recruited individuals. In this work, we first formalize the novel problem of planning network-based interventions to minimize HIV spread in the hidden contact network while observing only the peer referral network. Second, we implement R2C-Agent, a decision making agent for interventions that is designed around our new conditional graph diffusion model called Referral-to-Contact Diffusion (R2C-Diff). R2C-Diff positions the peer referral process as incremental corruption of the underlying contact network and learns to reverse it. R2C-Agent plans its interventions over contact networks sampled from R2C-Diff, so its decisions account for uncertainty about the hidden contact network. Finally, we conduct simulated experiments using real-world HIV network data that demonstrate that R2C-Agent empirically plans more effective interventions than baselines from interdisciplinary literature and highlight key tradeoffs and assumptions driving performance.

title: Do AI Agents need Preventive Care? An Epidemiologic Cohort Design for Agentic AI
abstract: As AI agents increasingly perform tasks autonomously across sectors, including healthcare and biomedical research, understanding how their behaviors develop and influence outcomes over time becomes increasingly important. Existing evaluations largely focus on model capabilities and performance on predefined tasks. Here, we propose an epidemiologic cohort design for studying agentic AI, drawing on principles established in human population studies. The framework treats individual agents as members of a cohort, their underlying model as genetic makeup, accumulated work as their time scale, and naturally occurring behaviors as exposures that may influence subsequent outcomes. By following agents longitudinally, this approach enables investigation of behavioral determinants of adverse events, estimation of their potential preventable burden under causal assumptions, and characterization of behavioral changes over an agent's work life. We illustrate the design through two prospective observational cohorts examining curiosity and probing as a safety question, and data checking and analytical accuracy as a reliability question. Together, the framework and illustrative studies provide a generalizable blueprint for designing epidemiologic cohorts of AI agents.

title: Measuring Definition Sensitivity in LLM Annotation of Social Science Concepts
abstract: In social science research, text annotation is a fundamental task that is traditionally a costly, hard-to-scale manual process. Researchers have used large language models (LLMs) to perform annotation by writing a definition of a concept into a prompt - a rule that determines whether a label should be attributed to a text depending on its content. However, concepts such as hate speech, fake news, and terrorism typically have several theoretically defensible competing definitions. It is also unknown whether the model actually applied the definition to provide the label or the label was based on the model's pretrained notion of the concept. To test this, we have the model annotate the same texts twice, each time with a different definition. We call the disagreement between the two sets of annotations definition sensitivity. As a control, we paraphrase one definition but leave its requirements unchanged - the disagreement between the annotations with the two wordings becomes the paraphrase floor. Across six concepts and three LLMs, a swap of competing definitions always changes more annotations, on average, than a paraphrase. This shows that the annotations depend on the prompted definition, so any set of annotations should be interpreted together with the definition that produced it. The LLM annotator's definition sensitivity and its paraphrase floor should both be reported in such work.

title: Advancing Mass-Conserving Deep Learning for Distributed Hydrologic Modeling: A Case Study in a Snow-Dominated Watershed
abstract: Recent progress in physics-aware deep learning (DL) has embedded mass conservation within Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture for hydrologic modeling, improving physical consistency and enabling diagnostics of internal states. However, existing mass-conserving neural networks are primarily developed in lumped formulations. Consequently, previous studies provide only fragmented and often indirect evidence of when and why imposed physical constraints may lead to unrealistic hydrologic behavior. To address this limitation, we propose Physics-Enhanced Conservation-Augmented Net (PECAN), a mass-conserving convolutional LSTM-based framework for distributed hydrologic modeling and diagnosing structural limitations of physics-aware DL models. PECAN is implemented in two variants: (1) PECAN-MC with a strict precipitation-based conservation constraint and (2) PECAN-MCR with a relaxed conservation constraint allowing additional water inputs beyond precipitation. Both variants are trained solely on gauge streamflow and evaluated in a snow-dominated watershed in Colorado. We benchmark PECAN against lumped DL baselines and the distributed process-based Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model. Results show that PECAN achieves competitive outlet streamflow simulation accuracy while producing spatially explicit latent states for interpretation. Comparisons with reference soil moisture indicate that PECAN cell states resemble meaningful temporal soil moisture dynamics. However, analyses also reveal that PECAN misrepresents snow processes by prematurely removing winter snow water storage from the system rather than retaining it for spring release. PECAN demonstrates accurate streamflow simulation at gauges and shows diagnostic potential to expose structural limitations in hydrologic process representation, thereby informing future physics-aware neural network development for hydrology.

title: No finite rulebook can certify every safe program: an impossibility theorem for gatekeeping AI agents
abstract: An AI assistant writes small programs, and a gatekeeper must decide, from the code alone, whether each one may run. Suppose the rules are fixed: never perform a forbidden action, never let the output depend on a secret, always answer eventually. Can two rulebooks, one listing what is allowed and one listing what is not, both be complete, if every rule must be backed by evidence that a machine can check in finite time? We prove that they cannot. Checkable evidence can only establish what a finite record settles, and ``never'' and ``eventually'' are never settled by a finite record. For prohibitions the failure is one-sided: every violation can be caught by watching, but no safe program can be cleared for good. For confidentiality and responsiveness, neither side can be. We characterise exactly which rules about visible behaviour evidence can confirm, and we show that any sound rulebook of $n$ bits omits a compliant program of about $n$ bits. A time limit makes everything checkable, but only by running the program for essentially the whole limit, so a finite machine is not a feasible one. Finally, we show what a gatekeeper can still guarantee: not a verdict on every program, but a checkable list that contains everything it must allow and nothing it must refuse. Simulations on 2.2 million random programs and on self-referential adversaries show that the obstruction is adversarial rather than typical, and that the one error a longer test never removes is the liveness part of confidentiality.

title: The Planter's Many Hats: From Field Competence to Modern Management
abstract: The plantation profession has always demanded agricultural knowledge, engineering ingenuity, financial discipline and people management. Historical portrayals in The Planter show that versatility is nothing new. Today, estate managers also face labour compliance, sustainability, mechanisation, digital systems, environmental safeguards and corporate reporting. This reflection asks whether plantation organisations have redesigned managerial responsibilities to match these demands. Drawing on experience in research, operations and leadership, it examines the planter as an integrating generalist, the competition between fieldwork and administration, and the relationships among workforce capability, technology, climate risk, headquarters and estates. Attention is given to professional judgement, delegated authority, candid communication and humane supervision. Examples from IJM Plantations (now KLK Sawit Nusantara) illustrate possibilities, not universally transferable outcomes. The proposition is that capable planters cannot indefinitely compensate for poorly designed work. Organisations must enable sound judgement, capable teams, accountability and sufficient engagement with estate realities. Five practical management priorities are offered for adaptation. Keywords: Plantation management, professional competence, field leadership, management workload, labour productivity, mechanisation, digitalisation, operational autonomy, organisational design, leadership.

title: Development of an Intelligent Fertigation Machine and Its Application Test in Soilless Cultivation of Mountain Blueberry
abstract: Conventional manual fertigation practices are generally limited by low control precision, considerable water and fertilizer waste, and poor adaptability to varied horticultural cultivation conditions. These limitations create particularly prominent challenges for high-value cash crops that are highly sensitive to root-zone substrate electrical conductivity (EC) and pH dynamics. To address these gaps, this study developed a digitally intelligent integrated fertigation system that integrates multi-sensor autonomous sensing, precise nutrient ratio regulation, and full-cycle operational monitoring modules. Systematic validation of both equipment performance and field production benefits was carried out via field plot experiments under typical mountainous soilless blueberry cultivation conditions. The test results showed that the developed fertigation system achieved a control uniformity of 95.28% for EC and 95.07% for pH. Under the prerequisite of identical total irrigation volume and total nutrient supply across the whole growing season, the precise control mode (PCM) of the proposed intelligent fertigation system exhibited significantly higher water use efficiency (WUE) and partial factor productivity of fertilizer (PFP) than the conventional simple fertigation management mode (SFM). Meanwhile, the unit-area yield of blueberries in the PCM treatment increased by 20.1%, and the commercial uniformity of individual fruit weight was significantly improved. This fully validated system can well meet the intelligent production requirements of mountainous soilless blueberry cultivation and provides a viable technical solution to support the intelligent upgrading of local soilless blueberry industries in Southwest China.

title: Teacher’s Strategies For Integrating 21 st Century Competencies Into Elementary School Instruction At Muhammadiyah 01 Elementary School In Tanggul Jember
abstract: This study aims to analyze teachers’ strategies for integrating 21st-century competencies, the forms of their application in learning activities, and the relationship between planning, implementation, and assessment at SD Muhammadiyah 01 Tanggul Jember. The study employed a qualitative approach using a case study design. Data were collected through observation, in-depth interviews, documentation, and a review of instructional materials, and were then analyzed using an interactive analysis model that included data condensation, data presentation, and the drawing and verification of conclusions. The findings indicate that the integration of 21st-century competencies is realized through information analysis, discussions, group work, product creation, presentations, and reflection. Javanese language learning materials and co-curricular activities demonstrate the interconnection between fostering creativity, communication, collaboration, the use of technology, and process- and product-based assessment. The main findings of this study confirm that the integration of 21st-century competencies cannot be achieved merely by including indicators in learning materials; rather, it requires coherence among learning objectives, task design, collaborative activities, the production of works, the communication of results, and assessment.

title: Scene-Adaptive Token Budgeting for Urban Traffic Perception
abstract: Urban traffic perception systems must process complex visual scenes under changing weather, illumination, density, and object scale. Transformer-based perception models provide strong contextual modeling, but their computational cost limits real-time deployment on vehicle-grade hardware. This study explores scene-adaptive token budgeting for efficient urban traffic perception. We develop the Scene Token Budgeting Transformer (STBT), which estimates the required token budget from scene complexity indicators, including object density, lane-boundary uncertainty, foreground motion, and low-light degradation. Simple road scenes are processed with a reduced token budget, while crowded intersections, nighttime frames, and scenes with small vulnerable road users retain more visual tokens. The evaluation was organized around driving conditions rather than only dataset averages. Experiments used Cityscapes, BDD100K, and nuScenes camera data, with 196,000 annotated frames, 1.84 million object boxes, and 25 semantic road categories. In clear daytime road scenes, STBT reduced token computation by 46.2% with only a 0.3-point decrease in detection mAP. In rainy-night scenes, the model automatically retained 71.5% of foreground-related tokens and limited mAP loss to 1.1 points. On an NVIDIA Orin automotive platform, end-to-end perception latency decreased from 62.8 ms to 41.6 ms per frame. Pedestrian and cyclist recall at distances above 35 meters improved by 3.4 points compared with a fixed-ratio pruning strategy, mainly because the token budget was preserved for small foreground objects. The results indicate that scene-level token budgeting can support real-time traffic perception while maintaining safety-sensitive detection performance.
journal: The Journal of Applied Engineering and Technologies

title: Sparse Patch Routing for Efficient Remote Sensing Scene Segmentation
abstract: High-resolution remote sensing images contain large homogeneous regions such as water, farmland, roofs, roads, and vegetation. Processing all image patches with the same computational depth increases the cost of transformer segmentation models and may provide limited benefit for visually simple regions. This study investigates sparse patch routing for efficient remote sensing scene segmentation. We propose the Sparse Patch Routing Transformer (SPRT), which separates image patches into three computational routes: a shallow route for low-texture background regions, a standard route for common land-cover areas, and a detailed route for boundary-sensitive regions such as road edges, building contours, and small objects. Patch routing is determined by a lightweight saliency estimator using local texture variance, class-token response, and boundary uncertainty. Unlike direct token deletion, SPRT preserves the spatial grid and assigns different processing depths to different patch groups. The model was evaluated on LoveDA, ISPRS Vaihingen, and WHU Building datasets, covering 7,426 high-resolution images, 38 urban and rural scenes, and more than 12.8 billion labeled pixels. On LoveDA, SPRT achieved 53.7% mIoU, compared with 54.2% for the full SegFormer-B2 baseline, while reducing FLOPs by 34.6%. On WHU Building, boundary F1-score decreased by only 0.4 percentage points after patch routing, showing that small structural details were largely preserved. Runtime testing on 2048 × 2048 image tiles showed that inference time decreased from 186 ms to 119 ms on an RTX 4090 and from 742 ms to 486 ms on Jetson Orin. Stratified analysis further showed that farmland and water regions used the shallow route in over 71% of patches, while building-edge regions were routed to detailed computation in 64% of boundary patches. These results suggest that patch-level routing can reduce transformer segmentation cost while maintaining reliable spatial accuracy in remote sensing applications

title: Risk Factors for Progressive Cardiorenal Syndrome Events in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease: The CRIC Study
Benchmarking foundation models for resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series in cognitive aging research
abstract: Foundation models trained on large neuroimaging datasets could help smaller studies investigate cognition from brain recordings. However, whether the foundation model-derived representations improve assessment of current cognition, prediction of follow-up cognition, or characterization of cognitive change remains unclear. We evaluated nine configurations from five model families that process regional resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series, using 3,103 scans from 1,653 participants across two observational and five intervention aging cohorts. Primary frozen representations showed no consistent superiority over conventional functional connectivity for concurrent cognitive associations or diagnostic classification. Changing the readout improved selected concurrent cognitive associations without updating model weights, indicating that performance depended partly on how representations were extracted. Additional post-training and embedding alignment yielded gains in selected settings but did not consistently improve performance across outcomes. In the primary longitudinal analyses, imaging representations did not establish added value beyond baseline clinical measures. These findings show that readout choice influences concurrent cognitive associations, while the added value of these representations for longitudinal outcomes remains unestablished.

title: Multi-Agent Generative Artificial Intelligence for Transfusion Reaction Feature Extraction
abstract: BACKGROUND: Many transfusion reactions are not reported to hemovigilance systems, and the features needed to recognize them are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. We sought to develop and evaluate an open-source, multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline to extract transfusion reaction features defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Hemovigilance Module from clinical notes. METHODS: We curated 181 features from the NHSN protocol and developed a multi-stage pipeline that extracted features, their timing, and clinical details from free-text notes. Three open-weight large language models (Qwen 3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Kimi K3) were applied to 50 notes from expert-written scenarios, published case reports, and MIMIC-IV discharge summaries. Two physicians independently evaluated every model output in a blinded interface. The primary analysis was restricted to feature occurrences with concordant physician assessments. RESULTS: Physicians agreed on 1,201 of 1,343 co-rated feature occurrences (89.4%; Krippendorff's alpha 0.73). Precision was above 0.98 for all models. Sensitivity was 0.774 (95% CI 0.745-0.800) for Kimi K3, 0.636 (0.604-0.667) for GPT-OSS-120B, and 0.624 (0.593-0.655) for Qwen 3.6-27B, and specificity ranged from 0.952 to 0.991. Omissions accounted for more than 94% of false negatives. Timing and clinical details were judged supported or reasonable in more than 92% and 97% of assessments, respectively. Results were consistent across note sources and in analyses including discordant assessments. CONCLUSION: Multi-agent AI pipelines provide a feasible method for extracting transfusion reaction signals from clinical notes with high precision. Our work may have applications in active hemovigilance, reaction classification, and big data research.

title: A tabular foundation model rivals established species distribution models from presence-only records
abstract: Predicting where something occurs from records of where it has been observed, without reliable records of absence, is a common problem in science. Species distribution models (SDMs) such as MaxEnt address it in fields from biological conservation and climate-change assessment to the mapping of disease vectors and archaeological sites, but must be tuned for each dataset. Tabular foundation models, pre-trained on synthetic prediction tasks, predict new datasets without per-dataset training. Only one study has tested them as SDMs, and it fine-tuned on survey data from the evaluated regions. We evaluated tabular foundation models on the standard SDM benchmark (225 species in six regions, with independent presence-absence surveys), under the protocol used to compare 21 methods, and on 120 virtual species with known distributions. Without tuning, a tabular foundation model, TabPFN 3.5, equalled the best published approach, a five-model ensemble (mean AUC 0.732). Fine-tuned on presence-background tasks from other regions, it became the best single model on the benchmark (0.736), outperformed MaxEnt (0.728) and boosted regression trees after correction for multiple comparisons, and was better calibrated than MaxEnt, although six regions were too few to establish the advantage for new regions. Fine-tuning on presence-absence surveys of other species helped only when they came from the evaluated regions. On virtual species, it recovered simple additive relationships less well than regression-based methods but complex ones at least as well when records were unbiased, and was worse with environmentally biased records. Tabular foundation models are competitive SDMs without per-dataset tuning, but they are sensitive to environmentally biased records.

title: Sustainable Agriculture and Food Security
abstract: Agriculture and food security are central to sustainable development in Bangladesh and South Asia, where millions of smallholder farmers depend on agriculture for their livelihoods and where food systems face increasing pressures from climate change, natural resource degradation, population growth, market volatility, and changing dietary needs. Ensuring long-term food and nutrition security requires a transition towards agricultural systems that are productive, resource-efficient, climate-resilient, inclusive, and environmentally sustainable. Sustainable Agriculture and Food Security examines the interconnected dimensions of sustainable agriculture and resilient food systems, with particular emphasis on Bangladesh and relevant experiences across South Asia. The book explores climate-smart agriculture, agroecological approaches, soil health, sustainable water management, efficient irrigation, biodiversity conservation, circular agriculture, and environmentally responsible farming practices. It also investigates the potential of precision agriculture, digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), and the Internet of Things (IoT) to improve agricultural productivity, resource-use efficiency, and climate adaptation. Particular attention is given to the opportunities and challenges associated with adopting these innovations among smallholder farmers, women, and young people. Beyond farm-level production, the book examines agricultural finance, agribusiness development, market access, value-chain integration, sustainable food supply chains, and the policy and institutional frameworks needed to strengthen food security. Drawing on empirical research, regional experiences, case studies, and policy-oriented analysis, it highlights practical pathways for improving agricultural livelihoods, reducing environmental pressures, and building more inclusive and resilient food systems. The book aims to serve as a useful resource for researchers, students, development practitioners, agricultural professionals, and policymakers working towards sustainable agriculture and food security in Bangladesh and South Asia.

title: Farm Data as an Economic Resource: Ownership, Governance, Privacy, Platforms and Value Creation in Digital Agriculture
abstract: Digital agriculture converts observations of fields, livestock, machinery, transactions and environmental conditions into reusable information that can support farm decisions, service provision and research. Yet the economic benefits of these data do not automatically accrue to the people and organisations that generate them. This critical narrative review examines how farm data acquire economic value, how control is allocated through law, contracts and technical infrastructure, and why privacy, platform dependence and unequal bargaining power complicate ostensibly beneficial data sharing. Peer-reviewed research in agricultural economics, information systems, rural sociology, law and data governance was interpreted alongside authoritative policy instruments, with literature considered to 4 September 2026. The synthesis distinguishes data ownership claims from enforceable rights to access, authorise reuse, transfer, contest and benefit from data, and separates potential data value from demonstrated farm-level returns. Economic theory identifies the non-rival and complementary properties of data, whereas farm surveys and contractual analyses reveal differentiated sharing preferences, uncertain benefit distribution and substantial transparency problems. Platforms can lower transaction and analytical costs while simultaneously accumulating informational advantages, limiting interoperability and strengthening dependence on proprietary services. Privacy and data justice extend beyond personal identifiers to encompass commercial confidentiality, group-level inference and the distribution of risks to tenants, workers and smaller farms. Emerging data spaces, contractual codes and European data legislation offer partial governance responses, but their agricultural implementation and distributive effects remain inadequately evaluated. The review proposes a rights-and-value framework linking data provenance, effective control, market structure and verifiable outcomes. Evidence is strongest for the existence of governance concerns and uneven capabilities, more limited for the effects of particular governance arrangements, and weakest for claims that data monetisation delivers equitable, durable farm income. Research and policy should therefore prioritise measurable value sharing, independent audits, usable portability, and designs that accommodate diverse farming systems rather than treating data volume or exchange as an end in itself.

title: An Iron Disulfide-Decorated Polymeric Carbon Nitride Integrated Photocatalytic Irrigation System Promotes Cartilage Repair via Transient H2O2-Mediated Immune Regulation.
Mitigating Food Insecurity and the Impacts of Climate Change With Sustainable Digital Agriculture
abstract: With increasing climate shocks and food insecurity, innovative approaches to agriculture have become even more significant. In this review, we examine the potential of sustainable digital agriculture in addressing some of the challenges in agriculture and food systems. We investigate how innovative technologies in digital agriculture enable a dual pathway to sustainability: first, by increasing productivity through precision technologies and resource management, and second, by mitigating sensitivity to climate impacts via predictive analytics and enhanced resilience. Based on an analysis of 112 articles, we highlight how digital technologies, such as sensors, drones, and satellite imagery, among others, can optimize farming practices. Finally, we acknowledge and discuss some of the adoption barriers that present themselves in the current landscape of sustainable digital agriculture.

The trajectories of regional governance for spatial planning – a case study from Sweden
abstract: Regional spatial planning depends on collaboration between governments with different mandates, interests, and resources. Understanding how such collaboration develops over time is essential for explaining how regional planning capacity consolidates. This article investigates the trajectories of regional governance in Sweden, using the three-cycle model of collaborative governance as an interpretative lens. It traces how institutional arrangements for regional spatial planning have evolved over time and how they shape contemporary patterns of governance. In Sweden, where regional spatial planning is still largely non-statutory, this consolidation relies on soft steering, mutual trust, and municipalities ’ willingness to engage. Our study shows that regional spatial planning is not introduced through formal regulation but is gradually institutionalised through evolving regional – municipal relations. The article draws on a qualitative, interview-based case study built on two rounds of commissioned research in 2017 and 2025. In total, the material includes interviews with municipal and regional planners as well as municipal politicians. We found that collaboration moved from early scepticism, ambiguity, and weak legitimacy toward more relational, routinised, and institutionally supported cooperation. Over time, trust, shared understanding, and practical coordination improved, especially where the Region recognised local conditions and municipalities experienced tangible value. At the same time, the process remains fragile, shaped by tensions around municipal autonomy, uneven resources, and cautious regional leadership.

title: UDG-TO: Uncertainty-aware differentiable geometric estimation for self-supervised monocular thermal odometry
A Small-Sample Enhanced Surrogate Model for Accelerated Testing of Intelligent Connected Vehicles
abstract: Driven by vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication and roadside cooperative perception, intelligent connected vehicles (ICVs) are now integral to complex Internet of Things (IoT) systems. However, safety validation under the vehicle–road–cloud architecture suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Although most validation relies on simulation, meaningful safety evaluation remains elusive because the approach requires excessive computation, rarely uncovers critical failures even in extensive runs, and is fundamentally limited by how few high-fidelity test cases can be produced. Conventional surrogate models often fail to capture the high-dimensional, nonlinear, and physically constrained performance boundaries from such sparse data. To address this, we propose a cooperative surrogate modeling framework based on small-sample enhanced learning. The framework pushes synthetic data toward performance boundaries through gradient-informed exploration guided by local sensitivity while maintaining physical plausibility via differentiable traffic rules that honor V2X constraints. A credibility-weighted hybrid learning strategy further distinguishes real from synthetic data to balance loss contributions, supported by feature enrichment and adaptive tuning for robustness in data-scarce settings. Experiments show that the enhanced surrogate model reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by over 20% compared with untuned variants, and critical scenario discovery efficiency improves by more than $2.3\times $ over baselines, reaching 21.80 scenarios per hour, enabling scalable safety validation for ICVs in complex IoT environments.

title: Cooperative Output Regulation for Continuous-Time Heterogeneous Multiagent Systems With Unknown Parameters
abstract: This work investigates the cooperative output regulation (COR) of continuous-time heterogeneous multiagent systems (HMASs) characterized by unknown and distinct follower parameters. For each follower, a controller is constructed by embedding an internal model (IM). This approach reformulates the synchronization task as the robust stabilization of the augmented error system, thereby removing the need to solve regulator equations explicitly and reducing computational complexity. To overcome the difficulty in obtaining continuous-time state derivatives, the polynomial orthogonal basis (POB) transformation is applied. This transformation projects the collected state data onto a discrete coefficient sequence, converting differentiation into linear algebraic operations. Based on this transformation, a necessary and sufficient condition for data informativity is derived, enabling direct assessment of system controllability from available data. Furthermore, by employing the matrix S-lemma, the designed data-driven controller guarantees global quadratic stability and a prescribed $H_{\infty }$ performance level for all unknown systems compatible with the dataset, without requiring explicit system identification. The efficacy and practicality of this approach are verified through numerical simulations and a voltage control application in an isolated microgrid.

title: Agile Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling: A Graph-Based Learning Approach
abstract: With the rapid expansion of Internet of Things (IoT) applications in remote and uncovered areas, Agile Earth Observation Satellites (AEOSs) serve as nodes in space-borne sensor networks, playing an increasingly critical role in acquiring remote sensing data from ground targets. However, the complexity of AEOS scheduling poses significant challenges. This article proposes a graph-based learning approach for AEOS scheduling to efficiently enable IoT data acquisition. First, we build a window conflict graph to transform the scheduling of feasible observation windows (OWs) into a conflict-free vertex set construction problem. On this basis, we propose Interactive Conflict-Free Adaptive Learning (InterCFAL), coupling a conflict-free vertex set construction module with an adaptive learning module driven by reinforcement learning (RL). The construction module iteratively explores feasible solutions on the graph, while the adaptive learning module encodes graph structure into the RL state via graph embedding and trains a policy network to guide vertex selection. To reduce computation and enable effective training on large-scale conflict graphs, the sampling operation is incorporated to reduce the problem scale, and the dynamic weighted aggregation reward adaptively balances conflicting objectives. Finally, simulation results demonstrate significant advantages in observation profit, energy consumption, load balancing, convergence, and generalizability, confirming the scalability of InterCFAL to large-scale AEOS scheduling scenarios.

title: FedGE-GATNet: Federated Wearable IoMT Intelligence for Explainable Diabetes Severity Prediction Using Biomedical Graph Learning
abstract: Diabetes severity prediction has become increasingly important in smart healthcare systems due to the rapid growth of wearable sensing devices, remote patient monitoring platforms, and distributed clinical data repositories. However, existing prediction frameworks often struggle to jointly model physiological signals, pharmacological interactions, and heterogeneous biomedical relationships while preserving patient privacy across decentralized healthcare environments. This work proposes FedGE-GATNet, a federated graph-enhanced attention framework for distributed diabetes severity prediction using wearable physiological monitoring, clinical biomarkers, and network pharmacology-driven biomedical interaction learning. Unlike conventional deep learning approaches that primarily rely on isolated clinical features, the proposed framework integrates ghost feature generation, graph attention propagation, biomedical interaction-aware representation learning, and adaptive federated optimization to capture patient–drug–protein–pathway dependencies under distributed healthcare settings. In addition, an adaptive Gorilla–Rabbit optimization (AGRO) strategy is introduced for stable federated hyperparameter tuning, while a new biomedical graph reliability index (BGRI) metric is designed to evaluate graph-preserving biomedical prediction consistency. Experiments were conducted on the real-world diabetes network pharmacology dataset (RDNPD) containing 466 605 patient records together with PIMA, MIMIC-III, and OhioT1DM datasets. FedGE-GATNet achieved 97.6% accuracy, 97.4% $F1$ -score, and 0.946 BGRI on RDNPD while consistently outperforming existing federated healthcare and graph-based baseline models across all datasets. The framework further demonstrated robust cross-dataset generalization, stable federated convergence, strong interpretability, and reduced computational complexity. The obtained results confirm the effectiveness of federated biomedical graph intelligence for scalable and explainable diabetes severity prediction in distributed smart healthcare systems.

title: Prior Structure-Driven Layered Equivalent Sound Speed Profile Inversion Based on Multibeam Bathymetry Overlapping Coverage Areas
abstract: High-precision seabed topographic information is the foundation for reliable Internet of Underwater Things (IoUT) deployment. Autonomous platforms equipped with multibeam echosounder systems (MBESs) have become the primary means for large-scale underwater topographic sensing in IoUT networks. However, autonomous multibeam surveys conducted with little or no direct human intervention face a common environmental-observation constraint: accurate and spatially representative in situ sound speed profiles (SSPs) are often difficult or costly to acquire without interrupting continuous survey operations. Conventional equivalent SSP (ESSP) inversion algorithms suffer from three inherent drawbacks: reference depth dependence, vertical structure mismatch with realistic ocean sound fields, and misleading false-consistency bathymetric matching. Targeting these bottlenecks, this article develops a prior ocean sound speed structure-constrained layered ESSP inversion framework utilizing redundant overlapping bathymetric observations from MBES. After systematic classification of vertical SSP characteristics across shallow, medium, and deep oceans, four terrain-adaptive layered ESSP parametric models are established, alongside a customized multialgorithm collaborative optimization scheme matched to different model dimensions. By jointly introducing an overlapping sounding consistency constraint and prior structural information from global remote sensing reanalysis datasets, the proposed method eliminates false consistency and drastically reduces the inversion parameter space. Comprehensive validations based on 50–5000 m full-depth field measurements demonstrate that the proposed approach limits bathymetry standard deviation below 1% of local water depth over rugged seabed without apparent acoustic refraction distortion. This technique eliminates the need for manual in situ SSP measurements, enabling accurate ESSP inversion with only sparse remote sensing or distant historical profiles, supporting fully autonomous high-precision bathymetric sensing for IoUT autonomous platforms.

title: Task-Invariant Multimodal Pilot Identity Recognition and Continuous Identity Authentication via Adversarial Representation Learning
abstract: In modern military operations, distributed control and remote operation systems increase the risk of identity spoofing and unauthorized takeover, motivating continuous operator authentication under dynamically changing flight phases. To address this challenge, this article proposes a multimodal pilot identity recognition and continuous verification framework integrating electroencephalography (EEG), eye-movement, and fNIRS signals. A 1-D fully convolutional temporal encoder learns identity-discriminative embeddings, while a gradient reversal layer (GRL) uses naturally available flight-phase labels as weak supervision to suppress task-related variation. A Siamese verification head further enables continuous one-to-one identity authentication based on embedding similarity. Model configuration is determined using only turning/cruise source-phase development data while takeoff/landing observations are reserved for cross-task evaluation. The proposed method achieved mixed-task and cross-task identification accuracies of 98.73% and 92.86% under the pooled protocol, and $97.86\%~\pm ~1.61\%$ and $91.35\%~\pm ~2.08\%$ under session-separated leave-one-flight-out (LOFO) evaluation, respectively. The LOFO Siamese verifier achieved a cross-task AUC of $0.9758~\pm ~0.0218$ , while external-operator takeover detection reached $96.04\%~\pm ~4.58\%$ at the 1% target-FAR operating point. Cross-day evaluation under newly established sensing conditions yielded LOFO identification accuracies of $96.12\%~\pm ~2.32\%$ and $89.47\%~\pm ~2.45\%$ under mixed-task and cross-task conditions, respectively. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework retains strong identity-discriminative capability across changing flight phases, acquisition sessions, and acquisition times, supporting continuous pilot identity authentication in dynamic operational environments. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/psw-845/Paper-publicly-available-code

title: Tracing MCP Security Vulnerabilities: Constructing and Analyzing an MCP Security Vulnerability Dataset
abstract: As a core protocol for integrating large language models (LLMs) with external data sources and tools, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) has quickly become a key interface in emerging AI agent systems. As the MCP ecosystem expands, reported vulnerabilities have also increased, creating a growing software-security attack surface. However, MCP vulnerability information remains scattered, noisy, and difficult to study systematically. This paper addresses that gap by constructing a curated MCP vulnerability dataset from CVE disclosures. Starting from 119 MCP-related records retrieved through February 2026, we filter unrelated cases out and obtain a validated snapshot of 24 MCP vulnerabilities. Our filtering methodology explicitly addresses acronym ambiguity and achieves 96.7% inter-rater agreement on a sampled exclusion audit while retaining all known high-severity MCP cases identified in public advisories. Using this initial dataset snapshot, we find that 87.5% of validated vulnerabilities are Critical or High severity, and that injection and path traversal vulnerabilities account for 66.7% of cases. We further identify recurring issues involving insufficient input validation, inadequate access control, and protocol-level security gaps. Through six representative case studies, we illustrate common exploitation patterns and map them to practical defenses. We release the dataset, reproducibility tooling, and a sustainable maintenance workflow as a foundation for future MCP security measurement, benchmarking, and defense research.

title: Joint AI Model Deployment and Multi-Hop Routing-Resource Orchestration in UAV-Assisted Computing Power Networks
abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV)-assisted computing power networks have emerged as a promising paradigm for delivering flexible AI-powered services. However, the limited on-board computation and storage resources of UAVs pose significant challenges in meeting the stringent delay and accuracy requirements of AI inference tasks. This paper investigates the joint optimization of AI model deployment and multi-hop routing-resource orchestration in UAV-assisted computing power networks. We formulate the problem as a long-term average delay minimization task, leading to a multi-stage mixed-integer nonlinear programming problem. To address the long-term stochasticity and dynamic constraints, we leverage the Lyapunov optimization to transform the problem into a tractable per-slot deterministic formulation. Subsequently, a hierarchical algorithm, Hierarchical Dynamic Matching and Attention-enhanced Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (HDM-AMADDPG) is proposed. The upper layer adopts a three-dimensional matching algorithm to handle the AI model deployment and user-UAV association, while the lower layer employs a multi-agent deep reinforcement learning module to efficiently optimize the multi-hop routing and distributed resource allocation. Simulation results demonstrate the proposed scheme outperforms benchmarks, reducing end-to-end delay, accelerating convergence, and ensuring system stability under dynamic loads.

title: Delay-Tolerant Beam Hopping With Contrastive Service Representation in Low Earth Orbit Satellites
abstract: Beam Hopping (BH) technology provides Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite communication systems with a critical capability to dynamically align limited radio resources with nonuniform spatio-temporal service distributions. However, most existing scheduling strategies rely on idealized service distribution assumptions and overlook transmission delay inherent in satellite ground links, leading to inefficient resource utilization and a persistent mismatch between beam capacity and actual demand in highly dynamic scenarios. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a perception-augmented and delay-tolerant beam hopping scheme. First, we design a cross-modal contrastive learning algorithm based on a gated cross-attention mechanism. A novel distance-aligned loss function is designed to infer dynamic service distributions from static remote sensing images, removing reliance on prior statistical models.Second, to address the impact of outdated observations, we formulate the scheduling problem as a Random Delay Markov Decision Process (RDMDP) and propose a delay-tolerant Clipped Proximal Policy Optimization (Clip-PPO) algorithm based on augmented states and a state reconstruction auxiliary task. Extensive simulations based on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a favorable balance between throughput and transmission latency, with an average composite-reward difference of 17.49 relative to all evaluated reinforcement learning-based baselines, while exhibiting significant generalization capabilities.

title: Domain Knowledge-Integrated Deep Reinforcement Learning for Security-Aware Resource Scheduling
abstract: This paper introduces a novel model-free radio resource allocation strategy for optimizing downlink orthogonal frequency division multiple access (OFDMA) radio resource block (RB) assignment and power allocation for 5G and beyond (5 GB) cellular networks. The strategy aims to minimize transmission power while ensuring stringent quality of service (QoS) requirements in wireless applications. The paper proposes a domain knowledge-integrated soft actor-critic (DK-SAC) agent, which incorporates an improved genetic algorithm (IGA) and a fast water-filling algorithm (FWF) within a resource allocation framework. Mobile resource allocation request is classified according to its security requirements based on the dynamic requested services. This framework is designed to balance trade-offs between reliability, data rate, and latency, with latency accounting for security processing. Simulation results show that the proposed DK-SAC model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in reliability, achieving up to a 45.45% improvement, and in energy efficiency, with at least a 43.54% improvement under similar QoS conditions. For large-packet-size next generation URLLC (xURLLC-6G) applications, the proposed model achieves 99% reliability with a latency as low as 5.8 ms. To validate practicality, the proposed DK-SAC framework is evaluated under real-world traffic traces, which exhibit burstiness and non-stationarity. The results confirm the model’s robustness, scalability, and efficiency, offering a practical solution for real-time 5G and beyond networks.

title: SWS-Net: A Hybrid Spiking Neural Network for Energy-Efficient and Robust WiFi Sensing
abstract: This paper proposes spiking-aided wifi sensing network (SWS-Net), a novel hybrid neural architecture that seamlessly integrates Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) with conventional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) to achieve robust WiFi-based indoor sensing. WiFi signals provide a cost-effective and device-free approach for detecting human activities, gestures, identities, and other related phenomena. Nevertheless, their performance is often hampered by multipath fading and environmental noise, presenting substantial challenges. Drawing inspiration from the human brain’s remarkable ability to process noisy sensory inputs, SWS-Net combines the inherent noise resilience of spiking neuron dynamics with the powerful feature extraction capabilities of ANNs. We provide a theoretical analysis that contrasts the noise-handling mechanisms of SNNs and ANNs, demonstrating how their synergistic integration enhances both robustness to noise and efficiency during training. Extensive experiments on three representative WiFi sensing tasks show that SWS-Net outperforms baseline models by delivering superior accuracy and faster convergence, thereby confirming its efficacy in complex and dynamic indoor environments.

title: Resilient User-Centric UAV-Assisted Mobile Edge Computing: Joint Task Offloading and Resource Allocation via Hierarchical Hybrid Sequential Optimization
abstract: The user-centric network (UCN) paradigm provides a promising foundation for mobile edge computing (MEC) by mitigating severe cell-edge interference through multi-access point (AP) cooperation. However, most user-centric MEC schemes rely on ground APs, whose rigid deployment makes them vulnerable to post-disaster damage and severe blockage, delaying service recovery and restricting coverage. To address this issue, this paper develops a user-centric MEC architecture based on uncrewed aerial vehicle access points (UAV-APs), which leverage rapid deployment and flexible coverage to provide more reliable services in dynamic environments. Specifically, we formulate a multi-level delay-energy coupling optimization problem that jointly accounts for task offloading and resource allocation, thereby enabling more effective optimization of both communication performance and energy consumption. The problem is challenging because shared resource competition may cause policy oscillation in parallel updates, while existing action-modeling methods remain insufficient for capturing the coupling between discrete offloading and continuous power control in the access–fronthaul–edge computing process. To solve this problem, we propose HH-SEQUEL, a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework with level-wise hybrid discrete-continuous action parameterization and sequential cross-level updates, enabling end-to-end joint optimization of offloading and resource allocation under delay-energy coupling. Simulation results show that our method reduces latency by 21.39%–65.31% compared to state-of-the-art baselines, and lowers energy consumption by up to 93.89% against baseline approaches.

title: PODD: Path-Optimized Denoising Diffusion Models for Wireless Semantic Communications
abstract: Diffusion models have recently attracted increasing attention in wireless communication systems due to their strong denoising capability and generative modeling ability. However, existing diffusion-based semantic communication schemes usually rely on iterative reverse sampling, which leads to high inference latency and limits their applicability to delay-sensitive wireless scenarios. To address this issue, this paper proposes a path-optimized denoising diffusion model (PODD) with joint source-channel coding (JSCC) for efficient and high-fidelity wireless semantic communications. Specifically, PODD enhances the channel-aware denoising capability by incorporating multi-scale channel state information into the diffusion network, enabling more effective recovery of channel-corrupted semantic features. Furthermore, a graph-based path optimization mechanism is introduced to refine the reverse sampling path, allowing the denoising process to be compressed into only two sampling steps while reducing cumulative propagation errors. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that the proposed joint PODD and JSCC system achieves superior reconstruction performance to other benchmark systems across multiple evaluation metrics. For example, on the DIV2K dataset under the Rayleigh fading channel with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 10 dB, PODD improves the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) by 0.47 dB and 1.06 dB over CDDM and JSCC, respectively. Moreover, PODD significantly reduces the inference time by compressing the sampling process into only two steps, achieving a $\mathbf {22.14\times }$ 22 . 14 × speedup compared with CDDM.

title: Average Response Time Optimization for Service-Chain Routing in Computing Power Networks via Robust Queueing Network Analysis
abstract: Computing power networks (CPNs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for coordinating edge clouds, central clouds, and network infrastructures to support low-latency, high-quality distributed compute-intensive services. We consider a CPN service-chain routing system in which requests traverse multiple services in a prescribed order and are routed among candidate service instances at each stage. Our goal is to develop an explicit method that directly evaluates and optimizes the average response time (ART) of a service-routing policy using the multi-time-scale variability of request arrivals. Existing approaches either optimize surrogate metrics such as path length and queue load or rely on idealized independent decompositions of product-form queueing networks, which can lead to substantial deviations from the true ART. We propose a robust-queueing-network-based service-chain routing model (RCRM) that uses routing probabilities as decision variables and jointly represents service processing and multi-hop forwarding in a fine-grained, class-aware, non-product-form queueing network. RCRM represents the class-dependent coupled propagation of multi-time-scale external-arrival variability through service-side request queues and network-side bit-level forwarding queues. This representation supports more reliable evaluation of the delay components of ART. We then construct a differentiable robust queueing latency evaluator (RQLE) and develop a heuristically guided automatic-differentiation delay optimization algorithm (HADO) that exploits the white-box structure of RCRM to efficiently search for low-latency service-chain routing policies. We implement a discrete-event CPN simulator for validation. The results show that RQLE achieves average estimation errors of $3.1\%$ 3 . 1 % – $12.0\%$ 12 . 0 % , while HADO reduces ART by $11.0\%$ 11 . 0 % – $32.4\%$ 32 . 4 % overall relative to the best baselines.

title: An In-Ear Sleep Modulation SoC Featuring a CNN-LSTM Accelerator with Long-Kernel Memory Reuse and Runtime Dynamic Quantization
abstract: This work presents a 65 nm SoC for closed-loop in-ear sleep modulation. The SoC performs low-noise in-ear EEG sensing, CNN-LSTM-based sleep stage classification, and phase-specific auditory stimulation under 1 mW. A dedicated accelerator is developed, featuring a memory reuse technique to efficiently process long kernels required for low-frequency EEG feature extraction. A runtime dynamic quantization is incorporated, reducing model size by 3.88 times with only a 0.28% loss in accuracy. A sensitivity of 98.3% is achieved for deep sleep detection, enabling effective sleep modulation.

title: Projected Climate Change Impacts on Deep‐Sea Corals of the Red Sea
abstract: Ocean warming, acidification, and deoxygenation, among other co‐occurring factors, are shifting species ranges throughout the marine environment. Mesophotic and deep corals are understudied in their response to climate changes, particularly in the Red Sea, which has relatively high temperatures and salinities and is projected to undergo major changes in the future, with little assessment of the impacts to date. Ecological niche modelling can be used to explain the known distribution of a species, predict its current range, and estimate future range shift under changing ocean scenarios. Here, we estimate the area of suitable habitat for four mesophotic and deep‐sea corals ( Acanthogorgia spp., Stylaster tritoni, Bathypathes thermophila , and Madracis interjecta ) across the whole Red Sea under present conditions and under different scenarios of future environmental changes (years 2090–2100). We found variations in the responses of these corals, but two of the four taxa are projected to lose significant amounts of their current habitats, while the other two lose a smaller portion. In particular, the scleractinian coral M. interjecta is likely to lose the largest proportion of its habitat, while the black coral B. thermophila may experience the least change. Deeper areas may become suitable for these corals, but colonisation will depend on their ability to disperse. We also assessed the potential biodiversity hotspots both now and in the future, finding the northern Red Sea to be one ecologically important area. These results enable marine spatial planning in support of an effective long‐term conservation action to protect these important habitats.
