journal: Journal of psychopathology and clinical science

title: Biological foundation models
publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

title: Persian Handwritten Digits and Symbols Dataset (PHDD): An Open Benchmark for Persian OCR and Pattern Recognition
abstract: This paper introduces the Persian Handwritten Digits and Symbols Dataset (PHDD), an open benchmark designed to facilitate research in Persian optical character recognition (OCR) and pattern recognition. The dataset comprises 40,214 grayscale images of handwritten Persian numerals and mathematical symbols, collected from about 200 volunteer students at the University of Zanjan. The dataset was processed through a fully automated pipeline developed in Python using OpenCV. The pipeline performs character detection, automatic cropping, denoising, normalization, and resizing to 28 × 28 pixels, yielding uniform, high-quality images stored in lossless PNG format. All preprocessing scripts and the full data-generation workflow are publicly available. Beyond dataset compilation, a convolutional neural network (CNN) was trained for feature extraction and multi-class classification, producing robust descriptor embeddings. A two-dimensional visualization of these learned descriptors using the t-SNE technique reveals compact, well-separated clusters, demonstrating the discriminative power of the extracted features. PHDD provides a valuable foundation for applications in deep learning, computer vision, image classification, and OCR, enabling reproducible studies in handwritten digit and symbol recognition.

title: Agentic AI in transforming agriculture: a review
abstract: Artificial intelligence-based agents are emerging as a transformative paradigm for agriculture, enabling autonomous perception, reasoning, decision-making, and coordinated action across complex data and operational environments. These systems could improve productivity, resilience, resource efficiency, and food security, while raising challenges related to robustness, interoperability, data governance, trust, equity, and regulation. This Review examines the rise of these systems in agriculture and outlines research priorities for their development and deployment.

title: Electronic structure, topological analysis, molecular docking and ADMET of a bioactive flavonoid glycoside from Dicranopteris linearis.
abstract: Kaempferol-3-O-(4″,6″-di-E-p-coumaroyl)-β-d-glucopyranoside (1), recently isolated from Dicranopteris linearis, exhibits α-glucosidase inhibitory activity, but the molecular features underlying this activity remain unclear. Here, density functional theory (DFT) was integrated with frontier molecular orbital (FMO), molecular electrostatic potential (MEP), quantum theory of atoms in molecules (QTAIM), non-covalent interaction (NCI), natural population (NPA), CLPO charge-transfer, electron localization function (ELF), localized orbital locator (LOL) and harmonic oscillator model of aromaticity (HOMA) analyses to characterize the electronic and topological architecture of 1. The HOMO and LUMO are predominantly associated with the two p-coumaroyl substituents, whereas the chromone C2[double bond, length as m-dash]C3-C4[double bond, length as m-dash]O unit contributes 61.1% to the LUMO+1. ELF and LOL analyses complemented this picture by characterizing electron localization across the molecule. QTAIM/NCI further identified a differentiated network of weak closed-shell interactions, whereas MEP highlighted carbonyl- and hydroxyl-centered electrostatic hot spots. NPA and CLPO charge-transfer analysis showed a push-pull chromone, a resonance-assisted 5-OH⋯O[double bond, length as m-dash]C4 hydrogen bond and no through-space charge transfer between the π-stacked coumaroyl groups. Molecular docking against processing α-glucosidase I from Saccharomyces cerevisiae (PDB ID: 4J5T), providing the primary structural context for the experimentally reported α-glucosidase inhibitory activity (IC50 = 22.5 µM) and exploratory docking against human maltase-glucoamylase (MGAM; PDB ID: 3TOP), suggested preliminary binding poses involving key pocket residues and complementary hydrogen-bonding, π-mediated, and hydrophobic contacts. The electronic features identified computationally provide an electronic framework for interpreting the experimentally reported α-glucosidase inhibitory activity. ADMET profiling additionally indicated limited passive permeability and negligible predicted CNS exposure.

title: A review of micro- and nanostructural cues in 3D-printed scaffolds: regulating cell fate for anisotropic tissue regeneration.
abstract: Anisotropic tissues rely on spatially organized cells and extracellular matrices to maintain directional mechanical, electrical, and transport functions. Reconstructing this organization remains challenging because restoring tissue volume or gross anatomy alone cannot reproduce the local structural microenvironment that guides cell behavior and tissue maturation. Advances in three-dimensional (3D) printing provide increasing control over fibers, grooves, channels, and other micro- and nanoscale features, creating opportunities to regulate cell-material interactions through defined structural cues. This review summarizes recent progress in the design of micro- and nanostructural cues in 3D-printed scaffolds and discusses how these structures influence cell alignment, migration, differentiation, phenotypic maturation, and matrix organization across anisotropic tissues. Particular attention is given to the relationship between structural parameters, cell fate, and tissue-specific functions in muscle and tendon, neural, vascular, and other anisotropic tissue models. Current studies demonstrate that structural organization can guide cellular responses and contribute to tissue maturation and functional regeneration; however, these effects are frequently intertwined with matrix composition, mechanical and electrical properties, biochemical signals, and cellular components. Moreover, mechanistic evidence and well-controlled structure-function studies remain concentrated largely in vitro, while in vivo validation relies predominantly on small-animal models. This review therefore highlights the need to define structure-specific cellular responses, establish stronger mechanistic links between structural cues and cell fate, and validate their functional relevance in physiologically representative models, providing a framework for the rational design of 3D-printed scaffolds for anisotropic tissue regeneration.

title: A 3D Implementation of an Elastoviscoplastic Model and Application to Creep-Driven Slow-Moving Landslides
abstract: To analyze problems involving creep-driven slow-moving landslides interacting with structures and infrastructure and gain useful information for risk management, numerical modeling is the most comprehensive tool. When resorting to numerical simulations, appropriate constitutive modeling is key to capture the time-dependent behavior of geomaterials. However, a drawback of advanced constitutive models accounting for time dependency is the high number of parameters involved, which are commonly calibrated based on site-scale monitoring data, without accounting for the characteristic creep behavior of the material. This paper describes the implementation of an existing elastoviscoplastic model in a three-dimensional (3D) finite-difference software. The model, called SHELVIP (Stress Hardening Elastic Viscous Plastic), was derived from the classical theory of elastoplasticity by adding a viscoplastic component based on Perzyna’s overstress theory. After illustrating the model and the implementation procedure, the steps to tune the constitutive parameters, especially the viscoplastic ones, are described. First, the viscoplastic parameters are determined at the laboratory scale through an analytical calibration process based on laboratory creep tests. Then, tuning of some parameters at the site scale is performed, while other parameters are kept unchanged from their laboratory-scale value being representative of the intrinsic creep behavior. The final set of parameters can be used to run predictive analyses for problems of engineering relevance. The analytical calibration is exemplified with reference to triaxial creep tests on Palombini clays. Then, the implemented SHELVIP model is validated by comparing numerical, analytical, and experimental creep strains at different deviatoric stress levels. A three-dimensional numerical model of the interaction between a deep-seated landslide and an existing motorway tunnel is developed. The capability of the constitutive framework to catch the time-dependent landslide movement is demonstrated by comparing monitoring data with the corresponding numerical results. The model is then used to run predictive analyses aimed at investigating the slow-moving landslide–infrastructure evolution.

title: Importance of Uncertainty Representation and Design Exploration Method for Robust Aerodynamic Optimization
abstract: This study examines the impact of uncertainty propagation and design exploration techniques on robust airfoil optimization processes. The RAE2822 airfoil geometry is selected as the case study and parameterized using the class/shape transformation (CST) method. The functional relationship between design inputs and outputs is modeled using a computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-driven surrogate model based on Gaussian process (GP) regression. Uncertainty calculations are performed using Monte Carlo sampling (MCS) and polynomial chaos expansion (PCE). In addition, the effects of different design exploration methods are analyzed using deductive design exploration (DDEM) and inductive design exploration (IDEM). The results indicated that the DDEM method is sensitive to the choice of uncertainty propagation technique, leading to variations in the optimization results. In contrast, solutions obtained using the IDEM method are found to be independent of the uncertainty propagation approach and more robust than those from the DDEM method. Furthermore, the robustness metric provided by IDEM makes it a practical and efficient method for robust airfoil optimization processes.

title: Unsteady Aerodynamic Prediction of a Variable-Sweep Morphing Wing via Steady–Unsteady Data Fusion
abstract: Variable-sweep wing aircraft demonstrate pronounced unsteady aerodynamic characteristics throughout the wing morphing process. Accurate prediction of unsteady aerodynamics remains a critical challenge due to complex flow physics and high computational cost. Traditional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods are precise but time-consuming, and purely data-driven surrogates often lack robustness when applied to unseen flow conditions. To address these limitations, this study proposes a steady–unsteady data fusion framework for rapid and reliable prediction of unsteady pressure distributions and aerodynamic coefficients of a variable-sweep wing undergoing cosine-type sweep motions. The framework integrates a steady prediction module with an unsteady correction module, leveraging the complementary strengths of the data sets. Steady-flow data provide broad parametric coverage over Mach numbers, sweep angles, and angles of attack, whereas unsteady data offer high temporal resolution and capture dynamic response features. The fusion model generates a base pressure field from the steady module and learns unsteady corrections from time-resolved simulations, achieving both accuracy and generalizability. Performance is evaluated across three distinct validation scenarios: same-period validation, cross-period validation, and cross-Mach/angle-of-attack validation. Results showed that the fusion model reduces pressure field errors by more than 50% and decreases lift and drag coefficient errors by nearly an order of magnitude compared with a purely unsteady surrogate. This study demonstrates that combining steady and unsteady data yields a computationally efficient and robust surrogate model, offering a practical tool for rapid and accurate unsteady aerodynamic prediction of morphing wings.

title: Boundary Performance Enhancement Monitoring Based on Smart Bearing Service Performance Indicators
abstract: Boundary-condition anomalies in continuous girder bridges redistribute support reactions and internal forces, yet long-term reaction monitoring is seldom connected to field intervention and assessment. We developed a support-reaction monitoring workflow for force-measuring adjustable bearings. Here, smart refers to continuous sensing, remote transmission, and controllable in situ height adjustment rather than autonomous diagnosis or actuation. Three long-window indicators, normalized reaction time mean (NRTM), normalized reaction time variance (NRTV), and reaction time correlation coefficient (RTCC), were derived from statistically steady traffic windows to suppress individual-vehicle effects. Simulations of a 60-m + 80-m + 60-m variable-section girder showed convergence after 6 h, with NRTM, NRTV, and RTCC errors of 0.00%, 1.06%, and −1.34%, respectively. The indicators were only weakly affected by changes in traffic parameters, while NRTV and RTCC recovered stable values at signal-to-noise ratios of at least 30 dB. Up to 30°, a simplified skew influence-surface check yielded small NRTM, NRTV, and RTCC deviations of 0.18%, 0.87%, and −1.19%, respectively. This supports the use of resultant reactions within the tested skew range. Field implementation involved an in-service, skewed, variable-section, continuous steel box-girder bridge equipped with 12 force-measuring adjustable spherical bearings. Indicators were calculated using a 9-h sliding window with 10-min steps. Under open traffic conditions, the bearing height underwent four stages of adjustment (1–2 mm each), during which the monitored time series of indicators changed accordingly. The postadjustment shift toward finite-element targets provided a relative assessment of the intervention outcome. These results support the use of indicators with engineering records and finite-element analysis to assess boundary anomalies, staged adjustment, and relative postadjustment changes under routine traffic.

title: Reliability Analysis of Unsaturated Soil Slopes Using Advanced Surrogate Models: A Comparative Study of PCE-MCS, K-MCS, and Gradient-Based Methods
abstract: Probabilistic stability analysis of soil slopes is essential for reliable geotechnical design due to pronounced uncertainties in soil strength and hydraulic parameters. Although crude Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) provides a robust benchmark, its prohibitive computational cost and the limitations of gradient-based methods such as FORM and SORM in handling nonlinear and non-Gaussian performance functions restrict their practical applicability. To address these challenges, this study conducts a comparative analysis of advanced surrogate-based reliability methods, specifically polynomial chaos expansion–enhanced Monte Carlo simulation (PCE-MCS) and kriging-enhanced Monte Carlo simulation (K-MCS), against traditional gradient-based methods such as the first-order reliability method (FORM) and second-order reliability method (SORM) for evaluating the stability of unsaturated finite soil slopes. The crude MCS serves as the benchmark. The work examines the predictive accuracy and computational efficiency of these methods in estimating the probability of failure ( p f ). Parametric studies demonstrate nonlinear variations in p f with mean and coefficient of variation of stability number ( c / γ H ), internal friction angle ( ϕ ), and fitting parameters of soil-water characteristic curve (SWCC) ( a f / γ H , n f , and m f ). In terms of computational efficiency, surrogate-assisted approaches provide orders-of-magnitude reductions in wall-clock time compared to crude MCS. When normalized with respect to PCE-MCS (unity), K-MCS requires only 1.85 times the computational cost, whereas FORM/SORM requires approximately 28 times. In contrast, crude MCS incurs computational costs exceeding four orders of magnitude for large sample sizes. Statistical testing confirms that stochastic methods (K-MCS, PCE-MCS) significantly outperformed gradient-based methods (FORM, SORM). Although no statistically significant difference is observed between K-MCS and PCE-MCS ( p -value = 0.83), K-MCS exhibited slightly narrower confidence intervals and lower mean error (0.0116 versus 0.0153), indicating marginally greater robustness. Moreover, K-MCS maintains point-estimate error percentages below 8% across most scenarios, with PCE-MCS below 11%. In contrast, FORM showed maximum errors of up to 50.67%, followed by SORM with errors as high as 31.97%. The study also includes Sobol’ sensitivity analysis to identify the influence of each input parameter on the factor of safety. Comparisons of Sobol’ indices derived using post-processed PCE, PCE-MCS, and K-MCS reveal consistent results, with friction angle ( ϕ ) identified as the most influential parameter (total-order Sobol’ index = 0.66). To facilitate practical application, the study concludes with developing design charts using kriging for target reliability indices of 3.0. These charts provide an important tool for slope stability assessment, enabling precise and efficient evaluations under unsaturated soil conditions. The findings emphasize the efficacy of PCE-MCS and K-MCS as robust and computationally efficient surrogate modeling techniques for quantifying the probability of failure of unsaturated soil slopes and facilitating reliability-based design optimization of finite slopes.
journal: Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering

title: Method for Determining Lateral Groundwater Inflow and Initial Conditions of 1D Hydrodynamic Models for Large and Medium-Sized Rivers Based on Steady Flow Calibration
abstract: To enable the direct and efficient determination of lateral groundwater inflow and initial hydrodynamic conditions in one-dimensional (1D) hydrodynamic models for large and medium-sized rivers, we propose a steady flow calibration–based method to simultaneously determine these two key parameters. Taking preflood measured discharge as the benchmark, a hydrodynamic presimulation model with lateral groundwater inflow as the sole recharge is constructed. Numerical iteration drives the flow to steady state while lateral groundwater inflow is adjusted until the simulated discharge matches the benchmark. The lateral groundwater inflow thus determined serves as the constant input for the flood process, and the corresponding spatial distributions of water level and velocity under this steady state serve as the initial hydrodynamic conditions for flood simulation. Source-term calculations and stability conditions are optimized in the presimulation to improve accuracy and stability. The method is validated using historical flood data from the Tuhai River, China. For the typical events, the mean absolute error, root mean square error, and mean absolute percentage error remain low, demonstrating satisfactory accuracy. This method enables simultaneous quantitative determination of the two key parameters, significantly reducing parameter uncertainty, subjective biases, and numerical oscillations associated with their manual calibration. It improves simulation efficiency while maintaining numerical stability and simulation accuracy, offering an effective data-lean alternative for large and medium-sized rivers with stable preflood baseflow.

title: FEM Validation of Form-Found Shell Roofs Designed in Seismic Areas
abstract: Shell structures offer high structural efficiency when their shapes allow loads to be carried mainly through compression, making them particularly suitable for materials with limited tensile strength, such as masonry, unreinforced concrete, and unreinforced 3D-printed concrete. The purpose of this work is to evaluate the structural quality and practical reliability of shells obtained through a physics-informed neural network-based optimized constrained form-finding (PINN-OCFF) methodology. This form-finding approach explicitly accounts for both vertical and horizontal loading conditions at the design stage by identifying an isoresistant volume capable of withstanding these actions through pure compression. Unlike traditional form-finding methods that focus primarily on gravity loading, the PINN-OCFF strategy generates shell shapes intended to remain in compression under combined loading conditions relevant to real design situations. The study focuses on a shell designed through this PINN-OCFF framework and assesses its performance through finite-element method (FEM) analyses carried out in Abaqus, following modeling assumptions commonly adopted in engineering practice and required by design codes such as the Eurocodes, ACI, or the Italian NTC. The FEM results are compared with the membrane equilibrium predicted by the form-finding process in terms of the stress distribution, development of tensile zones, and overall structural response. To investigate the influence of boundary conditions, three different constraint configurations are considered: fully fixed edges, fully hinged edges, and hinges located only at the base supports. For comparison, a shell of uniform thickness is considered and analyzed under the same vertical and horizontal loads used during form finding. The analyses show that the shell designed through the PINN-OCFF form-finding process better preserves compression-dominated behavior under realistic modeling assumptions, even when horizontal loading conditions and nonideal boundary conditions are introduced. Compared to shells designed considering vertical loads alone or employing a uniform thickness, the optimized shell exhibits reduced bending effects and limited tensile stresses. These findings demonstrate that incorporating horizontal actions directly into the form-finding stage leads to more robust and practically reliable shell designs, supporting the use of the PINN-OCFF methodology as an effective preliminary design tool for compression-dominated shell structures.
journal: Journal of Structural Design and Construction Practice

title: Measuring Station-Area Functional Profiles of High-Speed Rail Stations through a Node-Place Approach: Nationwide Evidence from China
abstract: High-speed rail (HSR) stations are critical interfaces between national transport networks and urban systems, shaping both regional accessibility and local development. Yet, previous studies seldom offer a nationally comparable assessment of HSR station-area functional profiles, defined here as the combined performance and balance of transportation-related node functions and surrounding urban place functions within station areas. It remains unclear how railway-level attributes and city-level contexts jointly influence these profiles. This study proposes an integrated evaluation framework grounded in the node-place approach to quantify, classify, and explain the functional characteristics of HSR station areas. The framework combines a set of multidimensional indicators capturing transportation connectivity (node) and urban development attributes (place) through a weighted multicriteria evaluation to derive overall functional performance and incorporates an interpretable machine learning model to uncover nonlinear effects and interaction mechanisms among key determinants. A case study is conducted using 90 major HSR stations in China within the 15-min walking zone. Results show that the station-area function evaluation index is low on average but highly heterogeneous across space. Stations in eastern and northeastern China more often exhibit balanced node-place profiles, whereas stations in western regions more frequently display functional deficiencies. A common structural pattern is that node-related functions exceed place-related functions, indicating that network accessibility is not consistently matched by surrounding urban development. Railway-level attributes explain more variance than city-level factors, with station built time emerging as the most influential determinant. Its interactions with distance to the city center, station building area, and urban population shape distinct station-area functional profiles within threshold ranges. These findings provide an evidence base for differentiated station-area planning and targeted investments, supporting the transformation of HSR stations into integrated, multifunctional urban nodes.
journal: Journal of Transportation Engineering, Part A: Systems

title: Interpretable Hourly Flood Forecasting Leveraging Deep Learning Recurrence and Attention Mechanisms
abstract: Timely and precise flood forecasting at subdaily intervals is crucial for mitigating the adverse impact of flood events, particularly through early warnings that enable effective emergency response. This study investigated the efficiency of the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT), a state-of-the-art sequence-to-sequence deep learning architecture, for its efficacy in forecasting flood events with lead times from 1 to 24 h across the Atlantic and Gulf coastal regions of the US, extending from Maine to Louisiana. The TFT framework integrated time-dependent meteorological and hydrological variables along with several invariant catchment attributes to effectively model the temporal variability and spatial diversity of hydrological responses across different regions. Model performance was systematically assessed utilizing the Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), relative peak bias (RPB), and peak time bias (PTB), benchmarked across multiple forecast horizons and evaluated against both discharge observations and simulations from the physically based National Water Model (NWMv3.0). The TFT demonstrated superior predictive capability, achieving an average NSE of 0.83 for continuous hydrograph simulations across all catchments during the testing phase, significantly outperforming NWMv3.0, which had an NSE of 0.53. The proposed TFT framework incorporates antecedent observed streamflow as an autoregressive input, whereas NWMv3.0 relies primarily on meteorological forcings and physics-based process representations without directly utilizing the same observed discharge information during forecasting. Consequently, part of the superior short-term predictive performance of the TFT framework, particularly at shorter lead times, may be attributed to this additional information advantage associated with streamflow persistence and autocorrelation. An attention mechanism was utilized to perform feature importance analysis, which identified total precipitation, longwave radiation flux, and convective fraction as the dominant dynamic meteorological forcings predictors, and the catchment mean slope was the most important static attribute, underscoring the model’s interpretability for the area of interest. To enhance reliability further, a quantile regression loss function was incorporated into TFT to generate probabilistic discharge forecasts (instead of point forecasts) across seven quantiles. The associated 95% prediction uncertainty (95PPU) was evaluated rigorously using established hydrological uncertainty metrics, including the R -factor, P -factor, and the total uncertainty index (TUI). By leveraging the advanced capabilities of the TFT architecture, such as its capacity for quantifying feature importance and delivering detailed probabilistic forecasts, this study contributes substantive advancements to short-term flood forecasting methodologies. These outcomes support data-informed decision-making and resilience-building strategies in flood-prone regions, reinforcing the applicability of deep learning in operational hydrologic forecasting.
journal: Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management

title: How peer-activity leaders promote children's well-being: perspectives from a CBPR-based multi-stakeholder study in Southern Sweden.
abstract: BACKGROUND Adult role models and supportive environments are essential for children's health, well-being, and development. Participation in organised leisure activities and access to local meeting places strengthen children's social connectedness, safety, and resilience. In Malmö, Sweden, All-Activity Houses (AAHs) were established to promote children's well-being through free and easily accessible activities led by peer-activity leaders who work closely within the children's everyday environments. OBJECTIVE The aim of this study is to explore how peer-activity leaders perceive and promote children's overall well-being, and to identify key mechanisms within the AAH context that contribute to these processes. METHODS The study applied a participatory action research design with a Community-Based Participatory Research (CBPR) approach. Data were co-created through multiple focus group meetings using a multistage focus group method within the CBPR teams, complemented by field notes from participant observations. Nineteen peer-activity leaders from four AAHs participated in the study. RESULTS Five themes emerged, reflecting how peer-activity leaders promote children's well-being: building and sustaining trust; creating a safe place; applying flexibility in response to local conditions and children's needs; promoting equality; and providing care. CONCLUSION The findings suggest important mechanisms through which peer-activity leaders perceive themselves as contributing to children's well-being.
journal: International journal of qualitative studies on health and well-being

title: How social media-induced secondary traumatic stress affects depression: a moderated mediation model of self-compassion and problematic social media use in college students.
abstract: Background: Social media use has grown rapidly among college students, who constitute one of the most active user groups. However, exposure to negative and traumatic content on social media may lead to secondary traumatic stress (STS-SM), which may be linked to depression. This study examines the psychological mechanisms underlying the relationship between STS-SM and depressive symptoms among Chinese college students.Methods: A total of 1080 Chinese college students (382 females and 698 males; mean age = 19.07 years, SD = 1.08) completed web-based questionnaires including Secondary Traumatic Stress Scale for Social Media, Beck Depression Inventory-II, Self-compassion scale, and Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale. Age, gender, educational level, marital status, ethnicity, and subjective socioeconomic status were treated as covariates. Mediation and moderation analyses were performed to examine the role of self-compassion and problematic social media use (PSMU) in the relation between STS-SM and depression using the PROCESS macro in SPSS.Results: STS-SM was found to be positively associated with depression (r = 0.48, p < .001), and this correlation was mediated by self-compassion (b = 0.09, 95% CI [0.07, 0.11]). Moreover, the effect of self-compassion on depression was moderated by PSMU, with the effect being stronger for students with high PSMU (b = -0.32, p < .001) than those with low PSMU (b = -0.12, p < .001).Conclusions: STS-SM contributed to increased depressive symptoms by reducing individuals' levels of self-compassion, with the effect of self-compassion on depression moderated by PSMU. These findings underscore the importance of regulating traumatic content online and highlight self-compassion training as a promising intervention, particularly for those with PSMU.

title: AlphaNet7: a multi-head physics-informed neural network for latent parameter discovery in variable-order fractional systems
abstract: Solving high-dimensional inverse problems in variable-order fractional dynamical systems from sparse observations remains a major challenge in scientific machine learning. Standard Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) rely on soft residual penalties, which frequently induce gradient pathologies or encounter conservation discrepancies when applied to non-local fractional operators. To address this limitation, we propose AlphaNet7, a constrained multi-head PINN architecture for the simultaneous inverse identification of compartment-specific, time-varying fractional orders and transmission dynamics. The proposed architecture combines a shared feature-extraction backbone with eight independent prediction heads, jointly inferring multiple latent quantities while implicitly integrating the governing phenomenological equations through a custom autograd-compatible piecewise differentiable explicit fractional forward solver. AlphaNet7 is applied to a seven-compartment nonlinear epidemiological system governed by the non-singular Caputo-Fabrizio fractional operator. From two macroscopic surveillance streams, the network estimates a regularization-guided, constraint-dependent set of seven phenomenological effective fractional orders rather than genuine biological memory parameters. In the reference run, inferred compartment orders span approximately 0.688 to 0.864 (mean 0.753), whereas a single-head global-order model achieves identical reconstruction error (RMSE = 0.0028) and removing the diversity penalty contracts compartment means to between 0.740 and 0.774 (RMSE = 0.0021). Under regularization-guided optimization, the multi-head model captures nonlinear transitions in exposure and recovery alongside quasi-stationary institutional plateaus; this alignment reflects post hoc temporal coincidence with policy shifts rather than causality. Furthermore, the inferred regime yields a modest reduction of roughly 2% to 3% (1.38 to 1.35) in the definition-driven, phenomenological fractional reproduction metric. Because the explicit solver numerically constrains trajectories to the discretized governing dynamics, AlphaNet7 outperforms fixed-order baselines in calibration and out-of-sample forecasting, reducing forecast error by 30.2% to 63.1% across rolling hold-out splits under unified normalization. This provides a prior-constrained framework for effective parameter estimation in variable-order fractional systems.

title: The series of genetic codes that preceded our own.
abstract: We produce a working hypothesis for the steps by which the canonical genetic code might have been constructed. We assume amino acids were added in the order inferred from their enrichment or depletion in ancestrally reconstructed sequences dating back to the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA) relative to that in ancient but post-LUCA controls. To convert this ordering into a time series of 64-codon genetic codes, we followed the "2-1-3 rule" that information appeared first at the middle codon position, then mostly at the first before the third, with purine vs pyrimidine distinctions tending to precede distinctions between purines or between pyrimidines. Two notable deviations from the 2-1-3 rule suggest an ancestral promiscuity between valine/isoleucine/methionine, and between alanine/threonine, to produce "statistical proteins." The same promiscuities enable amino acids to be added in order of appearance at successive nodes in the cladograms of Class I and Class II aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase catalytic domains. Trifonov's previous amino acid ordering did not produce this consilience, with both a worse fit to the 2-1-3 rule, and discordance of synthetase trees with the order. More support for late resolution of hydrophobic promiscuity comes from post-LUCA differentiation between the synthetases of valine and isoleucine, in a manner dependent on 2 conserved tryptophans. The observed promiscuous activities of synthetases, and deep mutational scanning data on which amino acid substitutions are best tolerated, also align well with our reconstructed time series of genetic codes. As a working hypothesis, this series can guide research on random peptides, urzymes, and substitution models.

title: Performance of an infliximab precision-guided dosing tool from a capillary blood-based self-collection device in inflammatory bowel disease patients.
Rp-Bp and the Ribotools box for translatome profiling.
abstract: We present the Ribotools "box" for the analysis of matched ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) and RNA sequencing data. Ribotools can be used in standalone mode or in combination with Rp-Bp for Ribo-seq quality control, open reading frames discovery, translation efficiency, and differential expression analyses. In this work, we use Ribotools to profile the differentiation of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) into cardiomyocytes to reveal a remarkably coherent transition from plastic, signaling-driven to stable, structurally committed cardiac cells, staged through multiple layers of translational control. Together with complementary proteomics, the resulting dataset provides a rich multi-omics resource for investigating the hiPSC model of cardiac lineage commitment. Additionally, we present a reproducible and extensible pipeline for benchmarking translation efficiency analysis tools. Ribotools and Rp-Bp are available on Bioconda and help to make research accessible and reproducible. Detailed documentation, test datasets, and tutorials are available at https://ribotools.readthedocs.io and https://rp-bp.readthedocs.io.

title: Macronuclear Development During Conjugation in Blepharisma sinuosum and B. stoltei: Insights Into the Diversity of Macronuclear Formation in Ciliates.
abstract: Sexual reproduction is one of the crucial driving forces of evolution. Ciliates, single-celled eukaryotes with nuclear dimorphism, undergo a unique sexual process, conjugation, during which the macronucleus (MAC) and micronucleus (MIC) are extensively reorganized. Previous studies have shown that macronuclear development in Blepharisma can involve functionally differentiated micronuclei. Here, we investigated the conjugation process in two multi-micronucleate species, Blepharisma sinuosum and B. stoltei. In B. sinuosum, approximately two-thirds of MICs enter meiosis, but only one meiotic MIC completes the divisions that generate pronuclei; the remaining MICs persist as somatomicronuclei and develop into secondary MAC anlagen. The new MICs undergo variable additional mitoses, producing different MIC numbers among exconjugants. In both B. sinuosum and B. stoltei, primary MAC anlagen derived from the synkaryon and secondary MAC anlagen derived from somatomicronuclei show coordinated late development, supporting a model in which both nuclear sources contribute to the developing MAC. Compared with B. sinuosum, B. stoltei exhibits greater individual variation in the number of meiotic MICs, new MICs, and primary and secondary MAC anlagen. These results expand the species-level cytological basis for understanding the diversity of macronuclear development during ciliate conjugation.
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology

title: Innovation dynamics and sustainability in manufacturing: leveraging open innovation and dynamic capabilities
abstract: The purpose of this study is to evaluate how manufacturers today face mounting demands from stakeholders to adopt innovative manufacturing systems that mitigate the negative societal and environmental effects of their operations. Consequently, manufacturing processes are constantly evolving. Open innovation (OI) systems present a promising avenue for manufacturers to develop dynamic capabilities (DCs), thereby enhancing their long-term performance. However, despite its potential significance, empirical research linking OI, DC and sustainable manufacturing performance (SMP) remains relatively scarce, especially concerning the simultaneous minimization of environmental impact, economic viability and social acceptability. This study rigorously investigates the intricate relationship between various OI systems (namely outbound, inbound and coupled) and their impact on SMP through the mediating influence of DC within the context of large-scale manufacturing enterprises. Using a robust quantitative research design, the authors surveyed 346 employees from prominent Malaysian manufacturers. Data collection utilized a 5-point Likert scale questionnaire drawn from established literature. The authors then used partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) for comprehensive data analysis, resulting in the validation of 11 out of 12 research hypotheses. The findings reveal that both inbound innovation and coupled OI exert direct, positive influences on the social, economic and environmental facets of manufacturing performance. Conversely, outbound innovation predominantly affects economic and environmental performance. A key insight from this study is the mediating role played by DC in shaping the relationship between OI and SMP. This underscores the critical importance for manufacturers to invest in developing DC to maximize the positive impact of OI on SMP. The study emphasizes the importance of fostering DC to leverage the potential benefits of OI for SMP improvement. The findings can guide manufacturers in adopting strategies that simultaneously address environmental concerns, economic sustainability and social responsibility. Unlike prior studies that treat OI as a unitary construct or assert DC’s mediating role by citation alone, this study disaggregates OI into inbound, outbound and coupled forms, and grounds DC’s mediating function in its sensing, seizing and transforming microfoundations, showing that mediation strength scales systematically with each OI mode’s knowledge-integration demands (variation accounted for [VAF] ranging from 22.34% to 68.67%). This mechanism-level, differentiated account rather than a uniform DC–OI–SMP relationship is the study’s central conceptual contribution.

title: Human–AI interaction in academic knowledge co-creation: a typology based on a systematic literature review
abstract: This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) contributes to knowledge co-creation in academic writing, focusing on systematic literature reviews (SLRs) as a representative and consequential form of structured knowledge production. It develops a typology of human–AI interaction that reveals how intellectual responsibility, decision-making and dialogue are distributed between human researchers and AI systems. A systematic review of 120 publications from Scopus and Web of Science was conducted to analyse applications of AI in SLRs. Studies were coded along two dimensions derived from human–AI interaction theory: (1) decision-making delegation and (2) iterative dialogue between humans and AI. Using deductive thematic analysis, the research identified distinct interaction types and synthesised empirical patterns into a transparent framework. The analysis reveals three types of human–AI interaction: AI-Supported, Collaborative and Partner-like. The AI-supported type treats AI as an assistive tool for automating repetitive tasks while preserving full human control. The collaborative type represents dialogical co-creation, where humans and AI engage in iterative prompting and feedback cycles. The partner-like type reflects hybrid partnership and partial delegation, where AI contributes analytical reasoning and interpretation under human oversight. Together, these types form a continuum of knowledge co-creation processes in which AI evolves from an efficiency tool to an epistemic partner. The dataset was limited to English-language sources indexed in Scopus and WoS, and coding relied on reported practices that varied in transparency. Future research should include experimental or longitudinal studies to assess how different interaction types affect review quality, transparency and ethical outcomes. The typology extends knowledge co-creation theory by including non-human (AI) agents as active participants in the SECI process and the dialogical model of co-creation. The typology provides a framework for researchers, institutions and editors to assess how AI contributes to academic knowledge production. It supports responsible integration of AI in SLRs by clarifying levels of delegation and dialogue. The model encourages teams to document prompting cycles, maintain ethical oversight, and develop competencies for reflexive, transparent collaboration with AI systems. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is the first to conceptualise SLRs as sites of human–AI knowledge co-creation, linking knowledge management theory with evidence on AI-assisted academic writing. It proposes a theoretically grounded typology that clarifies AI’s role in distributed knowledge creation and offers practical guidance for transparent and ethical research practice.

title: From engagement to loyalty: the mediating roles of brand trust and social media brand posts
abstract: The purpose of this study is to examine how social media brand engagement influences brand loyalty in the smartphone industry. Particular attention is given to the mediating roles of customer engagement with social media brand posts and brand trust, thereby clarifying the mechanisms through which engagement translates into enduring consumer–brand relationships. The study collected survey data from 585 smartphone users in Jordan. Measurement validity was established through confirmatory factor analysis, and hypotheses were tested using a structural path model, providing robust statistical evidence of the relationships among the engagement, trust and loyalty constructs. Social media brand engagement positively influences brand loyalty, both directly and indirectly through brand trust. Aggregated post-level engagement exerts a weaker effect, contributing modestly to loyalty. Disaggregated analyses reveal that engagement behaviors differ in impact: liking significantly influences trust and loyalty, whereas commenting and sharing do not. Serial mediation is not supported for aggregated post-level engagement; a significant sequential pathway emerges through liking, trust and loyalty. Customer engagement theory is advanced by differentiating between brand-level and post-level engagement, revealing that visible engagement behaviors are not uniformly valuable. Trust emerges as the dominant relational pathway driving loyalty. Situated within Jordan’s smartphone industry, the study extends the contextual relevance of engagement research in emerging markets. Managerially, the findings prioritize trust-building strategies over surface-level engagement indicators.

title: Financial feasibility of employee ownership under the Danish succession model
abstract: We examine the feasibility of employee-financed succession under Denmark's new framework, which lets owners transfer ownership to employees through a cooperative holding structure with deferred capital gains tax. We develop a cash-flow model yielding closed-form feasibility conditions that incorporate the statutory dividend threshold and tax deferral, with simulations and a stochastic extension quantifying liquidity risk. Feasibility turns on short-run liquidity rather than profitability. Because dividends are pro rata, funding a stake of any size requires the operating company to distribute its entire equity value; this “dividend leakage” to non-participating owners is the root of the constraint. The maximum sustainable multiple rises with payout and falls with leverage, leaving high-valuation firms unreachable; a smaller stake does not help, as feasibility is independent of the ownership share. Feasibility therefore hinges on concessions outside the dividend channel: tax-exempt seller gifts or employee contributions. The baseline abstracts from bargaining and from heterogeneity beyond payout and leverage; an appendix shows earnings risk tightens the feasible set. The results clarify why employee buyouts are viable in some firm contexts but not others and inform the statutory review due after three years. They indicate that using differentiated cash-flow rights, so the employee entity captures more of a given distribution, would widen reach at no cost to either party. The selection mechanism favors mature, stable firms. Reaching high-growth sectors requires instruments beyond the current framework. To the best of our knowledge. This is the first formal feasibility analysis of the Danish model, connecting institutional tax design to economic viability.
journal: Journal of Participation and Employee Ownership

title: Operationalising pedagogical policy enactment to enhance quality assurance and student satisfaction in higher education
abstract: This study aims to integrate, operationalise and evaluate previously developed pedagogical policy guidelines within an institutional quality assurance (QA) matrix to examine their implementation and association with student satisfaction outcomes in higher education (HE). UK-based HE department was used as a longitudinal case study. Data collection involved auditing the adoption of pedagogical policy guidelines across 44 sampled modules and National Student Survey (NSS) themes, alongside analysis of corresponding NSS outcomes. Regression, thematic and comparative analyses were conducted to examine the relative associations between policy adoption and student satisfaction. Student satisfaction increased across the analysed NSS themes, alongside increased policy adoption. Pedagogical practices demonstrated positive associations with student satisfaction outcomes, while organisational elements exhibited comparatively weaker associations. The findings support a differentiated and prioritised approach to pedagogical policy enactment. The policy prioritisation and pedagogical integration (PPPI) model provides a staged framework for prioritising and operationalising pedagogical practices within HE curriculum design and QA processes. The study extends existing pedagogical policy literature beyond framework development towards implementation-oriented evaluation. It operationalises previously developed pedagogical policy guidelines through audit-based evaluation and examines associations between policy adoption and student satisfaction outcomes.

title: Zillow’s iBuying gamble: when algorithms meet reality
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to provide a decision focused teaching case that enables students to examine Zillow’s entry into iBuying, analyze the limitations of algorithmic forecasting under changing market conditions, and evaluate the strategic tradeoffs involved in scaling an AI driven business model. This case was developed exclusively from secondary sources falling into four categories: regulatory and corporate sources (Zillow Group, Opendoor Technologies and Offerpad Solutions quarterly shareholder letters and Form 8-K filings, FY 2020 through FY 2022; Rich Barton’s shareholder letters); contemporaneous journalistic sources (Bloomberg and CNBC); industry analytical sources (Mike DelPrete’s iBuyer market reports); and public methodology disclosures from Zillow Research providing the Zillow Home Value Index trajectory in Figure 2 and Table 2 (in case file) and the Zestimate accuracy data in Table 3 (in case file). All quantitative claims in the case body and Table 1 (in case file) were cross-referenced against the corresponding SEC filings, which were treated as authoritative when press accounts differed. The Q3 2021 home purchase figure of 9,680 corresponds to the Zillow Q3 2021 shareholder letter; an earlier figure of 3,805 (Q2 2021 purchases) was identified and corrected during case development. A review of published cases in major case repositories, including The Case Journal and SAGE Business Cases, located cases addressing Zillow’s broader business and the iBuying sector, but none that positions the algorithmic-pricing failure as a prospective strategic decision; this case differentiates itself by foregrounding model brittleness under distributional shift as its analytical core. No primary data collection was conducted, no information has been disguised and all named individuals appear in their public capacities. Ethics review board approval was not required. In October 2021, Rich Barton, co-founder and CEO of Zillow Group, faced a decision about the future of Zillow Offers, the company’s three-year-old algorithmic iBuying division. Internal data showed that Q3 2021 home acquisitions had reached 9,680, more than 2.5 times the Q2 volume of 3,805, while sales velocity, renovation capacity and pricing-model calibration had failed to keep pace. Inventory tripled in a single quarter to 9,790 homes. In Phoenix and Atlanta, the rapid home price appreciation that had supported the model’s unit economics was beginning to moderate. Barton had to decide whether to continue scaling, pause and recalibrate or pivot more fundamentally. The case is set at the inflection point in mid-October 2021, before the company’s October 18 pause and before the November 2 wind-down. Students are positioned inside the decision rather than evaluating it retrospectively. The Teaching Note epilogue summarizes the wind-down, the housing super app pivot and the 2022 outcomes for Opendoor, RedfinNow and Offerpad. This compact case is designed for upper-division undergraduates studying strategic management or technology strategy. This case is appropriate for upper-level undergraduate courses in Strategic Management (particularly modules on competitive advantage, digital strategy and strategic failure analysis) and for upper-level undergraduate courses in Management Information Systems or Technology and Innovation Management (particularly modules on algorithmic decision-making and AI deployment). The case may be adapted for MBA elective courses on strategy and technology with depth adjustments. It is appropriate for in-seat, hybrid and online modalities. It is not recommended without modification for introductory undergraduate courses, as it presupposes familiarity with basic competitive strategy and business model concepts and with elementary statistical reasoning.

title: VIPA: View-Invariant Projector-Based Adversarial Attack
abstract: Projector-based adversarial attack aims to physically manipulate real-world scenes by projecting adversarial patterns, thereby causing deep image classifiers to produce incorrect predictions. However, existing stealthy projector-based adversarial attack methods model the project-and-capture process in a single and static view, limiting their view-invariant capability and practical applicability in dynamic environments. In this paper, we introduce View-Invariant Projector-Based Adversarial Attack (VIPA), a novel method designed to overcome these limitations by achieving both view-invariant and classifier-agnostic adversarial attacks in the physical world. We first leverage a view-invariant projector-camera system simulation method to model the physical interactions between projected patterns and real-world surfaces. To ensure robustness and stealthiness of the attack across different views, VIPA optimizes adversarial projections by aggregating simulated attack losses from multiple views. This joint optimization across diverse views helps maintain robustness regardless of the viewpoints. Finally, the optimized patterns are physically projected into real-world scenes, where they successfully fool various classifiers from different viewpoints, thereby enabling robust and practical view-invariant adversarial attacks. Our experiments in both targeted and untargeted attacks demonstrate that VIPA consistently achieves higher attack success rates than existing methods, while also enhancing stealthiness and ensuring minimal perceptual degradation across all tested views.

title: Reciprocal associations between overparenting and nonsuicidal self-injury in Chinese adolescents: The roles of emotional granularity and self-differentiation.
abstract: Nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) is a prevalent public health problem among adolescents. Focusing on the Chinese cultural context, this study examines the reciprocal relationships between overparenting and NSSI, as well as the mechanisms that may account for this link. Participants were all Chinese adolescents (N = 419, 47.30% girls) with an average age of 13.49 years old (SD = 0.99), drawn from a three-wave longitudinal study with 1-year interval between each wave. A cross-lagged panel model was constructed to explore the bidirectional associations between overparenting and NSSI in adolescents, and a moderated mediation model was constructed to verify the mediating role of emotional granularity and the moderating role of self-differentiation. The key findings were as follows: (1) There were reciprocal cross-lagged effects between overparenting and NSSI among adolescents. (2) Overparenting not only directly predicted the occurrence of NSSI but also indirectly influenced it through the mediator of emotional granularity. (3) Self-differentiation moderated the effect of overparenting on emotional granularity. Findings highlight the significance of considering dynamic interrelations between distal and proximal factors for the adaptive development of adolescents.

title: Dual Constraints of Microbial Carbon Use Efficiency and Mineral Protection Govern Necromass Accrual
abstract: Increasing soil organic carbon (SOC), central to food security and climate mitigation, is increasingly recognized as being mediated by microbial necromass C (MNC) accrual. However, how microbial production and mineral preservation jointly govern MNC accrual under contrasting resource conditions remains unclear. Here, we analyzed soils from 14 long‐term fertilization experiments (up to 47 years) to assess how edaphic and climatic conditions regulate the response of MNC accrual to manure (M) and non‐manure (NM) fertilization treatments. We found that the primary constraints on MNC accrual varied with resource availability, with microbial production under resource‐limited conditions and mineral preservation under resource‐abundant conditions. Under resource‐limited conditions, M treatments increased MNC by up to 122%, with changes tightly coupled to SOC gains. This accrual was associated with increases in dissolved organic C and microbial C use efficiency, indicating a production‐constrained pathway in which manure inputs alleviate substrate limitation and promote microbial C allocation toward biomass production and necromass formation. Conversely, under resource‐abundant conditions, MNC responses to fertilization were weaker (+56%) and uncoupled from SOC gains. Instead, MNC accrual was primarily associated with mineral protection capacity (e.g., Fe and Al oxides), consistent with a preservation‐constrained pathway. Overall, microbial processing and mineral preservation represent context‐dependent constraints on MNC accrual under contrasting resource conditions. These findings underscore the importance of resource context for site‐specific C management and for understanding soil C dynamics under global change.

title: Climate‐Driven Oceanographic Changes Shape Larval Dispersal Success in the Southern Ocean
abstract: Although climate‐driven changes in ocean circulation are increasingly recognized as key drivers of marine ecosystem structure and dynamics, their consequences for the early life stages of deep‐sea fishes remain difficult to quantify. In the Southern Ocean, variability in frontal systems such as the Polar Front (PF) may influence larval dispersal and retention, with direct implications for recruitment. We investigated how interannual variability in ocean circulation and egg production shapes larval dispersal and retention in suitable recruitment areas of a large body size deep‐sea fish species, Patagonian toothfish ( Dissostichus eleginoides ), around the Kerguelen Plateau. We developed an integrated modeling framework which combined spatially explicit models of egg production with 24 years (2000–2023) of Lagrangian dispersal simulations driven by satellite‐derived geostrophic currents to quantify successful larval retention. Ontogenetic changes in distribution and fecundity were accounted for to model egg production, allowing retention metrics to reflect spatial heterogeneity in reproductive output. Larval retention rate in suitable recruitment areas varied from 9% to 28% over the study period. PF‐associated jet intensity was significantly associated with larval retention variability: years characterized by stronger PF‐associated circulation showed lower larval retention, with more larvae advected away from the shelf toward the eastern part of the plateau. The latter part of the time series, particularly after 2010, was characterized by stronger year‐to‐year fluctuations, a higher contribution of the North‐West recruitment area, and more frequent low‐retention years. Building on new findings on toothfish spawning dynamics and long‐term altimetry data, we showed for the first time that there is the potential for self‐recruitment in the northern part of the Kerguelen Plateau (French EEZ). We also discussed the implications for fishery management since PF‐associated indices may help interpret past recruitment trends and offer useful early‐warning for future recruitment anomalies.

title: Revealing the Widespread Bias of Extinction Risk in the Antarctic and the Southern Ocean
abstract: Accelerating environmental change in the Antarctic and Southern Ocean (ASO) necessitates robust extinction risk assessments to inform conservation priorities. Nevertheless, no systematic, region‐wide baseline of extinction risk currently exists for tracking ASO biodiversity responses to ongoing change, a significant barrier to global biodiversity monitoring. Here, we conducted the first ASO‐wide synthesis of current extinction risk knowledge for plants, animals and Fungi. This included examining biases in current assessments, the distribution of Threatened species and their associated threats. Using a data‐inclusive workflow, we compiled 8908 assessments representing 4970 species, more than doubling the number of ASO species assessed compared with any single source. As expected, assessments were heavily biased towards vertebrates (58% assessed), while invertebrates, despite their ecological prevalence, were markedly underrepresented (6% assessed). Among vertebrates, mammals had the highest proportion of Threatened species (26%). Birds within the ASO were disproportionately Threatened (25%) compared to the global average (11%), with the greatest threat for ASO species being ‘Biological Resource Use’. The sub‐Antarctic Islands had the highest density of both Threatened species and assessment effort, whereas many Antarctic species remain unassessed. Additionally, Threatened species have the lowest protected area coverage of any conservation status. These pronounced assessment biases highlight the need for more balanced, representative and data‐inclusive extinction risk assessments to be able to effectively detect conservation status change. This work represents an important step in ensuring ASO representation in global biodiversity monitoring frameworks, strengthening the capacity of these frameworks to detect, attribute and respond to future biodiversity changes.

title: When Drought Is Not Drought: How Metrics Bias Estimates of Ecosystem Water Limitation
abstract: Anthropogenic warming and shifts in global precipitation regimes are increasing rainfall variability and the frequency of intense precipitation events, raising uncertainty about how conventional meteorological drought indices capture ecosystem water limitation. This uncertainty arises from two key issues: temporal aggregation, as most meteorological drought indices are based on monthly integrated summaries, and drought definition, because atmospheric water deficits do not necessarily translate into vegetation water stress. Here, we quantified ecosystem gross primary productivity (GPP) responses to drought using three approaches: (1) monthly meteorological drought identified from monthly standardized precipitation evaporation index (SPEI), (2) daily meteorological drought defined by daily SPEI, and (3) ecological drought defined using an indicator of actual vegetation water limitation. Comparing monthly and daily SPEI‐based drought isolated the effects of temporal aggregation, while comparing daily meteorological and ecological droughts quantified the influence of drought definition. Across 130 eddy‐covariance sites spanning multiple biomes and climate zones, we analyzed 6691 drought months identified using monthly SPEI. Daily SPEI data revealed that within months classified as meteorological drought, nearly 50% of days did not coincide with atmospheric water deficits owing to daily rainfall variability. As a result, monthly SPEI overestimated GPP responses (20.60% ± 5.28% increase) relative to daily SPEI (4.61% ± 1.21% increase). In contrast, daily meteorological drought metrics underestimated drought‐induced suppression of GPP by ~46% compared with ecological drought, demonstrating that atmospheric drought metrics do not fully reflect water stress experienced by vegetation. Our results show that both temporal resolution and drought definition can bias estimates of ecosystem drought responses, underscoring the need for finer‐scale temporal and ecologically relevant measures of vegetation water limitation to improve understanding of biosphere–climate interactions in an increasingly drought‐prone world.

title: Compounding Human and Bioclimatic Factors Driving the Global Fire Crisis
abstract: Over millennia, social and ecological systems have been shaped by fire and have in turn shaped fire regimes. However, recent decades have seen an escalating “fire crisis” characterized by an increasing incidence of large, intense wildfires, most notably in forests. Voices in the academic literature and media often attribute the fire crisis to a narrow range of mechanisms, for example, fuel management or climate change. This failure to acknowledge the complexity of causes leads to simplistic framings of risk, and ultimately, proposed solutions that are either not feasible or may lead to undesired outcomes. In this review we outline the human and bioclimatic factors that are driving this fire crisis. Factors reviewed include the impacts of colonial legacies, which disrupted Indigenous land stewardship and traditional burning practices over centuries; policies of fire suppression; population growth, urbanization and land management practices; biotic disturbances such as insect outbreaks and invasive plant species; and climate change, which is affecting both fire regimes and social‐ecological resilience to fire. Many of these factors co‐occur leading to complex interactions and, often, unexpected outcomes. Our review highlights that climate change is now having a compounding effect, building on a multitude of other factors to drive the fire crisis. Addressing this crisis requires first acknowledging its complexity and moving beyond simple framings of risk. We suggest solutions will vary across different places and through time, but may include supporting Indigenous land stewardship, adopting flexible fire responses, shifting societal expectations from aggressive fire suppression to “living with fire”, and fostering resilient social and ecological communities.
