title: Comparative study of yield, purity, morphology, and LPS-induced cytokine responses of BMDMs and thioglycollate-elicited PEMs.
abstract: Mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM) and mouse peritoneal macrophages (PEMs) are the most commonly used primary cells in immunology studies. Direct and complete data for these models in the resting state are lacking. Cell yield, purity, and shape, and LPS-induced cytokine secretion profiles of BMDM and PEM under consistent experimental conditions. Femurs and tibias were removed from the same batch of C57BL/6 mice, and bone marrow was extracted. BMDMs were differentiated for 7 days with 20 ng/mL M-CSF. The mice were intraperitoneally given 3% sulfoglycolate medium, and PEMs were harvested 3 days later. Morphological changes of each type of cell were measured from day 0 until the mature state of resting. Cell yield was measured by hemocytometer and flow cytometry of F4/80+ CD11b+ double-positive cells. For functional comparison, mature macrophages were stimulated with LPS, and the secretion levels of IL-1β, IL-6, IL-12, IL-23, TNF-α, CCL5, CXCL9, and CXCL16 in culture supernatants were measured by ELISA at 6 h, 9 h, and 12 h post-stimulation. For their size and structure, mature BMDMs have an elongated spindle shape and connection. Mature PEMs are generally round or oval; some cells are polygonal after adhesion. The net yield ([2.41 ± 1.79] × 107/animal) and purity ([96.93 ± 0.53] %) were much higher than PEMs ([2.54 ± 0.15] × 106/animal, [71.18 ± 0.83] %), and they were statistically significant. The cell viability was higher than 93% for both cell types, with no difference between them. Upon LPS stimulation, PEMs secreted significantly higher levels of IL-1β and IL-6 at all measured time points and IL-23 (at 12 h) compared to BMDMs (P < 0.0001). BMDMs produced greater amounts of IL-12 (at 9 h and 12 h) and TNF-α (at all time points). For chemokines, CXCL16 was higher in PEMs at 9 h and in BMDMs at 12 h, while CXCL9 was elevated in BMDMs only at 12 h. CCL5 showed no significant difference between the two cell types at any time point. The rest of the BMDMs and PEMs differ very much in size, yield, and purity. They also exhibit distinct cytokine and chemokine response patterns upon LPS stimulation. In vitro modeling studies apply them in different ways. BMDMs are better suited for experiments with a large number of targets, and PEMs have shorter maturation cycles. The choice between the two models should consider both baseline characteristics and their distinct functional response profiles. Researchers should choose a cell model that best suits the experimental constraints.

title: Differentiation in ant-eating spiders based on offensive and defensive exploitation of ants
abstract: Ecological speciation via host-race has been documented in several herbivores and parasitoids. Analogous prey-race has recently been suggested to explain the diversity of specialised ant-eating spiders. Two sister species from the Iberian Peninsula, Zodarion alacre and Z. andalusiacum (Zodariidae), possess almost identical copulatory organs, but differ in body size and colouration. Zodarion spiders exploit different ant species offensively (as prey) and defensively (as mimetic models). Here we tested the hypothesis of prey-race diversification in these two species via offensive and defensive exploitation. We studied the diet of both species using metabarcoding, recorded their circadian activity in the field, investigated their mimetic similarity to ants, and modelled visual perception by potential predators. We found that both species feed on ants but Z. alacre hunted larger ant species than Z. andalusiacum. Their circadian activity was different too, with Z. alacre being active mainly during day while Z. andalusiacum mainly during night. Zodarion alacre appear to imitate Messor ants in movement, colouration, body shape, and size. Zodarion andalusiacum is similar to sand in colouration, moves less, and thus probably uses background matching. We conclude that divergent (offensive and defensive) exploitation of ants could have lead to diversification of the two ant-eating spiders.

title: Enter the Tomatrix: Model-Driven Ideotype Design for Dwarf Tomato in Vertical Farming
abstract: Artificial lighting accounts for most of the energy consumption in vertical farms, emphasizing the need for crops that use light efficiently. We aimed to develop and assess dwarf tomato ideotypes with architecture optimized for light absorption and carbon assimilation in vertical farming. A dynamic functional–structural plant model simulated canopy light absorption and carbon assimilation at planting densities of 35, 50, 65, and 80 plants m-2. We applied Morris sensitivity analysis to screen for influential traits, then Bayesian optimization to identify optimal trait combinations. Leaf angle, leaf curvature, and leaflet angle were the dominant architectural traits influencing canopy absorption of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) and carbon assimilation across all planting densities. In simulations, optimized ideotypes converged towards more erect leaves with moderate curvature, improving vertical light distribution, reducing photosynthetic saturation in upper leaves, and increasing light availability deeper in the canopy. Fruits affected the canopy light balance: by the end of the simulation at 80 plants m-2, they absorbed 16% (carbon assimilation ideotype) and 23% (reference architecture) of total absorbed PAR, making fruit shading a constraint on canopy carbon gain. Simulations showed that ideotypes optimized for carbon assimilation could achieve density-dependent yield improvements, with simulated fruit dry mass increasing by up to 12% at 80 plantsm-2, compared to 2% at 35 plantsm-2. The simulations suggest that coordinated adjustments in leaf orientation traits can increase yield in dense canopies, and that ideotypes should be designed and reported for specific planting densities. This two-step workflow provides a reproducible route for ideotype design and breeding for resource-use efficiency in controlled-environment agriculture.

title: Understanding the impact of co-occurring diseases on aerial hyperspectral detection: A UAS case study with grapevine leafroll virus and downy mildew.
abstract: Grapevine disease prevention and management challenges sustainable viticulture globally. Comprehensive vineyard monitoring is time- and labor-intensive, especially in regions where multiple pathogens regularly cause co-occurring infections. We used a visible-to-near-infrared (VNIR) imaging spectrometer mounted on an uncrewed aerial system (UAS) to monitor two New York State vineyards affected by grapevine downy mildew (GDM) and Grapevine Leafroll-associated Virus 3 (GLRaV-3). Four UAS datasets were collected during the 2024 growing season, accompanied by ground scouting, physiological measurements, and PCR diagnostics for a subset of vines. Partial least squares regression (PLSR) models detected GLRaV-3 symptoms with symptomatic-class F1 scores of 0.69-0.72 in August, and models differentiating GDM-only from GLRaV-3-only symptoms achieved accuracies of 0.55-0.82 after down-sampling. To test whether co-occurring GDM impacted accurate GLRaV-3 detection, we compared PLSR recall for GLRaV-3-only vines with recall for vines showing both GLRaV-3 and GDM symptoms. Across three datasets, recall differences (co-occurring minus GLRaV-3-only) were +0.4, +9.0, and -4.6 percentage points and all 95% confidence intervals included zero, suggesting that co-occurring GDM did not consistently reduce GLRaV-3 symptom classification accuracy. This study provides a direct, field-based evaluation of aerial imaging spectroscopy to detect co-occurring grapevine diseases in commercial vineyards. Our results suggest that UAS VNIR data can be informative amidst the biological complexity of ongoing operational agricultural systems. Early-season disease monitoring remains challenging, and larger representative studies are needed to better quantify co-occurrence effects on disease identification via aerial imaging spectroscopy.

title: Intrinsic noise reduces fluctuation frequencies in a cross-repressilator model motivated by stem cell differentiation.
abstract: The dynamical effects of intrinsic noise in gene regulatory networks (GRNs) can be significant when the number of molecules is low. In previous work, we proposed a new conceptual model, comprising a network of three transcription factors (TFs) that mutually inhibit each other (i.e. a 'cross-repressilator', also referred to as a 'toggle triad'), that offers a route to reconcile the direct fate restriction (DFR) and progressive fate restriction (PFR) hypotheses for stem cell fate choice. In the deterministic case, the cross-repressilator model generically displays three kinds of dynamics. Between the multipotent and fate-specified regimes there exists a third, initially unanticipated, intermediate oscillatory regime that provides a mechanism for environmental signals to influence fate choice. Here, we analyse in detail a stochastic version of the cross-repressilator model. Our findings reveal that, as the system size reduces, intrinsic noise systematically lowers the characteristic frequencies associated with fluctuations both in the multipotent state and in the oscillatory regime. Hence, while the cross-repressilator conceptual model points to a possible resolution of the DFR/PFR dichotomy, the effect of noise is to reduce the number of oscillatory cycles that would be present and thus to accelerate movement of the cell state towards differentiation during the fate specification process.
journal: Journal of the Royal Society, Interface

title: Differentiable emulation for high-dimensional Bayesian calibration of nuclear reaction models
Gentle push: Fine-tuning foundation models for complex oxide surface reconstructions
Housing finance and affordable housing delivery: evidence from Punjab, Pakistan
abstract: This study aims to evaluate the Punjab Affordable Housing Program (Apni Chhat Apna Ghar, ACAG) as a finance-enabled affordable housing initiative in Punjab, Pakistan, examining its operational performance, financial sustainability and inclusion across districts. This study analyses administrative data from all 36 districts of Punjab using descriptive statistics, operational performance indicators, Pearson correlation analysis, district rankings, exploratory ordinary least squares regression and k-means cluster analysis. The programme recorded 114,316 approved applications, 102,029 loan disbursements and 78,693 completed houses. Mean district disbursement, completion and recovery rates were 89.50%, 77.39% and 6.35%, respectively. Programme scale was strongly associated with approvals, disbursements and completions. Recovery performance was positively associated with disbursement efficiency and female participation but negatively associated with programme scale. The recovery model showed strong explanatory power, whereas completion outcomes were only weakly explained by district-level administrative variables, indicating that post-disbursement implementation factors influence housing completion. The analysis relies on district-level administrative data and cannot identify household-level causal relationships. Future research should incorporate household and implementation-level variables. The findings highlight the importance of strengthening post-disbursement support, repayment management and gender-responsive outreach while adopting differentiated district-level implementation strategies to improve programme performance and long-term financial sustainability. This study provides one of the first empirical district-level evaluations of a provincial finance-led affordable housing programme in Pakistan, offering evidence on how operational efficiency, financial recovery and inclusion interact to shape affordable housing delivery in the Global South.
journal: International Journal of Housing Markets and Analysis

title: Organisational capabilities, corporate sustainability and firm competitiveness of coffee enterprises in Vietnam's Central Highlands: co-creation in an international trade context
abstract: This study examines how marketing capability, digital capability, and supply chain capability influence corporate sustainability and firm competitiveness among coffee enterprises in Vietnam's Central Highlands. It also investigates the moderating role of co-creation in the relationship between corporate sustainability and firm competitiveness. Drawing on the Resource-Based View, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, Stakeholder Theory, and Service-Dominant Logic, the study analyses data from 236 coffee enterprises using SmartPLS 4 and PLS-SEM. Corporate sustainability is modelled as a higher-order construct including economic, social, and environmental dimensions. All hypotheses are supported. Marketing capability, digital capability, and supply chain capability positively affect corporate sustainability, with digital capability showing the strongest effect. Corporate sustainability strongly enhances firm competitiveness and mediates the effects of organisational capabilities on competitiveness. Co-creation also positively moderates the sustainability–competitiveness link. The study is limited by its cross-sectional design, self-reported data, and regional focus, which may constrain generalisability. However, it shows that competitiveness depends not only on internal capabilities but also on sustainability-oriented practices and stakeholder collaboration. This study integrates key organisational capabilities into a unified framework explaining how corporate sustainability enhances firm competitiveness in an export-oriented agricultural context. It also highlights the mediating role of sustainability and the moderating role of co-creation in strengthening sustainable competitiveness in an emerging economy.
journal: Journal of Agribusiness in Developing and Emerging Economies

title: Dynamic cortical connectivity underlying proprioceptive processing during NMES-induced hand movements: Insights from an acute deafferentation model.
abstract: OBJECTIVE Neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) is a promising modality for restoring sensory feedback in upper-limb prosthetics. However, the dynamic cortical mechanisms underlying the perception of NMES-evoked muscle contraction, particularly under conditions of sensory loss (e.g., amputation), remain poorly understood. This study investigates the time-varying effective connectivity of the sensorimotor cortex in response to NMES using the ischemic nerve block (INB) technology to model acute deafferentation. METHODS 64-channel EEG data were recorded from 11 able-bodied participants under a 2×2 factorial design involving INB states (before vs. block) and stimulation intensities (above vs. below motor threshold). The adaptive directed transfer function (ADTF) combined with graph theoretical analysis was employed to quantify dynamic causal interactions in the Beta band (15-30 Hz). RESULTS The NMES-evoked cortical response progressed through three stages with monotonically increasing network segregation and integration (PFDR ≤ 0.01 for all stage-wise comparisons). During the ischemic nerve block (INB), the clustering coefficient (CC) and global efficiency (Ge) decreased under above-threshold stimulation (cluster-level PFDR = 0.019 and PFDR = 0.013, respectively), whereas below-threshold stimulation elicited a transient CC increase (150-525 ms, PFDR = 0.019) followed by late Ge reductions. The differentiation of the network response between above and below motor-threshold stimulation was reconfigured rather than abolished during deafferentation. At the regional level, deafferentation attenuated contralateral somatosensory and ipsilateral motor driving, whereas ipsilateral somatosensory outflow was relatively enhanced. CONCLUSION NMES-evoked muscle contractions modulate the dynamics of sensorimotor networks by acute deafferentation. Acute deafferentation attenuates network integration and increases the relative contribution of the ipsilateral hemisphere. SIGNIFICANCE These electrophysiological markers may inform the design and evaluation of closed-loop sensory feedback for neuroprostheses.
journal: IEEE transactions on neural systems and rehabilitation engineering : a publication of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society

title: Physics-Driven Extraction of Dynamic Fluid Asset from Monocular Video with Generative 3DGS.
abstract: Existing methods for dynamic 3D scene synthesis from video rely on per-frame deformation fields optimized through pixel-level reconstruction losses. While effective for closed systems such as elastic solids, these approaches face challenges with open systems like fluids where material continuously enters and exits the scene, topology changes freely, and no stable point correspondence exists across frames. We propose a simulation-driven alternative that optimizes the parameters of a fluid simulator to reproduce dynamics observed in a single-view video, rather than fitting per-point deformation to pixel values. Our framework leverages generative 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models to obtain initial fluid geometry including unseen surfaces, estimates a physically grounded velocity field from surface motions with a physics-constraint correction algorithm, and converts it into a divergence-free, grid-based representation. A differentiable Affine Particle-In-Cell (APIC) simulation then optimizes effective simulation parameters, such as viscosity, boundary conditions, and inflow/outflow velocities, to match the observed dynamics. Because the dynamics are governed by forward simulation, the output assets are inherently editable, interactive, and temporally extendable, which reconstruction based approaches cannot readily provide. Stage-wise ablations confirm that each stage is necessary, and hyperparameter sweeps show the pipeline to be robust without sensitive per-scene tuning. Our method handles various liquid fluids, including inviscid and viscous types, demonstrating the potential for automatically creating simulation-ready 3D fluid assets from readily available internet videos.
journal: IEEE transactions on visualization and computer graphics

title: Integration of peripheral blood lymphocyte subsets and cytokines enhances prognostic stratification in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma.
abstract: Immune dysregulation is involved in multiple myeloma (MM) pathogenesis and progression yet current staging systems do not incorporate indicators of immune status. We retrospectively included 260 newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM) patients with baseline data of peripheral blood (PB) lymphocyte subsets and cytokines from Tianjin Medical University General Hospital. Through majority voting across seven survival prediction algorithms and subsequent Cox analysis, cluster of differentiation (CD)3+CD8+ T-cell absolute count and interleukin (IL-10) were identified as immune prognostic predictors to construct the immune risk score. A comprehensive prognostic nomogram was subsequently established by combining this score with high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities, serum calcium and serum lactate dehydrogenase. Shapley additive explanation analysis ranked the immune risk score as the leading contributor to the final model. The nomogram achieved a cross-validated 3-year time-dependent area under the curve for overall survival (OS) of 0.825. The model was further evaluated in a temporal validation cohort. In exploratory analyses within our cohort, the nomogram showed better prognostic performance than the established staging systems and further stratified outcomes among patients receiving anti-CD38 antibody-containing regimens. The model was deployed as an exploratory online calculator for convenience. These findings require independent external multicentre validation before implementation.

title: Resolving the Multiple Controls of Biomass Production Efficiency in Woody Plants
abstract: Plants assimilate carbon through photosynthesis to support biomass production (BP), autotrophic respiration ( R a ) and the synthesis of non‐structural compounds. Biomass production efficiency (BPE), the fraction of assimilated carbon allocated to BP, is one key factor influencing ecosystems' potential to store carbon. However, there is no consensus on the controls of BPE, and even the sign of its response to growth temperature is unclear. By means of statistical hypothesis testing using the largest observational dataset to date on annual BPE ( n = 514 records) from evergreen and deciduous woody plants, we confirm earlier findings that BPE declines with stand age and is greater in deciduous plants. However, we also show that BPE declines toward more organic, sandy, or alkaline soils and increases with climatic aridity, while declining with warmer growing seasons and increasing with warmer winters. Such a dual temperature response is consistent with additional carbon costs due to the need for cold‐hardening processes, and reconciles contradictory published reports of both positive and negative effects of temperature on BPE. Notably, our analysis provides novel evidence that BPE is significantly higher in species associated with arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi than in those associated with ectomycorrhizal (EcM) fungi and mixed EcM–AM associations. Our analysis explains the observed BPE patterns better than dynamic global vegetation models (DGVMs) from the TRENDY (Trends and Drivers of the Regional‐Scale Terrestrial Sources and Sinks of Carbon Dioxide) project, which show a weaker correspondence with observations. In particular, our model captures reduced BPE in boreal regions, consistent with the predominance of ectomycorrhizal (EcM) species there. This study advances understanding of the global controls of BPE, and suggests a route toward the improved representation of plant growth in vegetation and land surface models.

title: Embracing the Heterogeneity Within Particulate and Mineral‐Associated Organic Matter for the Next Generation of Soil Carbon Questions
abstract: Soil organic matter (SOM) is a complex and dynamic substrate central to the functioning of terrestrial ecosystems. Because of its heterogeneity, SOM is routinely parsed into physical fractions with more uniform composition and behavior. Over the last several years, particulate (POM) and mineral‐associated (MAOM) organic matter have become the most widely adopted of these fractions, which has given the field a shared, comparable framework for resolving the first‐order heterogeneity within SOM. As fractionation has become routine, however, it has become clear that POM and MAOM identity alone cannot resolve the finer, second‐order variation that additional mechanistic inference requires. This is in part because the fractions are operationally defined composites, whose properties vary across composition, formation pathway, and behavior. Conceptualizing them as the terminal state of analysis collapses each fraction to its central tendency, flattening the distribution and obscuring the structure on which more complex questions depend. Here we propose embracing this within‐fraction heterogeneity rather than averaging over it, treating POM and MAOM as composite distributions whose internal structure underlies the variation in how they form, persist, and function. We suggest that this view can be operationalized via two complementary approaches: tailoring fractionation methods to target subpopulations most relevant to a question, and pairing fractions with orthogonal measurements. Together, these resolve the within‐fraction distribution that bulk measurements integrate over, narrowing the analysis onto the most explanatory slice of the bulk SOM. Similar to the original framework, we do not aim to prescribe a certain methodology, but rather a way of thinking about heterogeneity within SOM, in which a separation is justified by the understanding it produces rather than the data it generates. This way of reasoning allows POM and MAOM to continue linking organic matter to its functions, and in doing so supports more informed stewardship of soil carbon.

title: Forecast Evaluation for Functional Data
abstract: This paper proposes methods for comparing the accuracy of two competing sets of functional forecasts. This is increasingly relevant as many economic and financial forecasters are interested in predicting variables which are observed as functional data objects. However, to date there has been very little research on formal statistical tests to evaluate the relative accuracy of competing functional forecasts. We propose a suite of novel tests, building on the classic Diebold‐Mariano test, to provide formal statistical guidance on forecast accuracy in the case of functional data. We derive the asymptotic properties of the tests, including their self‐normalised versions, and demonstrate the validity of analytic or bootstrap‐based critical values. We investigate the finite sample performance of the tests using Monte Carlo simulations. We illustrate the use of our method by comparing forecasts of the U.S. yield curve based on forward rates with a random walk benchmark.

title: Hybrid temporal learning for contact-resistance forecasting of AgSnO₂/Cu contacts under DC endurance testing
abstract: Contact resistance does not follow a monotonic trajectory during repeated switching because arc erosion, surface-film breakdown, material transfer, melting, and resolidification act at the same time. We formulate near-term contact-resistance prediction as a temporal forecasting task using 96,433 complete switching records from an FD-12# AgSnO2/Cu contact pair tested under a 36 V, 10A resistive DC load, together with sparsely sampled surface morphology. Each forecast uses the preceding 300 operations to estimate the mean resistance over the next 200 operations. A Random Forest represents statistical descriptors of recent electrical history, while a temporal convolutional network (TCN) learns from the raw multivariate sequence. The two estimates are combined using the weight selected on validation data. On the chronological test set, the RF-TCN ensemble yields R² = 0.5261, MAE = 0.1614 mΩ, and RMSE = 0.2141 mΩ, compared with R² = 0.4399 for the history-mean baseline and lower performance for either individual branch. The ensemble retains R² = 0.5771 on 28 fully disjoint 500-operation windows. Moving-block bootstrap analysis gives an ensemble-versus-Random-Forest ΔR² of 0.0487 with a 95% interval of [0.0148, 0.0843]. Sparse morphology is kept as auxiliary state information rather than as the primary predictor: direct concatenation reduces generalization, whereas low-weight late fusion provides only a small correction. For this dataset, dense electrical history provides the main information for local resistance forecasting, while the results also show the limitations of fusing low-rate morphology with cycle-level data.
journal: International Conference on Communication, Sensing, and Intelligent Computing (CSIC 2026)

title: Optical monitoring-oriented simulation of agricultural ecosystems using an extended Lotka-Volterra model
abstract: This paper presents an optical-monitoring-oriented mathematical framework for simulating interactions in agricultural ecosystems using an extended Lotka-Volterra model. The framework introduces carrying capacity, prescribed seasonal forcing, chemical inputs, and selected interspecies interactions. Its state variables and time-varying forcing terms establish a mechanistic representation compatible with agricultural optical-monitoring workflows, in which imagederived vegetation indices and crop-condition estimates may be mapped to crop-state variables and scenario descriptors. The system is solved numerically with the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method to examine qualitative trajectory changes under different scenario settings. The simulations illustrate periodic fluctuations and the sensitivity of system trajectories to seasonal and chemical inputs. The framework links optical agricultural monitoring concepts with ecosystem-dynamics analysis and supports the interpretation of crop-condition information within mechanistic simulation.
journal: International Conference on Communication, Sensing, and Intelligent Computing (CSIC 2026)

title: Oxygen fugacity, temperature, and pressure of Siberian eclogitic diamonds: Implications for the Archaean convecting mantle redox state
abstract: Kimberlite-borne eclogite xenoliths ultimately derive from ancient subducted oceanic crust. Some specimens still record the chemical and redox conditions of their igneous protoliths, allowing a view into contemporaneous convecting mantle sources. However, accurate reconstructions are limited because eclogites have been exposed to metasomatism in the subcontinental mantle for billions of years. Here, we investigated garnet and clinopyroxene inclusions, both touching and nontouching pairs, in 19 eclogitic diamonds from the Siberian craton, hence shielded from post-entrapment overprint. Inclusion compositions indicate average sampling depths of 180 to 280 km, temperatures of 1030° to 1540°C (±60°C), and redox conditions, for most of the samples, oxidized enough for diamonds to have originated from water(carbonate)-rich fluids. The reconstructed bulk composition points to basaltic oceanic crust formed from an Archaean convecting mantle region that was more oxygen-depleted than today, providing compelling evidence of redox heterogeneities in the source rocks of ancient oceanic crust.

title: Defining epidemiologically relevant units of cholera transmission in sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Much remains unknown about cholera transmission dynamics in Africa. Applying both traditional phylogeographic techniques and innovative methods for combining epidemiologic and genomic data, we identified three to four distinct “cholera transmission units” within which cross-border cholera transmission has been more frequent. These units can be grouped into two major transmission clusters, one in Western Africa and bordering countries and one spanning the Central, Eastern, and Southern regions. Simulation studies show that these clusters can be used to assess the risk of international spread of introduced cholera strains and identify heterogeneities in the speed of international spread based on outbreak location. Our methods further allow us to infer cholera incidence attributable to specific lineages in the absence of sequencing data. This work has clear implications for cholera control.

title: Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars
abstract: Mars is reputed to lack ongoing volcanic activity. However, marsquakes were revealed recently, and clues to volcanism younger than tens of million years have accumulated. While sulfur dioxide, so far undetected, could testify to ongoing eruptive activity, evidence of active magma chambers may be better identified by seepage of halogen gases, such as hydrogen chloride (HCl). Observations by Atmospheric Chemistry Suite led to the widespread observations of HCl at part-per-billion levels in the atmosphere of Mars during the warm perihelion period, attributed to aerosol-atmospheric sources. Here, we report HCl detections during the cold aphelion season that are isolated in the Alba Mons region. We also identify fresh and narrow (<1 meter) fissures in this area, which we interpret to be potential HCl pathways rooted into magmatic bodies at depth. Our results are best explained by ongoing igneous processes in the Martian interior.

title: METTL3-mediated m 6 A modification of DNMT1 enhances ovarian cancer progression
abstract: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC), the most lethal subtype of ovarian cancer, is often diagnosed at advanced stages and remains associated with poor clinical outcome. In this study, we identify a critical oncogenic role of the RNA methyltransferase METTL3 and the N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) RNA modification pathway in HGSOC. Suppression of METTL3, either genetically or pharmacologically, and depletion of its binding partner METTL14 impair ovarian cancer proliferation and tumor progression. Mechanistically, we show that METTL3-mediated m 6 A deposition enhances the translation of DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1), the primary maintenance DNA methyltransferase responsible for preserving genome-wide methylation patterns and silencing tumor suppressor genes. Pharmacological inhibition of DNMT1 induces widespread DNA hypomethylation and up-regulation of the tumor suppressors TNFAIP3 and FBXO32. Consistently, METTL3 suppression reduces DNMT1 abundance and derepresses TNFAIP3 and FBXO32 expression. Knockdown and rescue studies further reveal that DNMT1 primarily mediates METTL3-dependent regulation of cell migration, whereas the antiproliferative effects of METTL3 suppression are likely driven by additional downstream targets. Collectively, these findings identify the m 6 A-METTL3-DNMT1 axis as a mechanistic link between RNA and DNA methylation pathways and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in HGSOC.

title: Stony coral symbioses show variable responses to future ocean conditions
abstract: Coral reefs support over a quarter of marine species and nearly a billion people worldwide but are also among the ecosystems most threatened by anthropogenic impacts. There is long-standing debate about whether coral symbioses will be disrupted or respond adaptively under future ocean conditions. Using a factorial 2.5-year future-ocean mesocosm experiment across eight coral species representing the major coral lineages, we tracked symbiont community shifts within replicate fragments from the same individual coral. Some corals exhibited stochastic divergence, whereas others showed deterministic shifts in symbiont community composition. Heat stress generally reduced symbiont diversity and promoted predictable restructuring, consistent with deterministic adaptation to moderate thermal stress but stochastic accumulation of diversity under extreme conditions. We propose that adaptive and stochastic responses represent endpoints along a continuum of host-orchestrated symbiont sorting. This study bridges coral reef ecology with broader host-microbiome theory, offering an integrated perspective on how symbiotic systems may respond to environmental change.

title: A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease progression
abstract: Identifying the neurobiological basis of cognitive vulnerability is essential for preventing Alzheimer’s disease (AD). We derived the Alzheimer’s Resilience-Vulnerability Connectome (ARC) by contrasting SuperAgers (SA), an extreme phenotype of preserved late-life memory, with AD using resting-state fMRI. ARC distinguished SA from AD in a discovery cohort ( N = 290; AUC = 0.85) and replicated independently ( N = 143), involving prefrontal, temporal, and insular networks and associating with brain age. Applied to cognitively unimpaired adults (discovery: N = 818; replication: N = 497), ARC-based subtyping revealed SA-like and AD-like subgroups with comparable baseline cognition but divergent longitudinal trajectories. AD-like individuals exhibited faster cognitive decline, greater amyloid-β accumulation, and higher AD conversion risk. Exploratory GWAS nominated CLYBL and FRMD6 as candidate novel loci associated with the subtype difference. These findings suggest that ARC captures a continuous connectomic dimension of cognitive aging spanning SA, cognitively typical aging, and AD, highlighting the potential of functional connectomic variation for early risk stratification in AD.

title: Local translational program at the muscle-tendon junction endows domain identity in muscle syncytia
abstract: How cells establish specialized subdomains is a fundamental question in cell and tissue biology. Skeletal muscle fibers, among the largest cells in the body, are multinucleated and form distinct regions such as the neuromuscular and myotendinous junctions (MTJs), the latter forming a critical interface between muscle and tendon that transmits contractile force. While transcriptional heterogeneity among myonuclei has been described, whether local translation contributes to domain identity remains unknown, largely due to the lack of tools for domain-specific manipulation. Here, we introduce MTJ-AAV, a viral system that enables selective genetic targeting of MTJ myonuclei. This approach allowed MTJ-specific ribosome tagging and revealed extensive translational regulation underlying MTJ biology and its remodeling during exercise. Untranslated regions of these transcripts were sufficient to control regionalized translation. Notably, the Krüpper-like factor–family transcription factors emerged as translationally up-regulated targets at the MTJ, where they drive local gene expression. Our findings establish local translation as a key layer of subcellular specialization and provide a versatile toolkit for dissecting spatial molecular regulation within muscle syncytia.

title: Clinically derived micro- and nanoplastic uptake drives spatiotemporally confined metabolic stress revealed by bond-selective imaging
abstract: Although microplastics and nanoplastics (MPs/NPs) are pervasive environmental contaminants, our understanding of cellular toxicity remains incomplete, as adverse effects are often attributed to long-term intracellular accumulation, while the spatiotemporal onset of cellular damage remains poorly defined. Here, we use chemical bond–selective stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy and cell models that decouple continuous exposure from intracellular retention to directly visualize clinically derived MP/NP-cell interactions. Cellular stress occurs primarily during MP/NP exposure, accompanied by alterations in lipid droplet (LD) composition. In contrast, following extracellular removal, intracellularly retained MP/NP become largely inert, with recovery of lipid metabolism and cellular functions. Lipidomics identifies arachidonic acid (AA) as a key dysregulated metabolite, and SRS imaging further reveals transient, spatially confined AA enrichment in MP/NP–proximal LDs during uptake. Phospholipid coating of MP/NP attenuates LD alterations and cytotoxicity while preserving particle internalization, establishing uptake-driven metabolic stress, rather than long-term intracellular retention, as a primary source of MP/NP–induced damage.

title: Persistent bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters over 800,000 years
abstract: The stability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major uncertainty in projections of future climate. However, direct evidence for AMOC tipping behavior on orbital timescales remains scarce. Here, we reconstruct the strength of Iceland-Scotland Overflow Water, a key lower branch of the deep Atlantic circulation, over the past 800,000 years by combining 12 current-speed records from North Atlantic sediment cores with a data-driven hybrid model. The resulting reconstruction reveals persistent alternation between weak (glacial) and strong (interglacial) circulation modes, pervasive millennial-scale variability within both regimes, and systematic asymmetry between weak-to-strong recoveries and strong-to-weak collapses. Threshold and phase-space analyses show that regime shifts occur within a narrow window of atmospheric carbon dioxide and sea level and often follow hysteresis-like loops. Although bistability persists throughout the last 800,000 years, its sensitivity and timing evolve through time. These findings provide long-term, high-resolution, data-driven constraints on the bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters and its implications for AMOC resilience in a warming world.

title: On-going retinal neuronal degeneration despite clinical stability in glaucoma
abstract: Glaucoma, a leading cause of irreversible blindness, involves progressive retinal ganglion cell loss. Early detection of this neurodegeneration is critical, yet current clinical methods often identify disease only after substantial damage has occurred. This preliminary study used high-resolution adaptive optics–optical coherence tomography (AO-OCT) to track individual retinal ganglion cells in patients and healthy volunteers over 3 to 5 years. Results revealed higher neurodegeneration in glaucoma compared to normal aging. We observed 4.16 to 6.86% annual decrease in cell density in glaucoma, far exceeding the 0.27% cell loss rate observed in the healthy volunteer group. Critically, AO-OCT detected progression significantly earlier, identifying cell loss 0.74 years before conventional OCT and 1.49 years before visual field testing. These findings demonstrate AO-OCT as a more sensitive tool capable of monitoring glaucomatous damage with superior precision, potentially representing a major advancement over current clinical imaging.

title: Oxygen-mediated projection microstereolithography for sub–100-μm zirconia dental veneers
abstract: High-resolution vat photopolymerization of ceramics is constrained by light scattering, which broadens cured features, and by shallow penetration, which limits interlayer bonding. This trade-off is particularly damaging for microscale structures such as no-preparation dental veneers. We introduce an oxygen-mediated projection microstereolithography strategy in which an oxygen-permeable release film creates an interfacial inhibition field in high-solid–loading zirconia slurry. Rather than uniformly reducing curing, oxygen preferentially filters low-dose scattered light at pattern edges while preserving curing in the projected core. This anisotropic inhibition reshapes the accuracy-depth trade-off, enabling optimized multilayer printing of thin-wall zirconia. The process enabled reproducible fabrication of ∼80-micrometer zirconia veneers with high trueness, improved marginal adaptation, and handling-related strength comparable to substantially thicker milled veneers. The approach provides the potential for minimally invasive dental restoration and a general strategy for high-resolution additive manufacturing of strongly scattering ceramic suspensions.

title: BCLAF1 links RNA splicing to ATF4-dependent metabolic adaptation in acute myeloid leukemia
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is driven by genetic alterations and non-mutational mechanisms that disrupt normal hematopoiesis and support leukemic cell survival. While the mutational landscape of AML is well characterized, the non-genetic processes sustaining leukemic maintenance remain less understood. Using human AML cells and murine models, we identify BCL2-associated transcription factor 1 (BCLAF1) as a key regulator of leukemic progression through control of mRNA processing. BCLAF1 physically associates with core spliceosome components and regulates alternative splicing programs in leukemic cells. Mechanistically, BCLAF1 is required for productive splicing of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) mRNA, thereby sustaining ATF4 protein levels and downstream metabolic gene expression programs. Loss of BCLAF1 reduces ATF4 levels, leading to impaired de novo amino acid biosynthesis and increased sensitivity to venetoclax. Together, these findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism linking RNA splicing control to metabolic adaptation in AML, identifying BCLAF1 as a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

title: Hoxa10 governs lifelong skeletal stem cell maintenance and bone repair
abstract: Skeletal stem and progenitor cells (SSPCs) sustain bone homeostasis and regeneration throughout life, yet the transcriptional programs that preserve their identity remain poorly defined. Here we identify the distal Hox gene Hoxa10 as a cell-autonomous regulator of skeletal stem cell maintenance. Using inducible genetic deletion, lineage tracing, single-cell transcriptomics, and injury models, we show that loss of Hoxa10 leads to progressive depletion of SSPCs, impaired bone regeneration, and defective matrix organization. Mechanistically, Hoxa10 maintains the undifferentiated state of skeletal stem cells by restraining premature osteogenic, adipogenic, and chondrogenic commitment, while promoting collagen III production and collagen fiber alignment within regenerative niches. Hoxa10 -dependent regulation of extracellular matrix composition is restricted to primitive progenitors and is uncoupled from osteoblast differentiation. Notably, transient depletion of distal Hox genes in primary human SSPCs recapitulates the murine defects in proliferation, self-renewal, and differentiation restraint. Together, these findings define a conserved Hox-dependent program that preserves skeletal stem cell identity and regenerative competence, revealing how developmental transcription factors are repurposed to sustain the adult skeleton across the life span.

title: Ultrasound neural interface enabling acute spinal cord monitoring and blood flow modulation
abstract: The days following decompression surgery for acute spinal cord injury (SCI) are a critical period for postoperative monitoring. After wound closure, clinicians lack on-demand access to local spinal cord morphology and hemodynamics, and care therefore remains guided largely by systemic surrogates rather than direct postoperative insight into the injured cord. We present the Multimodal Ultrasound System for Injury Care (MUSIC), a temporary epidural ultrasound neural interface placed during standard decompression surgery to enable postoperative brightness-mode imaging, Doppler-derived hemodynamic monitoring, and future device-integrated ultrasound actuation. Across simulations, benchtop, human cadaveric, and porcine studies, MUSIC enabled on-demand visualization of cord structure, hematoma tracking, detection and longitudinal tracking of localized Doppler flow signatures attributable to the sulcal artery region, and, in healthy pigs, proof-of-concept focused ultrasound modulation of blood-flow velocity. MUSIC establishes a temporary postoperative acoustic interface that provides spinal cord information to inform monitoring, future management, and localized intervention strategies after SCI.

title: Common transcriptional changes in the brain during hibernation and Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Hibernation demands rapid brain adaptations, involving cycles of reduced metabolic rate during torpor, followed by brief periods of arousal. Previous studies show hibernation induces a drastic increase in Tau hyperphosphorylation, but a mechanistic connection to disease remains unclear. Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing on hippocampi of golden hamsters, we unveil large transcriptional shifts across the hibernation cycle in all cell types, especially glia. Common transcriptional changes in mitochondrial and ribosomal genes are observed in all different cell types. In addition, hibernation triggers an inflammatory-like response in microglia that in part resembles cell states observed in Alzheimer’s disease, but here in the absence of Aβ-accumulation and neurodegeneration. These findings reveal brain transformations that might help preserve vital functions under extreme conditions and they suggest that early cellular changes in AD may be a natural adaptive process.

title: Genetic dissection of cell type–specific congenital heart disease variants reveals ETS1 control of vascular smooth muscle cell fate
abstract: Numerous congenital heart disease (CHD) risk variants lie in cis-regulatory elements, yet the impact of variants in repressed and bivalent chromatin on cell type–specific heart development is unclear. Here, we generated a single-cell multiomic atlas of human cardiac differentiation by jointly profiling H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and transcriptomes in individual cells, classifying cis-regulatory elements into six chromatin states, enabling prioritization of 610 CHD-associated noncoding variants enriched in lineage- and state-specific regulatory elements, including repressive and bivalent regions. CRISPR knockin of selected variants perturbed nearby gene expression and impaired cardiac differentiation. Dissection of a Polycomb-marked variant near ETS1 (ETS proto-oncogene 1) revealed local H3K27me3 loss, H3K27ac gain, and ETS1 up-regulation, which redirects differentiation toward second-heart-field progenitors with epithelial characteristics at early stages and, ultimately, highly migratory ETS1 + vascular smooth muscle cells. Together, our work establishes a single-cell chromatin-state framework for interpreting noncoding CHD risk variants and uncovers an ETS1-driven program linking Polycomb-deregulated noncoding variation to aberrant vascular smooth muscle fate commitment during human cardiogenesis.

title: Unveiling the underlying spin mechanism in quasi-2D perovskite spin-polarized lasing
abstract: Spin-polarized lasers hold great potential in integrated photonic devices for secure communication, optical interconnections, and advanced optical devices, offering excellent properties superior to those of conventional lasers. Quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) perovskites are promising candidates for spin-polarized lasers, because their potential structural inversion asymmetry will result in strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC) facilitating spin injection and hence spin splitting of electronic bands. However, strong SOC involves a trade-off between spin injection and spin lifetimes. How to prolong spin lifetimes in the lasing regime while maintaining the optical gain make it challenging to sustain spin polarization for lasing. Here, we unveil the underlying spin mechanism and successfully realize quasi-2D perovskite spin-polarized lasing by suppressing fast spin relaxation through triplet exciton regulation using organic cations of phenylethylammonium (PEA) and 1-naphthylmethylamine (NMA). We identify the Bir-Aronov-Pikus (BAP) mechanism is the dominant spin relaxation mechanism preventing the achievement of spin-polarized lasing in quasi-2D perovskites. By modulating the reverse intersystem crossing of triplet excitons, the D’yakonov-Perel’ (DP) mechanism becomes to play a key role and results in a new-emerged prolonged spin lifetime of 35.4 ps at 77 K, which is ∼5 times that of the BAP-induced one. Consequently, spin-polarized lasing is realized below 200 K, and the threshold is 30.2% lower than that for linearly polarized excitation. This work underscores the potential of PEA-based quasi-2D perovskites in spin-polarized lasing and contributes to the rapid advancements in perovskite spintronic devices.

title: Self-charged toothbrush facilitates tooth healthcare maintenance
abstract: Toothbrushes have undergone no substantive improvements beyond their mechanical function for about 1118 years to date. Conventional toothbrushes often fail to establish an antibacterial environment on the tooth surface, allowing bacteria to recover and recolonize. Here, we developed an innovative self-charged toothbrush that integrates daily tooth brushing with piezoelectric functionality, synergizing both optimal mechanical properties and stable electrical activity. The self-charged toothbrushes can generate reactive oxygen species to disrupt bacterial membrane integrity and diminish bacterial adhesion by combining static antibacterial inhibition through surface potential with dynamic piezoelectric stimulation. Clinical evaluation revealed that the localized piezoelectric stimulation of self-charged toothbrushes can mitigate plaque formation and gingival inflammation. Mechanistic studies further revealed that the self-charged toothbrushes induced oxidative damage to the oral pathogenic bacterial membranes, thereby impairing the ATP-binding cassette transporter pathway. Hence, this study developed a concept of piezoelectric PVDF toothbrushes that combine physical cleaning with sustained antibacterial effect, thus highlighting the potential of self-charged materials in advancing oral healthcare.

title: Thermalization of quantum light induced by classical nonlinear wave dynamics
abstract: Thermalization of isolated quantum systems is an intriguing phenomenon at the forefront of contemporary physics. In this work, we demonstrate that nonlinear multimode optical platforms can be harnessed to induce effective quantum interactions between photons. Through numerical experiments, we reveal the thermalization of quantum light, specifically single- and two-photon states, propagating alongside classical light within multimode nonlinear optical systems. This thermalization is clearly manifested by the emergence of Rayleigh-Jeans and Boltzmann statistical distributions. Beyond providing a deeper understanding of how classical nonlinearities can be used to investigate quantum many-body dynamics, our findings enable the exploration of a broader range of complex quantum phenomena, including aspects of quantum phase transitions, within readily accessible classical optical settings.

title: N 6-methyladenosine–dependent ARv7 translation couples lactate metabolism with enzalutamide resistance in prostate cancer
abstract: Enzalutamide (Enz)–resistant prostate cancer (PCa) is a lethal disease that affects a broad population of elderly men. Experimental and clinical evidence has demonstrated that androgen receptor variant 7 (ARv7) plays a critical role in Enz-resistant (EnzR) PCa by functioning as a constitutively active transcription factor driving disease progression. However, the predictive value of the ARv7 transcript has not been fully recognized due to its low frequency in castration-resistant PCa. In this study, we identified ARv7 mRNA as an N 6-methyladenosine (m 6 A)–modified transcript. Enz treatment increases METTL3-dependent m 6 A methylation of ARv7 mRNA at the A1177 site, which is subsequently recognized by the reader protein YTHDC2, leading to enhanced translation efficiency of ARv7. Furthermore, EnzR PCa exhibited elevated lactate metabolism, which regulated AR transcription through promoter-mediated epigenetic modifications at H3K9 and H3K14. Reactivated AR exhibited enhanced phase separation to transcriptionally up-regulate YTHDC2 expression. In vivo experiments demonstrated that targeting the METTL3-YTHDC2-ARv7 axis represents a promising therapeutic strategy to suppress EnzR PCa progression. Moreover, the METTL3 inhibitor STM2457 synergized with Enz to inhibit tumor growth without observable toxicity. Collectively, our findings suggest that the clinical utility of ARv7 may need to be reconsidered in light of its m 6 A-dependent translational regulation.

title: Toxic mercury, aquatic ecosystem collapse, and the ancient Lowland Maya
abstract: Environmental impacts endured by the Lowland Maya during the Classic Period (250 to 920 CE) included droughts, deforestation, and soil erosion. Recent studies on mercury (Hg) pollution and cyanotoxins suggest that degraded water quality was also a stressor for the Pre-Columbian Maya. Hg in the Maya region is related to use of both elemental mercury and mineral cinnabar (HgS), the latter used as a red pigment. Questions, however, remain concerning the toxicity of Hg or the consequences of prehistoric Hg exposure on ecosystem and human health. Here, we show that Classic Period Hg concentrations in sediment cores from two lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula exceeded modern sediment Hg toxicity thresholds by orders of magnitude for centuries during ancient Maya occupation. Sediments also have evidence of aquatic food web collapse (algae, bacteria, cyanobacteria, ostracods, snails, and nonbiting midges), coincident with the time of high Hg concentrations, confirming that Hg toxicity was an additional environmental stressor for Classic Maya populations.

title: A disynaptic trigeminal circuit for the transformation and integration of oral chemesthesis in male mice
abstract: Chemesthesis, encompassing oral sensations such as spiciness and coolness, is an important yet incompletely understood component of mammalian chemical sensing. Unlike taste or olfaction, these sensations are conveyed primarily through trigeminal pathways; however, how modality-specific peripheral signals are processed and transformed along central ascending pathways remains poorly understood. Herein, we delineate the structural and functional organization of an ascending trigeminal-brainstem-parabrachial circuit that mediates oral chemesthetic processing in male mice. Using viral tracing, in vivo calcium imaging, and chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations, we identify a genetically defined disynaptic glutamatergic pathway (trigeminal ganglion → spinal trigeminal nucleus caudalis → lateral parabrachial nucleus) that is both necessary and sufficient for capsaicin- and menthol-evoked defensive behaviors. Although peripheral TRPV1 + and TRPM8 + neurons retain a degree of modality bias, we observe substantial convergence of spicy and cooling signals within the spinal trigeminal nucleus, followed by sustained and synchronized population activity in vglut2 + neurons of the external lateral parabrachial nucleus. This hierarchical transformation from peripheral segregation to central integration reveals the organizational principle by which distinct chemesthetic modalities are progressively integrated along a trigeminal-mediated ascending pathway, providing a circuit-level framework for understanding how chemical stimuli are processed and coordinated to drive defensive behaviors.

title: Independent origin of genomic imprinting in placental fish
abstract: Genomic imprinting results in biased expression of one parental allele. Such non-Mendelian expression occurs in angiosperms and placental mammals, which share having an active paternal genome during maternal offspring provisioning. It is hypothesized that imprinting modulates conflict between maternal control of resource allocation and paternal control of resource acquisition. If true, then imprinting should evolve in any organism that evolves a placenta. Here, we demonstrate genomic imprinting in a placental poeciliid fish, Poeciliopsis prolifica . Using transcriptomes from reciprocal crosses between two inbred strains, we identified 84 protein-coding genes with robust evidence of imprinting in P. prolifica placenta. These include the teleost ortholog of mammalian imprinted gene, grb10 , and a pair of adjacent genes, dpp4 and gcga , with opposing effects on glucose metabolism that are oppositely imprinted in a fashion that potentially resolves parental conflict. Significantly elevated allelic DNA methylation on the promoters of two focal imprinted genes suggests epigenetic mechanisms of imprinting similar to those in mammals. We also discovered the convergent recruitment of a gene network associated with nutrient transport in mammals. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of genomic imprinting in a non-mammalian vertebrate and supports the potential role of imprinting in resolving parental conflict.

title: Cytoplasmic crowding drives intracellular viscoelastic increase during epithelial maturation
abstract: The cytoplasm is a crowded, active medium whose mechanical properties underpin essential cellular functions, yet how intracellular rheology adapts during tissue maturation remains unclear. Here, we examine the evolution of cytoplasmic viscoelasticity in Madin-Darby canine kidney epithelial monolayers as cell density increases. Using magnetic rotational spectroscopy, an active microrheology technique, we quantify zero-shear viscosity and elastic modulus throughout monolayer maturation. We uncover a substantial enhancement of intracellular viscoelasticity correlated with increasing cell density and a concomitant rise in cellular dry mass concentration. Hyperosmotic perturbations on subconfluent monolayers reproduce this effect, confirming cytoplasmic crowding as a driver of rheological changes. Notably, intracellular viscoelasticity scales linearly with dry mass concentration, suggesting a direct coupling between internal mechanics and cytoplasmic concentration during epithelial maturation. These findings establish a link between tissue-level organization and intracellular mechanics, highlighting cytoplasmic crowding as a regulator of epithelial homeostasis and providing a framework to connect rheology with tissue behavior.

title: IFNAR1 stabilization sustains CD8 + T cell persistence in IFN-high colorectal cancer liver metastases
abstract: Colorectal cancer liver metastases (CRC-LMs) are associated with poor survival and frequently resist immunotherapy, yet the mechanisms underlying this immune refractoriness remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify a tumor-intrinsic type I interferon (IFN-I)–high state in CRC-LMs associated with loss of the IFN-α/β receptor subunit 1 (IFNAR1) on effector T lymphocytes within immune-enriched perimetastatic niches. Reduced IFNAR1 expression stratifies patients with poor clinical outcomes. Transcriptional profiling of patient-derived organoids and complementary preclinical models revealed heterogeneous but recurrent tumor-derived IFN-I production in CRC-LMs. In IFN-I high contexts, sustained signaling promoted IFNAR1 internalization on effector CD8 + T cells, impairing their persistence, survival, and effector function. Pharmacologic or genetic stabilization of IFNAR1 on cell surface restored CD8 + T cell fitness and selectively enhanced T cell receptor– and chimeric antigen receptor–based immunotherapies in IFN-I high tumors. These findings define a context-dependent IFN-I high / IFNAR1 low axis that constrains antitumor immunity in CRC-LMs and identify IFNAR1 stabilization as a strategy to convert chronic IFN signaling from a suppressive barrier into a therapeutic vulnerability.

title: Pancreatic α cells function as MHC class II–dependent antigen-presenting cells in type 1 diabetes
abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease characterized by T cell–mediated destruction of pancreatic β cells, in which antigen presentation is essential. Although professional antigen-presenting cells initiate autoreactive T cell responses, whether endocrine cells contribute to antigen presentation within inflamed islets remains unclear. Here, we show that pancreatic α cells acquire major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II (MHC-II)–dependent antigen-presenting capacity during T1D progression. Reanalysis of single-cell RNA sequencing datasets from nonobese diabetic (NOD) mice and human T1D islets revealed progressive up-regulation of MHC-II associated genes in α cells. Immunostaining validated the increased of MHC-II level both in NOD mice and patients with T1D. Mechanistically, inflammatory cytokines activated the Janus kinase–signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT) pathway in α cells, leading to JAK-STAT–dependent MHC-II induction. Functionally, activated α cells internalized, processed, and presented exogenous antigens, acquired expression of costimulatory molecules, and promoted antigen-specific CD4 + T cell activation. These findings identify pancreatic α cells as nonprofessional antigen-presenting cells and expand the current understanding of antigen presentation in autoimmune diabetes.

title: Rapid, voxel-based 3D printing with yield-stress fluid inks
abstract: Despite decades of progress, 3D printing still presents trade-offs in what materials can be printed and at what resolutions, speeds, and part volumes. We introduce direct ink additive lithography, or DIAL, to alleviate these trade-offs when printing with yield-stress, complex fluid inks used to print functional materials. DIAL combines translational photopatterning with ink sheet deposition for rapid, voxel-based 3D printing. Using model DIAL inks with kilopascal-scale yield stresses, we evaluate how ink rheology influences printing and compare DIAL against digital light processing (DLP) and direct ink writing (DIW). Since DIAL enables fast, high-throughput, support-free, and large-area printing, we showcase its broad potential for producing functional materials by printing multiscale architected, multimaterial, structural electrolyte, and hydrogel structures that are difficult if not impossible to 3D print today.

title: A biofilm-derived peptide as an underwater adhesive
abstract: Wet adhesives that perform under water have broad applications in industrial and biomedical settings. To date, molecular designs for underwater adhesives have largely been inspired by marine animals including mussels and barnacles. Here, we propose bacterial biofilms as an alternative source of inspiration for underwater adhesives. Specifically, we demonstrate the application potential of a peptide derived from biofilms formed by the notorious pathogen Vibrio cholerae . We characterize the ability of this biofilm-derived peptide to adsorb onto various surfaces and to glue wet surfaces by using a combination of confocal microscopy, molecular dynamics simulations, atomic force microscopy, lap shear tests, and spectroscopic tools. We further show that the peptide can coaggregate with microspheres acting as an effective flocculant. Our results open new design possibilities for underwater adhesives inspired by natural biofilms.

title: A high robustness decoding technique for ultrasound modulated electroencephalogram
abstract: Ultrasound-modulated electroencephalography (USMEEG) has become a vital tool in neuroscience because it integrates millimeter-level spatial resolution with millisecond-level temporal resolution. However, under extremely complex scenarios, excessively strong or weak acoustoelectric signal coupling leads to severe distortion in USMEEG decoded signals. To address this, we developed a highly robust decoding algorithm based on the ultrasound pulse repetition frequency and introduced the acoustoelectric modulation ratio (AMR) to quantify different modulation scenarios. Across numerical simulations, phantoms, and validation using human steady-state visual evoked potential signals with data-level acoustoelectric coupling across 10 volunteers, the focused ultrasound phased array achieved an encoding spatial resolution of 0.79 millimeters. The proposed algorithm significantly outperformed four traditional methods, exhibiting higher precision under weak modulation (0 < AMR ≤ 0.6), moderate modulation (0.6 < AMR ≤ 1), and over modulation (AMR > 1) conditions, with average decoding correlations reaching 0.84, 0.90, and 0.89. This highly robust technique expands USMEEG applications and provides a technical foundation for high-performance noninvasive brain-computer interfaces.

title: Effector-triggered stomatal immunity prevents leaf invasion by bacterial pathogens
abstract: The phytopathogen Pseudomonas syringae must enter the leaf interior through natural openings such as stomata to cause disease. Plants restrict pathogen entry into the leaf through non–self-recognition–driven stomatal closure. P. syringae counters this stomatal immunity by deploying a range of toxins and effectors. Here, we show that stomatal immunity in Arabidopsis thaliana is reinforced upon recognition of the ubiquitous P. syringae type III effector AvrE1 by the resistance protein CAR1. CAR1 expression is enriched in guard cells, and its activation prolongs the effective duration of stomatal immunity. We also show that CAR1 prevents the invasion of leaf tissue by natural isolates of P. syringae , demonstrating that stomatal immunity provides a broadly significant barrier to host accessibility by P. syringae that carry the conserved effector AvrE1.

title: Dynamic redox reactivation of platinum sites for long-term glycolate electrosynthesis from polyethylene terephthalate wastes
abstract: Glycolates are indispensable in the health, chemical and pharmaceutical industries, whereas their mainstream production involve toxic chemicals and harsh operating condition. An alternative route for glycolate production is electrifying ethylene glycol (EG) that originates from polyethylene terephthalate (PET) but suffers from poor durability of active platinum site that tend to deactivate. Herein, we demonstrate a dynamic redox reactivation strategy, which alternates between working potential for oxidizing EG to glycolate and nonworking potential for reviving active platinum sites by the chemical reduction of adsorbed EG, realizing an unprecedented stability for over 3000 hours under average current density of ∼220 milliamperes per square centimeter. Upscaling this approach, the assembled electrolyzer drives a record current of 10 amperes at 1.18 volts for repeatable 40 batches of glycolates electrosynthesis, with each batch converting 48.0 grams of PET to 11.6 grams of glycolates (52.8% yield), 37.7 grams of p -phthalic acid (95.8% yield), 248.7 grams of NaHSO 4 (95.2% yield) and ∼11.5 liters of hydrogen, showcasing a considerable revenue of ∼$1072 per ton glycolate.

title: Massively parallel self-assembly of suspendable microcompartments for functional cell screening
abstract: Modern biology increasingly demands platforms that can compartmentalize and analyze single cells and cell-cell interactions at massive scale, yet existing compartmentalization strategies based on microfluidics suffer from critical limitations. Emerging lab-on-a-particle technologies such as nanovials enable anchored single cells or small groups of cells to be isolated and assayed in a fully suspendable and parallelized manner using standard instrumentation, although their open architectures can result in loss of growing or un-attached cells. Here, we introduce capped nanovials: self-assembling hydrogel compartments formed by docking spherical capping particles into bowl-shaped nanovials. We routinely achieve capping of >80% of all nanovials in a sample and >90% sorting yield by flow cytometry, making the capped nanovial system well-suited for preparing and running large-scale assays. Furthermore, we demonstrate stable clonal expansion of single mammalian, yeast, and bacterial cells; growth-based selections of >10,000 colonies; enhanced signal-to-noise in secretion assays; and high-purity selection of antibody-secreting cells based on activation of co-encapsulated T cell reporters (>30-fold signal, up to 100% selection purity). By combining the simplicity of a well plate with the functional precision of droplet microfluidics without requiring oil or custom instrumentation, capped nanovials realize accessible, high-throughput, and high-resolution experimentation.

title: Human carotid plaque risk imaging using multiparametric photoacoustic and ultrasound fusion (hCAPRI)
abstract: Assessing the risk of carotid plaque rupture remains limited because current imaging methods cannot provide both plaque composition and structural information in real time. Here, we present human carotid plaque risk imaging (hCAPRI), a multiparametric photoacoustic and ultrasound (PA/US) fusion method for real-time carotid plaque assessment. hCAPRI combines PA imaging for detecting intraplaque hemorrhage (IPH) with US imaging for evaluating the plaque structure. PA imaging measured IPH size and methemoglobin content, while US imaging assessed stenosis severity, calcification, and plaque thickness. Combining these PA/US parameters, we compute an hCAPRI score. In 171 carotid arteries (CAs) from 120 patients, hCAPRI revealed the relationships among the PA/US parameters. In 36 CAs validated with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), hCAPRI showed high agreement with MRI. The hCAPRI score achieved 89% sensitivity and 84% specificity for high-risk plaque classification. hCAPRI offers a low-cost, real-time, and contrast-free approach for carotid plaque risk imaging.

title: Lighting up necrotic neurons from traumatic brain injury with magnetic quantum dots to decode the cellular origin of MRI
abstract: The diagnosis of traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains heavily constrained by the limitations of conventional imaging techniques in visualizing the pathological events that determine the disease progression and outcome. To address this clinical challenge, we report a manganese-doped near-infrared quantum dot (QD) to intrinsically integrate the highly sensitive optical imaging with clinical compatible magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Taking the advantages of optical imaging powered by whole-brain clearing and cellular resolution three-dimensional (3D) panoptic imaging, in combination with the systematic in vitro cell studies on different types of cells involved in TBI, we disclosed the interpretable pathology reflected by TBI imaging through the highly sensitive fluorescence of magnetic QDs, i.e., after systemic administration, the nanoprobes were extravasated through the compromised blood-brain barrier and then selectively phagocytosed by activated microglia, which subsequently migrated into the regions rich in dead neurons and neuronal debris. This microglia-mediated tropism decodes the signal origin of MRI enhanced by the nanometer-sized contrast agent, thereby transforming the MRI from an anatomical tool into a pathological reporter. A biocompatible Fe 3 O 4 nanoparticle of similar size was also compared with the magnetic QD mentioned above for validating the translational merits of nanoparticles in MRI diagnosis of TBI.

title: Mechano-electrochemical energy harvesting and self-powered sensing via dynamic liquid metal–electrolyte interfaces
abstract: Wearable devices, stretchable sensors, and soft electronics benefit from harvesting ambient energy using compliant materials, yet existing approaches often face limitations in power density, scalability, and electrode adaptability. Here, we report a liquid metal mechano-electrochemical energy harvester (LMMEEH) that converts mechanical stimuli into electricity through dynamically regulated electrode-electrolyte interfaces. Mechanical motion changes the interfacial area and drives asymmetric Faradaic reactions associated with dynamic oxide formation and dissolution, generating electrical output. The fluidity, high surface tension, and self-renewing surface chemistry of liquid metals enable rapid interfacial reformation, large reversible deformation, and stable cyclic operation. The device achieves a power density of 140.2 microwatts per square meter and scales to a 40-unit array producing 2 volts. Spatial and temporal programming of the liquid metal interfaces further enables synchronized three-phase alternating-current generation. We demonstrate wave-driven emergency lighting, self-powered pressure sensing, and real-time physiological monitoring. This work establishes dynamic liquid metal electrochemical interfaces as a scalable strategy for soft mechanical energy harvesting and self-powered electronics.

title: Rapid activation kinetics of the NLR Swordholder underpin nonhost resistance to Phytophthora capsici in Nicotiana tabacum
abstract: Nonhost resistance (NHR) represents a durable phenomenon where plants resist nonadapted pathogens. While NHR holds substantial potential for engineering crops with broad-spectrum and durable resistance, its underlying molecular mechanism remains incompletely understood. The oomycete pathogen Phytophthora capsici is nonadapted to Nicotiana tabacum (Nt) but is virulent on the closely related Nicotiana benthamiana (Nb). Here, we demonstrated that both species encode the NLR Swordholder (Swh), which recognizes P. capsici AvrNt effector proteins. NtSwh restores NHR in ntswh mutants, whereas NbSwh confers only partial resistance. Mechanistically, NtSwh exhibits weaker autoinhibition mediated by its amino-terminal extension domains, enabling rapid immune signaling that prevent pathogen effector–mediated suppression; NbSwh’s stronger autoinhibition delays activation, permitting effector suppression. Heterologous expression of NtSwh in tomato enhances field resistance to P. capsici without yield penalty. These findings indicate that the kinetics of NLR can play a key role in defining NHR, in addition to the presence or absence of specific NLRs, providing insights into strategies for breeding durable crop immunity.

title: Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe, stratigraphic integrity, and confirming early inland dispersal: Evaluating peopling of the Americas modeling
abstract: Statistical models shape debates over the timing and geography of the initial peopling of the Americas, but their value depends on testing their assumptions against archaeological evidence. We examine the Apparent Stratigraphic Integrity Index (ASI), used to infer postdepositional mixing at Late Pleistocene sites and support a relatively late occupation of temperate North America. ASI describes vertical discontinuity in binned artifact-frequency profiles; it does not directly measure artifact movement or stratigraphic integrity. At Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe, Idaho, the 5-centimeter absolute-elevation bins used to calculate ASI do not reflect the actual stratigraphic positions of artifacts across the irregular LU2 surface on which LU3 loess accumulated. The resulting ASI value cannot support claims of large-scale vertical mixing. Independent chronological, stratigraphic, pedogenic, archaeological, and excavation evidence supports the integrity of the ∼16,000–calibrated-years-before-the-present occupation. Cooper’s Ferry/Nipéhe provides early inland evidence expected under coastal-migration models, showing that models should be evaluated against archaeological evidence rather than used to override it.

title: Direct regulation of a tRNA modification enzyme by ppGpp links stress signaling to translational control and biofilm development
abstract: Transfer RNA (tRNA) modifications influence decoding efficiency and translational fidelity, yet how they are integrated into bacterial signaling networks remains poorly understood. Here, we identify a direct connection between stress signaling and codon-specific translational regulation. We show that the alarmone guanosine tetraphosphate (ppGpp) directly inhibits MnmE (TrmE), a conserved tRNA-modification GTPase required for methylaminomethyl (mnm) modification of wobble uridine. High-resolution ribosome profiling in Bacillus subtilis revealed that loss of MnmE selectively increases ribosome pausing at AAG codons and reprograms translation of a subset of genes, including small open reading frames. Among these is a previously unrecognized AAG-containing leader peptide that controls expression of the biofilm repressor AbrB. Consistent with this mechanism, mnmE mutants exhibit constitutive extracellular matrix production and bypass the biofilm defect of a relA mutant. Together, these findings establish a pathway linking ppGpp signaling, tRNA modification, codon-specific translation, and multicellular development.
