title: Accumulated radicals by GHz femtosecond burst drive one-step superhydrophobic conversion
abstract: Short-lived radicals usually decay before they can drive long-range reactions, making laser-induced radical chain reactions difficult to sustain. Here, we used GHz femtosecond bursts to temporally couple excitation events, allowing reactive intermediates from preceding subpulses to remain available for subsequent reactions and favoring their transient accumulation relative to isolated-pulse excitation. Consistent with this temporally coupled process, the methylphenyl silicone resin/graphene/CuFe 2 O 4 /SiO 2 composite coating exhibits a threshold-like nonlinear wettability transition near 430 subpulses. Compared with the microsecond-spaced single-pulse femtosecond regime, the sub-nanosecond GHz burst produces more extensive chemical conversion, enabling one-step bond reorganization and phase transformation and yielding a low-adhesion superhydrophobic surface with a contact angle of 161° ± 0.7° without posttreatment. Pulse-timing–controlled radical-mediated chemistry thus provides a time-domain strategy for ultrafast materials synthesis.

title: Edge-Native Agentic AI for Scalable Knowledge Systems in Industrial Applications
abstract: Large-scale foundation models and language models provide strong general-purpose reasoning and generation capabilities, but enterprise deployment introduces additional system-level constraints beyond model accuracy. In domains such as healthcare, robotics-based automation, finance, data is heterogeneous, high-dimensional, temporally evolving, and tightly coupled with domain-specific policies and compliance constraints. Decision workflows are high-stakes and require consistency, privacy-preserving, and context-aware reasoning. Furthermore, these environments demand continuous personalization over longitudinal data and real-time contextual signals. We propose and deployed a unified edge-native agentic cognitive AI infrastructure (rolled out for digital health, in process for other use cases) that integrates locality-aware execution, dynamic context construction, and governance-aware reasoning to enable scalable, personalized, and compliant enterprise AI systems and introduce adaptive execution directly into the inference pipeline.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Building Production LLM Agents: An Evaluation-Driven Playbook
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are moving rapidly from demos to production, but the methodology for getting them there reliably remains fragmented: architecture, observability, evaluation, and online measurement are usually taught and built in isolation. This half-day tutorial presents a practical playbook for building, evaluating, and deploying LLM agents in high-stakes production settings like healthcare and finance. We cover modular context engineering, user simulation, tool and knowledge design, and - as the centerpiece - rigorous evaluation and harness optimization: calibrated LLM-as-a-judge pipelines, inter-rater reliability, and automated judge-prompt optimization, culminating in offline-online correlation that lets teams predict production impact before shipping. Principles are grounded in two regulated, high-stakes domains: customer support in finance and agentic AI in healthcare. Attendees leave with reusable recipes, evaluation code patterns, and a clear mental model connecting offline development to online outcomes. No production experience is required.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Artificial Intelligence for Data Engineering and Management Of Networked Systems (AI4DEMONS)
abstract: Modern networked systems generate massive volumes of heterogeneous and continuously evolving data, creating major challenges for data management, intelligent analysis, and cybersecurity. Traditional machine learning approaches often struggle to adapt to the scale, decentralization, and dynamic nature of contemporary network environments, motivating the need for adaptive, distributed, and knowledge-driven AI solutions. This workshop explores recent advances in AI-driven network intelligence and cybersecurity, with a particular focus on information and knowledge management techniques for distributed systems. Topics include Generative AI (GenAI) for synthetic network data generation and augmentation, Large Language Models (LLMs) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) for cybersecurity intelligence and threat analysis, continual and federated learning for privacy-preserving adaptive systems, adversarial learning and trustworthy AI, and agentic AI for autonomous and human-in-the-loop security workflows. The workshop also investigates retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), knowledge graphs, reasoning over structured and unstructured security data, intelligent orchestration, and scalable AI-enabled network analytics. By bringing together researchers and practitioners from AI, cybersecurity, networking, and knowledge management, the workshop aims to foster interdisciplinary discussion on resilient, intelligent, and trustworthy networked systems.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: VERIMEDIA: The second International Workshop on Media Verification and Integrity
abstract: The rapid growth of generative multimodal processing and dissemination technologies has enabled the creation of an unprecedented amount of realistic synthetic media. As a result, methods for assessing the integrity and authenticity of digital media play a crucial role across scientific, industrial, and societal contexts, as the realism of altered digital content continues to challenge forensic models. In this context, multimedia forensic systems must address factors such as social media preprocessing, heterogeneous data sources, distribution shifts, adversarial perturbations, and the trustworthiness of information, as well as disinformation detection. These conditions underscore the challenges of deploying digital content integrity tools that remain effective, robust, and explainable. Therefore, this workshop will highlight research advancements in multimedia forensics, deepfake detection, adversarial machine learning, and AI-generated media attribution. Particular focus will be on the deployment of autonomous AI agents for media verification, as well as lifelong media authentication, a forward-looking perspective on AI's role in safeguarding media integrity. The workshop gathers interdisciplinary contributions that advance the foundations and practice of robust and trustworthy multimedia forensics across different modalities, such as images, text, and audio, encouraging research that challenges existing assumptions and proposes forward-looking solutions across multimedia analysis.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: GenAI4SG: Generative AI for Social Good and Vulnerable Populations
abstract: Generative AI has become a general-purpose technology for producing text, images, code, and explanations across knowledge-intensive tasks. This opens new opportunities for social good in domains where expertise, data, and resources are scarce: rare diseases, low-resource education, accessibility, crisis response, and information integrity. Yet large-scale deployment also carries risks that fall hardest on disadvantaged communities, including hallucination, bias, privacy leakage, and high environmental cost. GenAI4SG brings together researchers working on retrieval-augmented generation, agentic systems, multimodal models, and knowledge-grounded AI to study how these technologies can be responsibly designed, evaluated, and deployed for social good, in line with the UN Sustainable Development Goals. We welcome technical, empirical, resource, demo, and position papers on methods, systems, datasets, benchmarks, and applications.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: HyperMind: Claim Resolution and Reputation Tracking for Trustworthy Multi-Agent LLM Aggregation
abstract: The quality of knowledge produced by multi-agent generative AI systems depends not on the capability of individual agents but on the reliability of the communication layer between them. When agents disagree, that reliability is entirely invisible: no outcome is recorded, no agent is accountable, and the system learns nothing. This paper presents HyperMind, a protocol that makes disagreements productive by treating each resolved dispute as a verifiable calibration event, through three co-designed components: a seven-state Claim Resolution Finite State Machine (FSM) issuing signed provenance receipts; a Beta reputation system updated exclusively from FSM-verified outcomes; and DiversityGuard, which detects and interrupts premature consensus. On a 100-question enterprise benchmark spanning five domains, HyperMind achieves the lowest Brier score on all four tested LLMs; paired-difference 95% BCa confidence intervals exclude zero on two models (Gemma-4-26B [+ 0.0321,+ 0.0913], Wilcoxon p=0.0005, surviving Bonferroni correction across four models; Qwen-3.6-35B [+ 0.0021,+ 0.0737], p=0.037, not correction-surviving), though the n=100 evaluation is underpowered for the remaining two models (5-6% power). The full run costs \0.005 per 100 questions, and every resolved claim produces an auditable chain of custody over agent reliability.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Agentic Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Evidence from Clinical Time-Series Explanation
abstract: Continuous physiological monitoring is central to emergency care, yet building trustworthy, clinically usable AI remains challenging. While LLMs translate complex physiological signals into natural-language clinical narratives, it remains unclear whether agentic reasoning frameworks improve the quality of explanations over zero-shot inference. We present Vivaldi, a role-structured multi-agent system for explaining multivariate physiological time series in emergency department settings. We evaluate through a controlled clinical pilot involving a small cohort of emergency medicine experts. Their assessments challenge the assumption that increasingly complex agentic reasoning uniformly improves performance. Our experiments show agentic pipelines substantially benefit non-reasoning and medically fine-tuned models, improving expert-rated explanation justification and relevance by +6.9 and +9.7 points, respectively. Contrarily, for reasoning models, agentic orchestration often degrades explanation quality, including a 14-point drop in relevance, while improving diagnostic precision (ESI F1 +3.6). We also find explicit tool-based computation is decisive for codifiable clinical metrics, whereas subjective targets, such as pain scores and length of stay, show limited or inconsistent changes. Expert evaluation indicates gains in clinical utility depend on visualization conventions, with medically specialized models achieving favorable trade-offs between utility and clarity. Together, these findings show that the value of agentic AI lies in the selective externalization of computation and structure rather than in maximal reasoning complexity, highlighting concrete design trade-offs that are broadly applicable to explainable AI in safety-critical healthcare settings.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Semantic Boundary: A Framework and Benchmark for Policy-Constrained Semantic Disclosure
abstract: Privacy-preserving AI systems must determine what information crosses from trusted collection contexts into downstream analytics, observability, evaluation, and agentic workflows. Existing approaches such as redaction, tokenization, and sanitized rewriting primarily limit disclosure by transforming surface representations. However, modern AI systems depend on feedback loops over operational traces (e.g., conversations, tool use, logs, and reports), and aggressive suppression can remove the semantic information they need for debugging, monitoring, evaluation, and learning. This challenge is particularly acute for longitudinal behavioural traces: interaction routines and inferred intent can function as identifying signatures even after explicit identifiers have been removed. Privacy and utility are therefore coupled through the semantic information that remains available after privacy-preserving transformations have been applied. We introduce Semantic Boundary, a framework for reasoning about what meaning may cross system boundaries under explicit disclosure policies and downstream purposes. Under this framework, sensitive inputs are transformed into policy-governed exports with transformation provenance before release to a downstream consumer. To evaluate alternative disclosure strategies, we construct the Semantic Boundary Benchmark (SBB), a counterfactual export-lattice benchmark over synthetic behavioural traces with injected sensitive attributes, quasi-identifiers, latent behavioural patterns, analytical tasks, and provenance targets. We find that risk-constrained selection on this lattice varies by registered purpose and linkage tolerance: surface-token suppression can coexist with persona re-linking; different tasks favour different lattice conditions; and forcing one condition across consumers incurs measurable utility regret. SBB makes these purpose-conditioned comparisons measurable and reproducible.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: LexSkill: A Systematic Chinese Legal Skill Framework with High-Quality Annotations and an Execution Harness
abstract: Agents in knowledge-intensive domains require not only knowledge retrieval, but also the skills to effectively use retrieved knowledge. Since domain knowledge is often highly complex, agents must possess strong reasoning capabilities in order to perform tasks effectively. In the legal domain, different legal systems exhibit substantial differences, and the reasoning logic for applying legal knowledge varies significantly across systems. Meanwhile, existing skill collections lack a systematic skill framework grounded in domain knowledge, limiting their scalability and extensibility. To address these challenges, we present LexSkill, a reasoning-oriented legal skill library for the Chinese legal system. Within this framework, legal experts construct 36 atomic skills, further organized into 180 sub-atomic skills and 2 compound skills. Since legal problem solving also requires grounded access to legal resources and coordinated reasoning across multiple steps, we further introduce Chinese-Law-Harness, which augments the skill library with MCP modules built over a case repository and a statutory repository, and incorporates a multi-agent system for skill orchestration and execution. Evaluations on existing legal AI benchmarks show that leveraging the skill library through the proposed harness significantly outperforms direct problem solving without structured support, verifying the effectiveness of our skills and harness.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Neuro-symbolic Recommender Systems
abstract: Recommender systems are a fundamental component of modern digital platforms, guiding how users discover information, products, services, and media content. Recent advances in deep learning have substantially improved recommendation performance. However, state-of-the-art approaches rely on black-box models whose limited interpretability and transparency hinder insight into their decision-making. This doctoral research investigates how symbolic methods can be integrated into neural recommender systems to improve interpretability while maintaining competitive recommendation performance. To this end, we study three complementary neuro-symbolic paradigms: (i) a hybrid model based on the cognitive architecture ACT-R; (ii) a differentiable fuzzy-logic network that learns rules describing user behavior for news recommendation; (iii) a relational transformer over knowledge-enhanced interaction graphs that enables cross-domain few-shot recommendation with feature-level attribution through in-context graph sampling. Preliminary results show that these paradigms achieve competitive accuracy while providing interpretable recommendations and transparent decision logic, highlighting the potential of neuro-symbolic paradigms as a foundation for more explainable and trustworthy recommender systems.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Sensing How Users Adapt to AI Decision Support: A Multimodal Eye and Mouse Tracking Study
abstract: AI decision-support systems that present data and explanations are now used in repeated, day-to-day work. Most studies, however, evaluate these systems from a single session and report static outcomes such as trust, reliance, and accuracy. My doctoral research asks a different question. How do users change the way they read and act on an AI system as they gain experience, and what does this mean for how such systems should present information and explanations? I treat this change as something to measure from behavior rather than from self-report, using eye and mouse tracking recorded at the same time. In a study where 14 users each completed three sessions of an AI-assisted forecasting task, two changes appeared together. The link between gaze and cursor position became weaker, which shows that visual attention became more independent of hand movement. Visual scanning also moved from a focal mode to an ambient mode. When I separated the two parts of this second change, it came almost entirely from longer eye movements, while the time spent on each fixation showed no reliable change. In short, users learned where to look, with no sign that they read each point faster. The largest change occurred over the panel that showed the model explanation. These early results support a thesis that uses behavioral sensing to evaluate and design AI systems that serve users from the first session through long-term use. They also point to a longer-term aim. Because users show consistent patterns in how they direct and reallocate attention, capturing these patterns is a first step toward transferring task expertise to less experienced users and, in time, to AI agents.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Knowledge-Driven Recommendations in Decentralized Systems: Integrating Federated Personal Data and Public Contexts
abstract: Modern recommendation systems force a critical trade-off between user data sovereignty and algorithmic personalization, while decentralized alternatives often struggle with data sparsity and reactive interventions that fail during high-volatility events, like decentralized finance liquidations. This doctoral research outlines a comprehensive framework that bridges sovereignty-preserving collaborative learning with predictive risk management. By fusing private personal knowledge graphs with public contextual data through computationally efficient retrieval-augmented generation and federated learning, the system generates highly tailored recommendations without exposing raw user data. Concurrently, it develops proactive, agentic architectures utilizing Survival Analysis and the physics of self-organized criticality to forecast individual time-to-event risks and systemic network fragility. By integrating these macroscopic and microscopic topological signals, the framework empowers automated agents to dynamically shift from yield-maximizing recommendations to minimally invasive, protective interventions, safeguarding users against cascading failures in decentralized ecosystems.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: SoilCast: An Interactive Machine-Learning System for Forecasting Soil Health under Climate and Management Scenarios
abstract: We present SoilCast, an interactive machine-learning system for real-time exploration of long-term soil health outcomes under alternative climate and agricultural management scenarios across Europe. SoilCast replaces computationally expensive process-based environmental simulations with pretrained surrogate models learned from more than 15 million simulator-generated samples. The system employs CatBoost-based state-transition emulators that predict changes in soil organic carbon, soil nitrogen, and crop productivity over successive 20-year periods, enabling recursive multi-step forecasts through 2100. To support reliable scenario analysis, SoilCast visualizes uncertainty intervals derived from empirical rollout errors on held-out spatial test regions, capturing the accumulation of forecast error over time. The application demonstrates how scalable surrogate modeling can transform complex scientific simulators into responsive decision-support systems for sustainable land management.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Real-Time Adaptive Tour Recommendation with Agentic AI
abstract: Tour-recommendation systems, including the recent wave of LLM-based travel planners, typically stop at plan generation: given a user request, they produce a single itinerary and stop. Once the trip starts, however, tourists are left to handle disruptions such as rain, growing queues, transit breakdowns, or user fatigue. We present AdaptTour, an agentic system that continues replanning after departure; its contribution is the overall control architecture. Mid-trip signals (weather, queue length, transit disruption, user fatigue, and free-text feedback) are fused into a single context snapshot, typed triggers pass through a debounced registry, and a replanner locks the executed prefix and re-optimises the tail, re-enforcing every constraint at each pass: money budget, accessibility, per-member vetoes and boosts, and carbon preference. The LLM is used only to score candidates, with a deterministic fallback for omitted candidates, and to generate the rationale presented to the traveller; selection, sequencing, routing, and constraint checking remain deterministic. Weather is live, while crowd, transit, and fatigue are simulated for the demonstration and explicitly labelled as such in the interface. The system provides a curated five-city catalogue of POIs (Singapore, Melbourne, London, New York, Paris), per-city fare tables, five travel modes, and OSRM-routed map polylines cached on disk for offline-capable visualisation. Source code, tests, and JSONL scenario traces are publicly available to support reproduction.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Learn to Compress or Compress to Learn? Shannon and Turing meet again in the LLM era
abstract: The year 1948 gave birth to two transformative pillars of modern computing: Claude Shannon's information theory, which gave rise to data compression, and Alan Turing's writings on intelligent machinery, which ignited the field of artificial intelligence. Today, nearly eight decades later, we are witnessing a profound hybridization of these once-distinct fields. As we push to efficiently store, process, and retrieve massive datasets across diverse data types, users, devices, and systems — from vector and graph databases to cutting-edge agentic memories — AI and compression can no longer operate in silos. In this talk, we investigate how Learning is fundamentally reshaping the fields of Indexing and Compression. We will focus on two challenging research directions: designing Learned Data Structures that fuse classical indexing with machine learning to achieve unprecedented efficiency, and developing next-generation Data Compressors driven by powerful autoregressive and diffusion neural models to reach new frontiers of efficacy. We will also examine the reverse direction — how Compression can reshape Learning through model compaction and comprehension. By unpacking the distinct computational advantages and current practical pitfalls of these lines of investigation, we will outline a roadmap for these research frontiers and hopefully inspire new cross-disciplinary collaborations.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: BenchGuard: A Calibrated, Adversary-Aware Triage Layer for Reward-Hacking Agentic Trajectories
abstract: Agentic AI systems are increasingly evaluated on executable benchmarks, and a now well-documented failure mode is reward hacking: agents inspect graders, spoof expected outputs, hijack binaries, or extract hidden test inputs. The dominant operational response is to monitor every trajectory with a strong LLM judge, but at 0.4–3.8 per 100 trajectories and several minutes of latency, judge-everywhere is impractical for the millions of runs produced by continuous benchmark development. We present BenchGuard, a strict command-only forensic triage layer: TF-IDF word n-grams over agent shell commands feed a class-balanced LinearSVC that is recalibrated with Platt scaling and reports prevalence-aware operating points. On Terminal Wrench's 5,984 paired trajectories, BenchGuard reaches ROC-AUC 0.928 [task-grouped bootstrap 95% CI 0.918, 0.939] at 50% prefix and TPR 0.70 at 5% FPR. We then run a head-to-head LLM judge experiment on the same balanced 100-trajectory sample under three configurations: command-only (judge AUC 0.806), full-context with a generic prompt (0.727, DeLong p=0.012 vs. BenchGuard), and full-context with a rubric-tuned prompt (0.837, p=0.237). BenchGuard is point-estimate-best across all three at 0 vs. 0.77–1.50 per 100 trajectories. Two cheap baselines (BM25 max-similarity AUC 0.451, a distilled hashed-n-gram MLP AUC 0.931) bracket the result: pure lexical similarity is insufficient, but capacity at this scale is also not the bottleneck. Three static lexicon-evasion attacks plus an LLM-paraphrase adversary that drops token-Jaccard to 0.42 cost only 0.013–0.030 AUC (-9 pp at TPR@5%FPR for the paraphrase); adversary-aware retraining recovers the static gap. Platt-recalibrated flag rates on a 34,029-trajectory external corpus drop from 13.3% (raw) to 0.4% (Platt p >= 0.99), demonstrating calibration transfer. We document a sharp construct-validity boundary: against the realistic union-negative class (legitimate solves + no-reward attacks), AUC drops to 0.700 and operating-point precision collapses — and we translate this into a three-step deployment recommendation. All code, data extracts, judge response logs (scores and verdicts), the LLM paraphrase outputs, and calibration models are released as a reproducible artifact.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Meta-ResGAD: Bi-Level Optimization for Topology-Adaptive Graph Anomaly Detection
abstract: Generative models have demonstrated significant potential in semi-supervised graph anomaly detection (GAD) by synthesizing pseudo-anomalies to mitigate extreme label scarcity. However, existing Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)-based frameworks face two key limitations: mode collapse during generation and poor topological adaptability. Specifically, traditional methods usually enforce rigid structural alignment, which wrongly treats normal heterophilic connections as anomalies, leading to performance degradation on heterophilic graphs. In this paper, we argue that these failures stem from indiscriminate learning, where models lack an adaptive mechanism to evaluate the quality and reliability of generated pseudo-anomalies and structural priors. To bridge this gap, we propose Meta-ResGAD, a novel bi-level optimization framework that introduces a ''learning-to-reweight'' paradigm into generative GAD. By reformulating GAD as a nested optimization problem, we divide the learning process into two levels: in the upper level, we utilize unrolled differentiation to optimize an upper-level Scorer using clean validation feedback; in the lower level, a structure-aware generation process explicitly decouples semantic and structural signals. Guided by meta-gradients, the Scorer acts as a dynamic sample filter that penalizes uninformative noise to prevent mode collapse, and adaptively down-weights unreliable structural priors to disentangle structural anomalies from normal heterophily. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world benchmarks demonstrate that Meta-ResGAD achieves state-of-the-art performance with robust topology-adaptive generalization, while maintaining the high inference efficiency and low memory consumption crucial for large-scale industrial deployment. Our code is now available at: https://github.com/TDSCX/AJAX.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Technology Forecasting through Data-Driven Analysis of Patents
abstract: Forecasting technology lifecycle phases is a key enabler of data-driven innovation scouting, helping coaches and decision makers anticipate future technological developments and plan accordingly. Patent data offers structured, time-stamped records of innovation activity, making it a valuable basis for modeling and forecasting technology lifecycle trajectories. In this paper, we propose a systematic, domain-agnostic framework for technology forecasting using patent count time series from the European Patent Office (EPO). After identifying trends that are likely to capture a complete technology lifecycle, we derive a universal eight-phase lifecycle pattern within the retained EPO series. Based on this pattern, we annotate the trends and evaluate a two-stage pipeline combining neural time series forecasting with lifecycle phase classification. The evaluation yields three key results: (1) a Transformer-seq2seq classifier achieves F1-macro~0.785 on the eight-phase labeling task using only raw patent counts; (2) the top neural forecasters converge to within MAE~7.85 patents (57% below Prophet), relative to the median per-series peak; and (3) the best combined pipeline configuration (Transformer-Direct paired with LSTM-seq2seq) predicts lifecycle phase transitions with a mean year-delta of 1.8~years and a median of 0.650~years, without relying on any domain-specific features or patent text content.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Mixture-of-Experts Enhanced Parameter-free Hypergraph Contrastive Network for Next Point-of-Interest Recommendation
abstract: Next Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation aims to predict a user's next destination based on historical check-in sequences. Existing works have achieved notable progress by capturing human mobility patterns through spatio-temporal context modeling and by injecting global collaborative signals via graph neural networks and hypergraph neural networks to alleviate data sparsity. However, indiscriminate fusion may leave heterogeneous mobility signals, such as spatial constraints, temporal habits, and categorical preferences, insufficiently differentiated. Additionally, learnable transformations in parameterized hypergraph convolutions may perturb topology-driven collaborative signals during multi-layer propagation, particularly on sparse interaction data. Moreover, the user's static preference representation and the sequence-encoded dynamic intent representation originate from different embedding spaces, resulting in semantic misalignment. To address these challenges, this paper proposes the Mixture-of-Experts Contrastive Parameter-free Hypergraph Network (M-CPHNet). Specifically, a relative time-gap encoding preserves diurnal rhythms via modulo-24 operations for fine-grained temporal intent modeling. A user-conditioned intent excitation gate coupled with an adaptive soft-routing mixture-of-experts module adaptively weights multiple experts to model complementary spatial, temporal, and categorical mobility patterns, yielding sequence intent representations. These are then fused with relative time-gap embeddings and absolute position embeddings, encoded by a Transformer, and aggregated via an attention query into a short-term dynamic intent. A parameter-free hypergraph convolution (Pf-HGConv) layer introduces no learnable weights in its propagation operator and performs normalized aggregation solely on the user–POI and category–POI co-occurrence matrices to obtain topology-enhanced global POI representations, thereby reducing parameterization-induced distortion. Hypergraph-sequence contrastive learning aligns the user's static preference representation with the short-term dynamic intent representation, mitigating semantic misalignment. Experiments on three real-world datasets show that M-CPHNet achieves higher observed performance than the evaluated baselines, with an average improvement of 4.8% in Acc@5 across the three datasets; under the reported experimental settings, its per-epoch training time on Foursquare-NYC is substantially shorter than that of STHGCN.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Offline Competence-Gap Mining for Motion Forecasting via Mode-Consistent Predictive Instability
abstract: Large motion-forecasting logs contain substantially more scenes than practitioners can inspect, motivating budgeted, model-aware data triage. We formulate competence-gap discovery as an offline retrieval problem for a frozen stochastic multimodal forecaster. A dropout-free reference pass supplies its highest-confidence mode as a per-scene reference future, and each stochastic pass is aligned to that future by nearest-mode selection. The resulting model-specific predictive-instability score combines trajectory displacement and confidence volatility for the tracked reference mode. On nuScenes and Argoverse, the method yields the strongest high-error retrieval and sparsification performance among the tested confidence and representation-distance selectors; on Argoverse, it also outperforms the tested diversity and representativeness selectors. Fine-tuning LAformer on 500 mined Argoverse samples under mixed-batch replay reduces held-out tail minADE by 3.9%, compared with 2.0% for low-confidence selection, while producing the smallest full-set minADE degradation among the tested deployable selectors. The same LAformer-mined subset reduces HiVT tail minADE by 3.4%, demonstrating that the selected samples remain useful for a second forecasting backbone. These results support the use of mode-consistent predictive instability for offline audit prioritization.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: End-to-End Delayed Matching Learning for Micro-View Order Dispatching in Ride-Hailing
abstract: Micro-view order dispatching (MICOD) is a critical task in ride-hailing platforms, aiming to optimize driver--order matching within limited spatiotemporal contexts. Prior works predominantly employ Reinforcement Learning (RL) to learn delayed matching policies. However, RL-based approaches often suffer from sample inefficiency and instability due to the need for extensive trial-and-error exploration. Furthermore, the combinatorial nature of dispatching typically breaks differentiability, preventing end-to-end alignment between prediction models and optimization objectives. In this paper, we propose DML, an End-to-End Delayed Matching Learning framework. Unlike RL, DML formulates order dispatching as a learning-from-expert problem inspired by imitation learning. By leveraging the insight that a global offline optimal matching (OPT) can be computed from historical data, DML constructs an expert in hindsight and avoids the need for online exploration. To effectively clone this expert behavior while enabling end-to-end training, we address two key challenges: expert decomposition and combinatorial differentiability. First, we construct a Delay-Augmented Bipartite Graph (DABG) and theoretically prove that the global OPT can be equivalently decomposed into local sequential learning targets. Second, we incorporate a differentiable optimization layer based on the Sinkhorn-Knopp (SK) algorithm and introduce a Batch-SK (B-SK) implementation to efficiently handle variable-sized graphs in parallel. Experiments on a real-world dataset collected from Didi Chuxing demonstrate that DML significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both matching quality and training efficiency.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: PrivMem: Privacy-Preserving Temporal Motif Mining over Cross-User Agent Memory Graphs
abstract: Long-lived AI agents increasingly store private memory graphs of user goals, retrieved documents, tool calls, failures, and repairs. Mining these memories across users is crucial for discovering recurrent operational patterns, yet the problem remains unsolved: raw graphs cannot be centralized, and even aggregate motifs can reveal workflows supported by only one or two users. Existing local differential privacy (LDP) frequency-estimation and pattern-mining methods optimize top-K recovery, but they have no principled release-time defense against rare-workflow disclosure. We argue that the missing axis is not a stronger randomizer but a safer server-side release policy. We present PrivMem, which extracts retrieval-causal temporal motifs on device, perturbs them with per-coordinate randomized response, and releases them through a shrinkage ranker, a public-schema risk gate, and a Benjamini--Hochberg calibrated false-discovery filter. The analysis proves per-coordinate ε-LDP, derives concentration for the unbiased support estimator, establishes a support-gap condition for top-K recovery, and shows that the release stack preserves privacy by post-processing. On a 240-user planted benchmark, PrivMem reduces in-schema rare-workflow leakage by over 35× at matched utility; at ε=1,0=8, it keeps top-20 F1 at 0.86 while cutting leakage from 0.27 to 0.007. It also drives out-of-schema leakage to zero and improves released-subspace clustering by over 10× ARI at ε=2. On a 1, 757-user real-trace corpus across eight LLM-agent domains, PrivMem releases exactly zero rare motifs at every threshold, while LDP baselines leak 0.28-0.57.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: APILaNet: Adaptive Physics-Informed Latent Network for Single-Sensor Forecasting
abstract: Forecasting river dynamics from sensor networks is often limited by sparse and noisy observations: in many catchments, operational monitoring provides only a single gauge and uncertain rainfall inputs. We propose an Adaptive Physics-Informed Latent Network (APILaNet), a trustworthy physics-constrained forecasting model that learns a 1-D latent dynamical field while enforcing mass conservation through a weak-form residual weighted by a learned, normalized space--time measure. The normalization stabilizes training across discretizations and concentrates constraint enforcement on transient, event-driven regimes. To improve identifiability under single-gauge supervision, APILaNet uses a monotone Lipschitz measurement layer to map latent states to observed levels, and a bounded event-aware scheduler that increases conservation and smoothness regularization during high-impact periods while preserving optimization stability. Across synthetic 1-D conservation benchmarks and multi-catchment hydrological forecasting, APILaNet improves accuracy relative to strong sequence baselines and yields markedly lower error during extreme events, with consistent gains in Nash--Sutcliffe efficiency.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: SGLP: Semantic-Guided Graph Structure Learning with LLM Structural Priors for Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation
abstract: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation (CDSR) mitigates data sparsity and cold-start issues by transferring user preferences across domains. Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) effectively capture collaborative signals, they struggle with the inherent structural sparsity present in individual domains. Specifically, users or items with few interactions become ''isolated nodes''. Traditional cross-domain methods fail to rescue these nodes because they rely on explicit, overlapping interaction topologies that are often missing, severely hindering message passing. In contrast, Large Language Models (LLMs) encode rich semantic knowledge yet lack the inherent ability to interpret collaborative graph structures. To address this limitation, we propose SGLP (Semantic-Guided Graph Structure Learning with LLM Structural Priors), a framework that leverages LLM knowledge as a structural prior to reconstruct sparse interaction graphs. Specifically, SGLP employs LLMs to generate Item Semantic Embeddings and User Global Semantic Profiles, establishing a robust semantic foundation. Distinct from traditional Graph Structure Learning (GSL) methods that rely solely on intrinsic node features, SGLP introduces a Semantic-Guided Graph Modeling module. This module applies differentiable structure learning to dynamically construct a task-adaptive hybrid graph, transforming unstructured semantic similarities into structured collaborative connections. To resolve distribution discrepancies between the reconstructed structural and semantic views, we enforce a Semantic-Behavioral Alignment constraint via contrastive learning. Furthermore, a Bi-Level Sequence Prediction strategy is introduced to alleviate negative transfer arising from domain shifts. Extensive experiments on three real-world Amazon datasets demonstrate that SGLP outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the efficacy of integrating semantic priors into graph structure learning for cross-domain recommendation.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Anytime-Budget Embedding Allocation for DLRMs via Continuous-Capacity Multiple-Choice Knapsack
abstract: Embedding tables dominate the memory footprint of deep learning recommendation models (DLRMs), yet existing compression methods usually assume that the deployment memory budget is fixed before training. This is inconvenient in production, where the same recommender may be served across hardware tiers, multi-tenant resource conditions, or changing A/B-test operating points. We study anytime-budget embedding allocation: train one DLRM once, then export a hard budget-feasible embedding layout for any memory target in a specified range. We propose Continuous-Capacity Entropy-Smoothed MCKP (CC-MCKP), a differentiable allocation layer that integrates the real-valued budget directly into the multiple-choice knapsack partition function through a smooth feasibility gate. Differentiating this continuous-capacity partition function yields per-table action marginals for training and an analytic budget shadow price for sensitivity analysis, while final deployment still uses a hard MCKP solve with conservative discretization to guarantee feasibility. We provide smoothness, marginal, shadow-price, hard-limit, finite-gate, and grid-consistency results for the layer. Across Criteo Kaggle and Criteo Terabyte, one CC-MCKP-trained model approaches independently trained per-budget specialists (within about 10-3 AUC on average) and provides the strongest average single-run accuracy, with its clearest gains at intermediate and unseen budgets and small reversals at the minimum-budget corner, where the feasible layout is unique. Hard export preserves zero budget violations, while one training run costs about 2× a plain model instead of the 13× of a per-budget specialist suite.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: EarthOracle: A Self-Correcting World Model with Observational Feedback for Long-Horizon Earth Forecasting
abstract: While deep learning models have achieved unprecedented success in short-to-medium-range weather forecasting, they universally suffer from error accumulation, spectral decay, and climate drift during long-horizon autoregressive rollouts. We argue that this stems from a fundamental paradigm flaw: treating forecasting as an open-loop ''one-shot extrapolation'' rather than the closed-loop ''predict-observe-assimilate'' cycle inherent in operational numerical systems. To address this, we propose EarthOracle, a self-correcting Earth World Model that explicitly embeds sparse observations into its inference loop. At its core lies a Differentiable Data Assimilation (Diff-DA) module, which dynamically injects heterogeneous and sparse observations (e.g., satellite radiances, buoy data, radiosondes) directly into the latent state using learnable uncertainty weights. Coupled with a novel self-correction training objective based on perturbation consistency, EarthOracle, actively digests new information to suppress error amplification over long trajectories. Furthermore, we introduce a Cross-Scale Memory mechanism that disentangles fast-evolving weather signals from slow-varying ocean-atmosphere coupled modes in the latent space, ensuring that observation feedbacks modulate the system at physically appropriate timescales. Extensive experiments on ERA5 (1979–2024) and multi-source sparse observations demonstrate that EarthOracle, significantly outperforms pure autoregressive baselines in Subseasonal-to-Decadal (S2D) forecasting. It maintains stable energy spectra and climatology over long rollouts, and matches the predictive skill of dynamical S2D models on critical teleconnection indices (e.g., ENSO, MJO) at less than 0.1% of their inference cost. By redefining long-term Earth forecasting from open-loop extrapolation to closed-loop assimilation, EarthOracle, provides a scalable and robust new paradigm for real-world AI climate prediction.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Exploring Semantics-Frequency Alignment in Diffusion Transformers for Financial Time Series Generation
abstract: Existing financial time series generation (FTSG) approaches predominantly model unconditional distributions, lacking the semantic controllability required to simulate deliberate market dynamics, such as macroeconomic shifts and geopolitical shocks. To bridge this gap, this paper studies text-conditioned FTSG that synthesizes realistic multivariate price sequences guided by natural language market descriptions. We propose Fin-CoDiT, a novel diffusion transformer framework engineered around a profound architectural inductive bias: the structural isomorphism between the hierarchical semantic depth of large language models (LLMs) and the spectral frequencies of time-series signals. To exploit this, Fin-CoDiT introduces a Semantics-Frequency Alignment mechanism via Grouped Routing Attention, which dynamically routes explicit LLM layers to their targeted frequency bands during the denoising process. To encode cross-variable dependencies of time series without violating the temporal arrow, we propose Time-Frequency Causal Variational Autoencoder, which strictly operates as a channel-wise bottleneck equipped with orthogonal causal convolutions to fundamentally eliminate future information leakage. Furthermore, it incorporates a branched decoder with in-network differentiable morphological projections, guaranteeing absolute physical market constraints (e.g., Pricehigh ≥ Pricelow). For the training and evaluation of this novel paradigm, we construct an automated multi-agent workflow that creates high-quality text-time series pairs from real-world market states spanning January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2025. Extensive experiments on treasury futures and ETFs demonstrate that Fin-CoDiT establishes a new state-of-the-art, significantly outperforming existing baselines in both generation fidelity and controllability.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: STMoE: Multi-Scale Mixture-of-Experts for Single-Cell Gene Expression Prediction from Histology
abstract: Predicting single-cell molecular state from routine histology could make spatial profiling more scalable, but existing histology-to- expression methods are mostly limited to spot-level targets, re- stricted gene panels, or organ-specific settings. This leaves three gaps for practical single-cell deployment: a lack of large aligned- cell resources, limited support for direct multi-organ prediction, and incomplete full-gene expression recovery from whole-slide images. We address these gaps by curating CellST-24M, a 23.94M- cell histology–transcriptomics resource spanning 66 studies, 25 organ categories, Visium HD, and Xenium, and by introducing STMoE, a WSI-only organ-routed prediction framework for full- gene single-cell expression inference. STMoE detects cells from H&E slides, encodes cell-centered and tissue-context crops with a frozen UNI2-h pathology foundation model, aligns image and expression embeddings with soft contrastive learning, and predicts full-gene profiles through organ-routed retrieval from training-only reference banks. On matched human lung benchmarks, STMoE achieves state-of-the-art cell-level performance, outperforming cell- adapted BLEEP, sCellST and GHIST under both in-domain and cross-patient settings. Across 22 organs, STMoE supports direct multi-organ prediction and achieves gene-wise Pearson up to 0.6451 and cell-wise Pearson up to 0.8379, while retaining approximately 60% predictive capability under cross-patient transfer. In down- stream marker-derived analysis, predicted profiles recover coarse cell-state structure with 0.5935 accuracy and 0.5922 balanced accu- racy. Together, CellST-24M and STMoE establish a benchmark and modeling framework for WSI-only, multi-organ, full-gene single- cell histology-to-expression prediction.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: EndoBudget: Capacity-Controlled Learning for Stable Information Systems under Endogenous Feedback
abstract: Modern information systems increasingly operate in closed feedback loops: recommenders shape exposure, retrieval and generation pipelines influence future content, agentic systems change the environments they query, and human-AI interfaces alter the logs used for subsequent training. In these settings, data are not merely sampled from an external distribution. They are endogenously produced by prior model decisions, creating deployment drift that can accumulate over time and change finite-run reliability estimates. This paper develops EndoBudget, a learning-theoretic framework for analyzing deployment discrepancy in information systems trained on feedback-generated data and for auditing explicit update budgets. We formalize closed-loop learning as a sequential process in which each deployed model induces the next data distribution. Our main generalization result bounds the long-horizon absolute deployment gap by a classical capacity-dependent estimation term plus an accumulated endogenous drift term. We further state a sufficient stability condition for temporal capacity budgeting: under an explicit update-stability condition, a summable budget yields finite feedback path length and convergence of the induced data distributions in complete metric spaces. An auxiliary continuous-time limit provides a formal view of the discrete retraining process as dynamics over probability measures. Controlled diagnostics and a semi-synthetic closed-loop recommendation study report finite-run measurements of cumulative exposure drift, absolute deployment-gap variability, exposure dispersion, and ranking utility for the compared update rules within the studied protocol. The framework provides a finite-run audit for stating, measuring, and evaluating explicit capacity and update constraints in adaptive information systems that retrain under long-term feedback, subject to the regularity assumptions made explicit below.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: PACE: Prediction-Conditional Conformal Expert Aggregation for Known-Only Hyperspectral OOD Detection
abstract: Closed-set hyperspectral image (HSI) classifiers are often deployed in scenes whose land-cover taxonomy is incomplete. In this setting, an unseen crop type, road material, or mixed surface may not look globally alien: it can lie near the known feature manifold and still be assigned to a known class with high confidence. We call this failure mode semantic absorption. It makes purely confidence-based, global feature-distance, and single logit-based scores unreliable, because the relevant question is whether the sample is plausible under the class into which the classifier absorbs it. We propose PACE, a known-only post-hoc framework for hyperspectral semantic OOD detection. PACE builds a prediction-conditional conformal anchor from class-geometry, global-support, and predicted-class-support evidence, converts heterogeneous OOD scores into conformal expert p-values, and combines compact expert sets by ACAT. A second conformal layer recalibrates the aggregate score into final p-values, which are used for OOD ranking and Benjamini--Hochberg (BH)-FDR-targeted unknown candidate mining. Across five HSI datasets under leave-one-class-out evaluation, PACE-Rank gives the best average AUROC and FPR95, while PACE-Discover gives the best AUPR-OOD and unknown recall at the BH target. All calibration and model selection use only known-center samples; no held-out-center samples, wild data, OOD labels, or target unknown labels are used.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Lance: A LANGUAGE-ANCHORED CLOSED-LOOP ESTIMATOR for Bridging Low-Level Image Fusion and High-Level Semantic Understanding in Remote Sensing
abstract: Remote sensing image fusion and semantic interpretation are usually optimized separately, so reconstruction quality need not preserve downstream retrieval utility. We propose LANCE, which uses structured language as an explicit, indexable semantic state. A frozen vision–language model maps the input to a closed-vocabulary text record; a language-conditioned generator fuses the imagery; and a dense verifier with a differentiable continuous summarizer re-describes the output. Text–text consistency and anti-collapse contrastive text–mask losses with negative queries close the loop without dense annotations or VLM fine-tuning. A variational EM formulation yields a per-step contraction result under regularity assumptions, distinguishing semantic faithfulness from verifier overfitting. Across seven test sets on GF2, QuickBird, WorldView-III, and WorldView-II, LANCE improves reduced-scale reference metrics by up to 11.7% (median 2.1%) over the strongest learning baseline. Independent evaluation using a held-out VLM and a supervised aerial detector yields gains of +6.4 mAP and +0.072 open-vocabulary F1 over the closest competitor. Text perturbations, cross-verifier transfer, and pseudo-RGB ablations examine the mechanisms underlying these gains. The framework connects image fusion to verifiable semantic representations for multimodal retrieval and knowledge management.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: MAPLE: Mamba-Based Adaptive Prototype Learning for Intent Disentanglement in Sequential Recommendation
abstract: Sequential recommender systems struggle to simultaneously capture persistent long-term preferences and volatile short-term intentions, while existing dual-stream architectures are computationally inefficient when handling long sequences and suffer from feature entanglement between the two interest streams. To address these issues, we propose a Mamba-based Adaptive Prototype LEarning and cross-intent contrastive alignment framework (MAPLE). MAPLE employs Mamba as the long-term encoder; its selective state space mechanism selectively retains important historical signals across the entire interaction sequence, making it well-suited for capturing stable long-term interest features with linear computational complexity. Meanwhile, the GRU-based short-term encoder focuses on a local tail window to model recent preference shifts. To decouple these two interest streams, we maintain a set of global semantic prototypes for each interest type and extract soft proxies as personalized semantic anchors through attention-weighted aggregation, thereby leveraging global intent consensus to enrich individual user representations. These proxies are further applied as contrastive anchors in a novel cross-intent InfoNCE loss, which treats proxies of the complementary intent stream as cross-intent contrastive anchors to promote semantic differentiation between long and short-term representations. Finally, we introduce an asymmetric dynamic gated fusion module that prioritizes long-term features as the main component and incorporates short-term features as the auxiliary component for next-item prediction. Experiments on four real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that MAPLE achieves highly competitive performance, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art models on rank-aware metrics.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: A Shared Task on Agentic AI in University Administration
abstract: Agentic AI systems combine large language models, information retrieval, planning, and tool use to act on behalf of users in complex digital environments. Evaluating such systems under laboratory conditions remains challenging because real-world environments are hard to control: executing AI agents in them is neither safe nor reproducible. We show that university administration provides a particularly suitable setting for Cranfield-style evaluations of AI agents in a laboratory. By reconstructing the digital environment available to university staff, we enable the systematic evaluation of interactive AI agents within human administrative workflows. TIRA's sandboxed execution environment allows submitted agents to operate safely on institutional data. Focusing on selected workflows, such as travel reimbursement, we organize the first shared task on agentic AI in university administration and contribute a reusable benchmark with expert-judged reference solutions. The shared task comprises two subtasks: in agentic retrieval, an agent only finds the documents relevant to a task instance; in agentic task solving, the agent also performs the task and produces the solution.
journal: Proceedings of the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management

title: Modality-Adaptive Expert Collaboration for Depression Detection Across Audio-Visual, Gait, and Personality Cues
abstract: Given the individual difference in depressive disorders, it is imperative to integrate multimodal cues to detect depression accurately, such as dialogue semantics, speech prosody, and facial expression. MPDD-AVG 2026 collects audio (A), video (V), personality(P), and gait (G) information, and defines three multi-modal combinations, namely A-V+P, A-V-G+P, and G+P, aims to achieve depression classification and PHQ-9 scale score prediction. Due to the limited-sample conditions and substantial heterogeneity between modalities, it’s difficult to reliably learn modality-specific information and distinguish depressive states near class boundaries. To address these challenges, we propose an adaptive criss-cross expert collaboration framework, which designs differentiated expert structures for depression detection based on the available modality conditions. For A-V+P and A-V-G+P, we use fine-tuned LLM experts for multi-stage classification, while for G+P, we adopt lightweight gait-personality experts with voting and conflict arbitration. We further introduce a route-constrained PHQ-9 score prediction strategy that combines segmented regression with pair-wise intra-class ranking to model both absolute scores and within-class relative differences. Experimental results on the Elderly track show that the proposed method outperforms baseline methods and comparison models across all three sub-tracks, demonstrating the effectiveness of modality-adaptive expert collaboration and segmented PHQ-9 score prediction for multimodal depression detection.
journal: Proceedings of the 1st International Workshop on Neurophysiological Intelligence for Human-Aware Multimedia

title: TTTR: Record, Replay, and Steer AI (Extended Abstract)
abstract: AI agent behaviors are difficult to reproduce because nondeterminism enters at multiple layers of the AI software stack, from tensor computation and token sampling to the external environment. TTTR is a record-replay framework that captures these sources and enables selective replay, allowing one layer to vary while others remain fixed. This supports cross-layer fault localization, counterfactual analysis, and reproducible evaluation of agent behavior.
journal: Proceedings of the Symposium on Rigorous LLM Systems

title: From data to decisions: ensemble deep learning framework for maize seed variety classification with explainable AI
abstract: Accurate and non-destructive identification of maize seed varieties is essential for maintaining seed purity, improving crop productivity, and supporting agricultural quality assurance. Although recent studies report high accuracies using advanced imaging and deep learning techniques, many rely on hyperspectral sensors or controlled acquisition environments, or offer limited interpretability, thereby restricting real-world adoption. This study investigates maize seed variety classification using low-cost RGB imaging and an ensemble deep learning framework, focusing on three widely cultivated Ghanaian varieties: Bhihilifa, Sanzal Sima, and Wang Dataa. In collaboration with Heritage Seeds Ghana, an expert-verified dataset of 17,724 maize seed images was curated under realistic acquisition conditions with an Apple iPhone 12. A baseline convolutional neural network (CNN) was developed for benchmarking, followed by transfer learning with DenseNet169, MobileNetV2, and Xception architectures. An ensemble framework integrating DenseNet169 and Xception was proposed to improve robustness and generalization. Across five-fold cross-validation, the ensemble achieved a mean accuracy of 98.89±0.17%, precision of 98.86±0.18%, recall of 98.80±0.17%, and F1-score of 98.83±0.17%. To enhance transparency, Grad-CAM and saliency maps were employed to visualize discriminative features influencing model decisions. Results demonstrate that accurate and interpretable classification of maize seed varieties is achievable using standard RGB imagery without specialized sensing equipment.
journal: International Journal of Informatics and Communication Technology (IJ-ICT)

title: Omega-3 DHA Targets P53-Mutant CRC Stem-like Cells via Membrane Disruption, Modulation of Differential Marker Genes, and Suppression of Self-Renewal Capacity.
abstract: P53-mutant colorectal cancer stem cells (CRCSCs) are characterized by multidrug-resistance, high self-renewal, and limited differentiation potential, which necessitates the development of novel compounds capable of targeting the molecular drivers of differentiation and stemness maintenance in CRCSCs, independent of p53 status. Given this, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) was selected as a promising therapeutic candidate and its ability to modulate differentiation marker genes and stemness maintenance in CRC stem-like cells was evaluated.P53-mutant (E204X) Caco2 cells, serving as a well-established model of CRCSCs, were treated with 50-150 μM DHA for 48 h. We then evaluated multiple parameters including cell number, metabolic activity, proliferation rates, and LDH release. Additionally, the expression of stemness (CD133) and intestinal differentiation marker genes (Muc-2 and CK-20) as well as clonogenic capacity were assessed. Bioinformatic analysis was performed to predict p53-binding sites within the promoters of CD133, Muc-2, and CK-20 for wild-type p53 and its mutant form.DHA significantly decreased cell numbers, metabolic activities, and proliferation rates after 48 h of treatment. Concurrently, DHA treatment disrupted cell membrane integrity, as evidenced by a marked increase in LDH release into the supernatant. The initially low expression levels of Muc-2 and CK-20 increased dramatically, whereas significant decreases were observed in CD133 gene expression. This was confirmed by significant reductions in self-renewal, plating efficiency, and survival fraction after 2 weeks. Bioinformatics analyses showed that while wild-type p53 binds to the promoters of three differentiation marker genes, the mutant-p53 (E204X) lacks such binding.DHA disrupts cell membrane integrity, modulates stemness and differentiation marker genes, and targets stemness maintenance through a p53-independent pathway, highlighting its cytotoxic and therapeutic potential against p53-mutant CRCSCs.

title: From molecular pathways to nanocarrier design: a translational framework for lipid-based nanoparticles in Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease, being a complicated neurodegenerative disoder affects cognitive as well as memory functions. Characterised by amyloid-β aggregation, along with tau hyperphosphorylation, and cholinergic dysfunction, this disease is also associated with oxidative stress and neuroinflammation. Conventional clinical interventions, like acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and novel monoclonal antibodies predominantly rely on symptomatic alleviation of symptoms. Nevertheless, these conventional treatments come across considerable constraints, like temporary effectiveness, lesser therapeutic reach due to the blood brain barrier, apart from additional adverse effects. To overcome these delivery obstacles and achieve intracellular targeting, lipid nanoparticles, such as liposomes, solid lipid nanoparticles, and drugs, that can effectively traverse biological barriers, and facilitate precise intracellular release. This review introduces a translational, pathway-integrated framework that connects key molecular mechanisms of the disease with rational design strategies of lipid nanocarriers. The review also illustrates how essential internal factors, such as lipid composition, ionizable lipid pKa, selection of helper lipids, PEG density, along with methods of endosomal escape, and the protein corona, affect brain targeting efficacy and toxicity. It further focuses on pathway-enforced nano lipidic therapeutic approaches, where nanocarrier design is tailored to cater to specific biological targets. Nano lipidic delivery of siRNA, miRNA, mRNA, monoclonal antibodies, and along with other neuroprotective agents has been emphasised. Additionally, advancements in surface functionalization, intranasal administration, as well as receptor-mediated transcytosis, and focused ultrasound-driven blood–brain barrier penetration have also been highlighted in this review. Therefore, it aims to bridge the gap between molecular pathology and formulation design through alignment of design principles that emphasize on nanocarrier properties and its relevance to disease-specific requirements, an approach that has never been comprehensively addressed in previous literature. Registration number of clinical trial: Not applicable Lipid nanoparticles carrying drugs, antibodies, or RNA are shown crossing the blood-brain barrier through transport receptors and escaping endosomes. Proposed therapeutic targets include amyloid beta aggregation, tau hyperphosphorylation, cholinergic dysfunction, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation. The figure lists improved cognitive function, reduced pathology, and precision medicine as potential impacts. Alzheimer’s disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that is driven by multiple pathological pathways. Lipid-based nanoparticles are a versatile platform to overcome the blood-brain barrier limitation to enhance brain-specific drug delivery in the current days. Integration of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) molecular pathways with rational lipid-based nanoparticle design strategies improves therapeutic outcomes. Personalised, multi-target, and image-guided treatments for Alzheimer’s disease with enhanced BBB penetration and clinical translatability may be made possible by precision-engineered and AI-optimized lipid-based nanoparticles.

title: Pathogen-specific positron emission tomography for Enterobacterales bone infection.
abstract: Aims Gram-negative bone infections involving Enterobacterales group of bacteria pose a growing concern, especially for orthopaedic surgeries and diabetic ulcers. Current imaging methods either identify morphological changes by CT and MRI, or inflammation, using white blood cell scans or 2-deoxy-2-[18F]fluoro-d-glucose ([18F]-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET). While valuable, these are not specific, resulting in delayed diagnoses. PET/CT using 2-deoxy-2-[18F]fluoro-d-sorbitol ([18F]-FDS) is a novel method for detecting living Enterobacterales bacteria in vivo, via a conserved sorbitol-specific bacterial pathway. In this study, we aim to evaluate [18F]-FDS PET/CT for detection and monitoring of Enterobacterales bone infection in a mouse model. Methods We adapted a murine model of Gram-positive implant-associated spine infection to a Gram-negative infection model. We compared microbiological techniques to imaging with [18F]-FDG and [18F]-FDS. We determined the standardized uptake value (SUV) ratios for detection of bacterial infection and response to therapy, in 48 mice with surgical implants infected with either Escherichia coli or Staphylococcus aureus and compared them to controls with surgical implants but no infection. Results Both bacteria induced substantial bone pathology with reduced bone density. [18F]-FDS PET could specifically detect implant-associated spinal infections due to E. coli with a mean SUV ratio of 2.2 (SD 1.3), which was substantially lower in S. aureus (0.7 (SD 0.2); p = 0.002) and uninfected mice (1.0 (SD 0.1)). In contrast, [18F]-FDG could not differentiate between the two bacterial infections or the control (p = 0.497). Finally, [18F]-FDS PET could determine antibiotic efficacy, and monitor infection over time. Conclusion We demonstrate that [18F]-FDS affords a highly accurate and clinically translatable detection of Enterobacterales bone infection. This novel modality offers a rapid and specific method to diagnose and monitor bone infections, inform medical decisions, reduce the need for surgery, and limit unnecessary antibiotic use. Similar approaches may be implemented to develop tracers for other bacteria.

title: Efficient angle-aware differentiable Mask3D modeling for inverse lithography
Satellite-derived vegetation indices and machine learning for food crop yield prediction: A systematic review of methods, performance and research gaps
abstract: Crop yield prediction is essential for global food security, but the current methods for yield estimation are labour-intensive, time-consuming and have limited spatial and temporal coverage. This systematic review focuses on consolidating the evidence from the 32 peer-reviewed studies published from 2018–26 that are concerned with using both satellite-derived vegetation indices (VIs) and machine learning (ML) to predict food crop yields. A preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA)-based search resulted in the identification of studies on rice, wheat, maize, soybean, sugarcane, sorghum and barley across different geographic regions. The evidence clearly shows that across all food crops, Random Forest (RF) is the most consistent ML technique, with an R² of 0.70–0.96 based on crop and region and deep learning approaches like long short-term memory (LSTM) and convolutional neural network (CNN) show higher temporal pattern recognition, but much greater numbers of labelled data are needed. Multi-index approaches consistently outperform single-index approaches, with those extracted from Sentinel-2 performing well in situations where normalised difference vegetation index (NDVI) loses sensitivity due to canopy saturation at high biomass levels in dense-crop canopies. Sentinel-2 is the most frequently used satellite platform (over 65 % of the analysed studies) and Google Earth Engine (GEE) has become the most used data processing environment. There are still gaps in the standardisation of benchmarking metrics, the representation of smallholder and tropical farming systems, the integration of data across phenological stages and the cross-regional transferability of models. This review consolidates evidence and presents clear priorities to move precision agriculture yield forecasting toward global food security applications.

title: MIGONet: a multiple-input graph neural operator with solver-free discrete manufactured-solution training
abstract: Surrogate modeling of transport requires operators that capture the combined influence of spatially distributed sources and Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, together with training datasets that can be generated at low computational cost. This work presents MIGONet, a multiple-input graph neural operator, and a discrete method of manufactured solutions (MMS) that trains it without solving a partial differential equation, using steady heat conduction as the model problem. In the discrete MMS procedure, temperature fields are prescribed a priori, and the source terms and Dirichlet or Neumann boundary data are evaluated with the same discrete operators as the reference finite-difference method (FDM), so every training sample satisfies the discrete governing equations by construction. Because the boundary data are derived from each field, a Dirichlet or Neumann condition can be assigned to every boundary segment of every sample, and the boundary specification becomes an operator input. MIGONet supplies representations of the complete source field and boundary data to every node before local message passing. On the rectangular domain, it is compared with a version without the complete-source encoder (MIGONet-local) and with the multiple-input operator network MIONet, using the same training data. MIGONet achieves mean relative temperature errors of 10.31% and 10.64% for curved-wire and Gaussian-spot heating, compared with 45.97% and 48.34% for MIONet and 72.25% and 67.82% for MIGONet-local. For 10,000 samples, discrete MMS reduces data-generation time from 486.65 s to 3.15 s relative to matched iterative FDM labeling. Separately trained MIGONet models are also evaluated on L-shaped, disc-shaped, and ring-shaped domains.

title: Beyond Account Ownership: Financial Inclusion, Digital Banking Use and Inclusive Development in Jalgaon District, Maharashtra
abstract: : The study draws on the conceptual discussion, literature and tabulated analytical material contained in the supplied thesis document. Jalgaon provides a relevant setting because its economy combines agriculture, commodity trade, small enterprises, services and urban activity, while its settlement structure includes a substantial rural population. The source material reports an dataset of 540 observations. Within that dataset, 75.2% of respondents are classified as financially included; 73.9% report insurance awareness; 60.7% report access to a Kisan Credit Card; and 43.0% report self-help group linkage. The article’s principal contribution is an integrated framework that connects access, usage, capability, product suitability, consumer protection and livelihood outcomes. It argues that district level inclusion strategies should combine reliable last mile infrastructure with financial literacy, assisted digital services, responsible agricultural credit and stronger customer grievance mechanisms. Before journal submission, all data must be replaced with verified primary observations and the statistical analysis rerun.
journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)

title: Integrating Geospatial Modeling and Multivariate Statistics for Assessing Soil Capability and Crop Suitability in the Arid Alluvial Floodplains of Middle Egypt
Current and emerging threats to honey bee health: a One Health perspective on antibiotic pollution.
abstract: Pollinators play a critical role in global food production and ecosystem health, yet high losses of essential honey bee colonies have been reported worldwide. Climate change, habitat loss, parasites, pesticides, and poor nutrition are established pollinator threats, whereas environmental antibiotic pollution remains poorly understood. Antibiotic exposure may independently affect bees or interact with these stressors, potentially compounding adverse health effects. Synthetic antibiotic residues and resistance genes enter the environment through the fertilization of soils with antibiotic-containing animal manure, animal wastewater discharge, and airborne antibiotic contamination landing directly on flowers and crops. While the effects of direct antibiotic exposure on honey bees have been studied, the consequences of indirect environmental exposure remain largely unknown. Foraging bees may encounter antibiotic contaminants in the environment, potentially disrupting their gut microbiome, altering behavior and physiology, and increasing susceptibility to pathogens. Contamination of honey bees and their products with antibiotics serve not only as indicators of environmental antibiotic resistance but also as a practical One Health model linking human, animal, and environmental health. Studying honey bee responses to agricultural contaminants provides insight into how antibiotic resistance and environmental stressors can move across ecosystems, affecting both pollinators and the broader public. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the multifactor threats to honey bees and their mitigation strategies, emphasizing the influence of animal production and antibiotic pollution on honey bee health. We highlight knowledge gaps in understanding the transfer of antibiotic resistance from agricultural environments to honey bees to enhance pollinator health and promote long-term ecological resilience.
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association

title: Unlocking the Reactive Role of CO₂ in the Pyrolysis of Heterogeneous Agricultural Residues: A Mechanistic Study and Predictive Modelling for Biorefinery Technologies
abstract: This study presents a systematic investigation into the pyrolysis of thirteen heterogeneous agricultural residues, categorised as cereal straws, high-lipid fruit seeds, and agro-industrial byproducts, across a temperature range of 300–800°C.
