title: Analysis of the Role of Agricultural Technology Adoption and Access to Financial Inclusion on the Development of Rural Areas in Indonesia
abstract: Rural areas in Indonesia support approximately one-third of the national population but continue to face challenges related to productivity, welfare, and infrastructure. Although agricultural technology adoption and financial inclusion have independently been associated with improved rural welfare, empirical evidence integrating both factors remains limited in the Indonesian context. This study aims to analyze the effects of agricultural technology adoption and financial inclusion on rural development and to examine the mediating role of financial inclusion in the relationship between agricultural technology adoption and rural development. A quantitative approach was employed using a cross-sectional survey of 300 smallholder farmers in several rural provinces of Indonesia. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The measurement model was assessed through indicator reliability, composite reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity using the Fornell–Larcker criterion and HTMT. The structural model was evaluated using path coefficients, bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples, R², and Q². The results show that agricultural technology adoption has a positive and significant effect on rural development (? = 0.312; p < 0.001). Financial inclusion also has a positive and significant effect on rural development (? = 0.458; p < 0.001). Furthermore, financial inclusion partially mediates the relationship between agricultural technology adoption and rural development, with an indirect effect of ? = 0.247 (p < 0.001). These findings indicate that technology adoption can generate greater rural development benefits when supported by access to formal financial services, credit, savings, and digital financial services.
journal: AJARCDE (Asian Journal of Applied Research for Community Development and Empowerment)

title: MECHANISM FOR DEVELOPING THE TRANSFER POTENTIAL OF AGRICULTURAL HOLDING LOGISTICS CENTERS
abstract: The article substantiates the theoretical and methodological provisions for developing a mechanism aimed at enhancing the transfer potential of agricultural holdings’ logistics centers. Transfer potential is interpreted as the ability of a logistics center to ensure the transmission, adoption, integration, and scaling of technologies, information, resources, managerial decisions, and logistics practices. It is established that its development depends not only on the availability of transport and warehousing infrastructure but also on the level of digitalization, personnel readiness, partnership interaction, institutional alignment, and route resilience. The proposed mechanism is presented as a system of organizational, economic, technological, information-analytical, institutional, and regulatory levers. Its structure comprises target-oriented, subject–object, resource–instrumental, process, and resultoriented components. The study outlines the diagnostic, design, implementation, coordination and adjustment, and performance-monitoring stages of the mechanism. The infrastructure modernization, digital integration, organizational partnership, regulatory harmonization, and environmental sustainability vectors of its practical implementation are substantiated. A methodological approach to assessing transfer potential is developed by combining basic infrastructure and logistics capacity with a mechanism activation coefficient. The basic component is calculated using storage capacity, the number of logistics nodes, multimodality, and freight-flow intensity. The proposed approach is tested using publicly available data on Kernel, Nibulon, and Astarta. The calculations show that Kernel’s basic index equals 0.992, Nibulon’s 0.784, and Astarta’s 0.303. These values primarily characterize the physical scale of the companies’ logistics systems, whereas their actual performance depends on digital integration, management quality, partnerships, and risk exposure. The practical significance of the proposed mechanism lies in its applicability to substantiating investment decisions, identifying digitalization priorities, diversifying transportation routes, and assessing development reserves of agricultural holdings’ logistics centers.
journal: State and Regions. Series: Economics and Business

title: Evaluating AI agents on the IUCN Red List assessor exam: Tradeoffs and opportunities for AI assistants in extinction risk assessments
abstract: The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species is the world's most widely used system for assessing the global extinction risk of species, underpinning conservation policy and action worldwide. However, due to funding constraints and limited assessor capacity, the Red List faces significant gaps in species coverage (less than 20% of plant species have been assessed) and challenges in keeping assessments up to date (over 30% are 10+ years old). Recent advances in AI open new opportunities for helping assessors increase assessment throughput and quality, but also raise concerns about trust and reliability, data security, cost, and environmental impact. As a starting point for considering these tradeoffs, this paper evaluates the performance of AI agents on the official IUCN Red List assessor training exam. On a benchmark of 101 exam questions, we show that several frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI reliably clear the exam's 75% pass mark. The top-performing model, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5, reaches 96% mean accuracy, increasing to 99% with majority vote over five attempts. Notably, the pass mark is now also reached by open-weight models running on local hardware: Alibaba's Qwen3.8 Flash, self-hosted on a single desktop Mac Studio, attains 81% mean accuracy (87% majority vote). This points to viable hosting alternatives where data security or sustainability concerns preclude sending data through external providers' data centres. Whilst the exam serves only as a capability floor, these results strengthen the case for thoughtful use of AI assistants in assessors' workflows, such as quality and consistency checks on draft assessments.

title: Explainable hour-ahead traffic-volume forecasting with condition-stratified evaluation: an interstate I-94 case study
abstract: Hour-ahead traffic-volume forecasting can support traveler information, staffing, and advance corridor management. However, reliable evaluation requires attention to data quality, temporal variation, and forecasting uncertainty. This study evaluates an auditable, condition-stratified forecasting framework using traffic observations from westbound Interstate I-94 in Minnesota. The Metro Interstate Traffic Volume dataset was audited for duplicate records, repeated timestamps, physically implausible rainfall observations, and missing hourly intervals. After preprocessing, 40,574 usable hourly timestamps yielded 28,855 valid gap-aware forecasting sequences with 24-hour input windows. The evaluated models included persistence, a 24-hour seasonal-naive baseline, LightGBM, XGBoost with and without weather variables, DLinear, GRU, a compact iTransformer-style model, and the Temporal-Mean Residual Network (TMRNet). Trainable models were evaluated using five prespecified random seeds. Performance was assessed through forecasting accuracy, paired statistical comparisons, direct forecasting horizons, rainfall-stratified errors, empirical prediction intervals, grouped permutation importance, TreeSHAP, and Integrated Gradients. XGBoost without weather achieved the lowest mean test MAE of 141.67 ± 0.31 vehicles/hour, followed by LightGBM (142.63 ± 0.41) and all-feature XGBoost (142.89 ± 0.56). TMRNet achieved a higher MAE of 220.34 ± 3.01 vehicles/hour. Removing weather variables from XGBoost produced an ensemble-mean MAE difference of −0.98 vehicles/hour relative to all-feature XGBoost (95% moving-block-bootstrap confidence interval: −2.21 to 0.12; Diebold–Mariano p = 0.106), indicating no statistically significant improvement. In a separate single-run sensitivity analysis, XGBoost achieved MAEs of 143.64, 182.65, and 197.44 vehicles/hour at the 1-, 3-, and 6-hour forecasting horizons, respectively. The test partition contained 5,371 zero-recorded, 353 light-rain, 45 moderate-rain, and two heavy-rain target hours. All 400 positive-rain test targets occurred within the final 909 valid test targets, making rainfall comparisons temporally confounded. At 90% nominal coverage, XGBoost achieved empirical coverage of 0.904 with a mean interval width of 661.02 vehicles/hour, compared with 0.903 and 945.69 vehicles/hour for TMRNet. Traffic history and temporal-cycle variables contributed more strongly to model predictions than direct rainfall inputs. The findings demonstrate the value of an auditable and condition-stratified approach to hourly traffic forecasting. Tree-based models generally outperformed the evaluated neural alternatives, while weather variables did not produce a statistically significant accuracy gain for XGBoost. However, the limited heavy-rain observations, temporal clustering of rainfall, and use of a single roadway restrict broader conclusions. The results do not establish heavy-rain robustness, suitability for sub-hourly traffic control, or generalization to other transportation networks.

title: Qingjin Desheng Pian attenuates NSCLC progression by suppressing neutrophil extracellular trap formation: involvement of the HMGB1/TLR2/MyD88 axis
abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Despite advances in immune checkpoint inhibitor-based therapy, a substantial proportion of patients derive limited benefit. In the tumor microenvironment, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) promote tumor progression and metastasis, representing a potential therapeutic target. Qingjin Desheng Pian (QJDS) is a standardized hospital preparation of traditional Chinese medicine that has been used clinically for primary and metastatic lung cancer. Although earlier studies have suggested antitumor effects of QJDS, its impact on NET formation and the underlying mechanisms in NSCLC remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate whether QJDS suppresses NET formation and to elucidate the molecular mechanisms. This retrospective study included 209 stage III-IV NSCLC patients who received QJDS plus chemotherapy or chemotherapy alone. NET enrichment was assessed by single-cell RNA sequencing and histopathology. Network pharmacology predicted potential targets. A syngeneic Lewis lung carcinoma model evaluated antitumor efficacy and intratumoral NET levels. In vitro , primary mouse neutrophils were stimulated with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) for NET induction, followed by QJDS intervention. Transcriptomic sequencing and weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified hub genes. Pharmacological rescue experiments using N4-acetylcytidine (N4A) were performed. QJDS prolonged progression-free survival, improved quality of life, and attenuated systemic inflammation. NETs were markedly enriched in NSCLC tumor tissues compared with adjacent tissues. QJDS dose-dependently inhibited tumor growth and reduced intratumoral NET formation and serum MPO-DNA levels in vivo . In vitro , QJDS suppressed NET release and attenuated NET-mediated migration, invasion, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and proliferation of lung cancer cells. Mechanistically, high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) was identified as a key hub gene through transcriptomic and weighted gene co-expression network analyses. QJDS significantly downregulated HMGB1, toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2), and myeloid differentiation primary response 88 (MyD88) expression in neutrophils, effects partially reversed by N4A. These findings indicate that QJDS attenuates NSCLC progression by suppressing NET formation through mechanisms involving the HMGB1/TLR2/MyD88 axis, supporting its adjuvant application in advanced lung cancer.

title: 6-pentyl-2H-pyran-2-one: from a fungal volatile metabolite to an ecological signaling hub for sustainable crop protection
abstract: 6-Pentyl-2H-pyran-2-one (6-PP) is a characteristic volatile secondary metabolite produced by Trichoderma species and was initially studied for its coconut-like odor and antifungal activity. Recent studies have revealed that 6-PP has broader roles in fungal ecology, influencing pathogen interactions, plant responses, and associated microbial communities. Here, we summarize recent advances in 6-PP biology, focusing on four aspects: the evolution of its biosynthetic model, the regulation of its production, its ecological functions, and its potential applications in crop protection. The discovery of the Pks1-mediated pathway has revised previous views based mainly on fatty acid metabolism and provided genetic evidence for 6-PP biosynthesis. We further discuss how environmental signals, intracellular signaling pathways, transcriptional regulators, chromatin modification, and metabolic states collectively influence 6-PP production. At the ecological level, 6-PP acts as a signaling molecule that affects pathogen fitness, plant growth and defense responses, and plant-associated microbiome assembly. Finally, we highlight strategies for translating 6-PP biology into agricultural applications through strain engineering, controlled-release formulations, and microbial consortium-based biocontrol. Key challenges include elucidating downstream biosynthetic steps, identifying plant perception mechanisms, clarifying the ecological effects of 6-PP on microbial communities, and validating its efficacy under field conditions. Addressing these knowledge gaps will advance our understanding of 6-PP as a potential ecological signaling molecule and support the development of sustainable crop protection strategies.

title: Phenotyping replication strongly influences genomic predictive ability in sweet sorghum (Sorghum bicolor [L.] Moench)
abstract: Genomic selection can accelerate breeding when the phenotypic and genomic information used to train prediction models is sufficiently reliable and relevant to the prediction target. Using a sweet sorghum breeding population evaluated in three Haitian field environments, we quantified the effects of phenotyping replication, training population (TP) size, TP–validation population (VP) genomic relatedness, and prediction model on genomic predictive ability for grain yield, plant height, stem weight, and total soluble solids. Increasing phenotyping replication consistently improved predictive ability across traits and environments and increased the precision of phenotypic estimates, with particularly large effects observed for grain yield. Larger TPs generally improved predictive ability; however, when TP sizes of 150 and 200 individuals were compared, the effect of increasing phenotyping replication was consistently greater than that of increasing TP size. Greater TP–VP genomic relatedness was also generally associated with higher predictive ability, whereas differences among prediction models were comparatively small and inconsistent across traits and environments. These results provide empirical evidence that genomic prediction performance in sweet sorghum depends not only on prediction model choice but also on the design and quality of the TP. In particular, for larger TPs, improving phenotyping precision through additional replication may provide greater gains in predictive ability than further increasing TP size. Genomic selection (GS) can increase the rate of genetic gain in crop breeding programs, but its effectiveness depends on the reliability of phenotypic data, the size and composition of the training population (TP), and the statistical model used to estimate genomic breeding values. These design choices are particularly important in resource-limited breeding programs, where phenotyping replication, TP size, and genotyping compete for the same resources. Using empirical data from a sweet sorghum [ Sorghum bicolor (L.) Moench] breeding population developed by CHIBAS, we evaluated the effects of phenotyping replication, TP size, training–validation population (TP–VP) genomic relatedness, and genomic prediction (GP) model on predictive ability (PA). Grain yield, plant height, stem weight, and total soluble solids were evaluated across three field environments. Few studies have evaluated these factors jointly using an empirical dataset. Increasing the number of phenotypic replications consistently increased PA across traits and environments and improved the precision of genotype performance estimates, with the largest effects observed for grain yield. Larger TPs also increased PA, but the magnitude of the benefit diminished as TP size increased. In particular, when larger TPs above 150 individuals were compared, the effect of increasing phenotyping replication was consistently greater than that of further increasing TP size. Greater TP–VP genomic relatedness was generally associated with higher PA, whereas differences among GP models were comparatively small and inconsistent across traits and environments. These results provide empirical evidence that GP performance in sweet sorghum depends strongly on the design and quality of the training data. Within the range evaluated here, when TP size increased from 150 to 200 individuals, improving phenotypic precision through additional replication generally produced larger effects on PA than further increasing TP size.

title: High-throughput canopy light interception using aerial LiDAR in maize
abstract: Canopy light interception is an important physiological trait that is traditionally measured using a light bar. However, this measurement is constrained by time and logistical challenges (days without clouds, only around noon, working in high temperatures), making it difficult to implement in large experiments such as those conducted in maize breeding programs. Recent advances in remote sensing, particularly the use of aerial LiDAR, have the potential for high-throughput characterization of canopy structures. Our objective was to evaluate whether aerial LiDAR can reliably estimate light interception and to determine its feasibility for deployment in commercial maize breeding experiments. To test this, aerial LiDAR data and light bar measurements were collected at five experiments varying in genotype, plant density, and irrigation treatments. Grain yield varied across experiments and treatments, from 3.8 to 24.6 Mg ha -1 , while maximum leaf area index ranged from 1.3 to 12.2 m 2 m -2 . Voxel canopy cover derived from LiDAR was strongly correlated with light bar light interception measurements across all environments and treatments (r = 0.96). A universal linear model, barely departing from the 1:1 line, showed high precision, low bias, and consistent performance across environments, with RMSE ranging from 5.5 to 7.9%. Experiment specific calibrations improved predictions by only 5% compared to the 1:1 (LiDAR voxel canopy cover equals light interception) and by 10% compared to the universal linear model, suggesting that individual experiment calibration is not needed. LiDAR light interception showed lower plot-to-plot error and higher treatment heritability than light bar light interception measurements. Furthermore, canopy light interception evolution curves over time derived from LiDAR data provided more accurate fits than those derived from light bar data in 98% of cases. We conclude that aerial LiDAR is an effective, high-throughput tool that can be used for measuring light interception in maize, providing more consistent and scalable data than traditional light bar measurements. A model in which LiDAR voxel canopy cover equals light interception works well across diverse conditions, and a workflow is described to support adoption. In the discussion, we further describe positive and negative aspects of the adoption of LiDAR compared to the traditional light bar, highlighting the value it provides for maize breeding, crop physiology, and overall field research.

title: CT-based navigation for acetabular cup placement in supine and lateral positions: a simulated surgery study using patient-specific 3D-printed pelvic models
abstract: Accurate acetabular cup placement is critical for the success of total hip arthroplasty (THA). The aim of this study was to evaluate the accuracy and precision of a CT-based, AI-driven navigation tool for acetabular cup placement in supine and lateral patient positions, using a patient-specific 3D-printed pelvic model with an embedded acetabular cup rim as a physical measurement reference. Twenty-six patient-specific pelvic models were generated from preoperative CT data. A virtual acetabular cup was added to each pelvic mesh, cropped to the rim, and 3D-printed together with the bone, yielding a physical cup reference embedded in the printed pelvis. The ground-truth cup orientation and position were defined within the planning application by overlaying a cup component template on the embedded rim. Each model was tested once in supine and once in lateral position in a paired design. Ten cases were repeated three times per position to assess intra-session precision. Outcomes were surface matching root-mean-square error (RMSE), cup anteversion, inclination, and depth errors. Analyses included two one-sided tests (TOST) for equivalence (±0.5 mm), Bland–Altman agreement, Levene's test, and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). Mean alignment-point RMSE was 0.26 mm (supine) and 0.28 mm (lateral); mean independent test-point RMSE was 0.30 mm in both positions, with TOST confirming equivalence within ±0.5 mm. Mean absolute anteversion error was 0.67° (supine) and 0.44° (lateral), with comparable inclination errors. Mean absolute cup depth error remained well below ±3 mm. Bland–Altman analyses showed narrow 95% limits of agreement between positions. All ICC(3,1) values for cup orientation exceeded 0.99 in both positions. The evaluated navigation tool achieved sub-millimeter surface matching, small cup placement errors, and excellent intra-session precision in both supine and lateral positions. The embedded-rim phantom enabled direct measurement of cup orientation and seating depth on the printed model and is applicable to other CT-based navigation systems.

title: Modeling the Impact of Climate Change on Onion (Allium cepa) Yield and Economic Production: A Multi-Model Approach
abstract: Although machine learning models for onions (Allium cepa) have recently emerged, process-based models are required to capture physiological responses under climate volatility. This study addresses this need by integrating the Agricultural Policy/Environmental Extender (APEX) crop growth model with an econometric framework to simulate onion yields and economic returns under shifting climate regimes. The APEX-onion model was calibrated for onions’ cold-weather dynamics and bolting partitioning, achieving robust multi-site regional validation (PBIAS = 2.48%, RMSE = 1.39 Mg ha−1). Decadal projections (2026–2035) across four CMIP6 models under the SSP245 and SSP585 pathways reveal that warmer conditions and elevated CO2 generally enhance yields (by 9–22%), whereas compound radiation and rainfall anomalies trigger severe water stress (>110 days) and yield penalties. An economic harvest ratio (EHR) model demonstrated that 100% unbolted harvests do not monotonically maximize farm profit due to wholesale price collapses under price-inelastic vegetable demand. Moderating marketable volumes (allowing an effective supply buffer averaging 39.0–42.6% and up to 46.5% during bumper years) protects farm revenue, whereas full marketable yields are essential during climate-driven shortages. This integrated framework provides actionable economic thresholds for agricultural climate adaptation.

title: The Association Between Neighbor Labor Exchange and the Adoption of Green Production Technologies Among Plateau Farmers: Evidence from the Use of Low-Residue Pesticides and Organic Fertilizers
abstract: The adoption of green production technologies (GPTs) is an important component of the agricultural green transition. However, under the combined pressures of persistent rural labor outmigration and population aging, limited attention has been paid to the relationship between informal mutual-aid institutions within rural communities and GPT adoption. Using cross-sectional survey data from 675 plateau farmers in western Sichuan, a bivariate Probit model and mediation analysis are employed to examine the association between neighbor labor exchange and farmers’ willingness to adopt and adoption behavior of GPTs and to explore the potential explanatory pathways. The results show that participation in neighbor labor exchange is significantly and positively associated with both farmers’ willingness to adopt and adoption behavior of GPTs, and the findings remain robust after a series of robustness tests. Participation in neighbor labor exchange is significantly and positively associated with both outcomes, and similar patterns are obtained in several robustness checks. Green quality cognition is also associated with neighbor labor exchange and both adoption outcomes, providing exploratory evidence of a potential indirect pathway. Formal between-group tests indicate that the positive association with willingness to adopt GPTs is stronger among farmers with better self-rated health. They also provide tentative evidence that the positive association between neighbor labor exchange and adoption behavior of GPTs is stronger among agriculture-dependent households. In addition, the average marginal interaction results indicate that the positive association between neighbor labor exchange and willingness to adopt GPTs is weaker among market-oriented households, whereas no statistically significant interaction is found for adoption behavior of GPTs. They suggest that rural mutual-aid networks, GPT-related information and training, and differentiated extension strategies warrant consideration in the promotion of GPTs in plateau regions.

title: Physical Prior Knowledge-Guided Reconstruction of Continuous Rice Canopy Spectra from UAV Multispectral Observations
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) multispectral imaging supports efficient crop monitoring but provides limited information on continuous spectral features. This study reconstructed rice canopy reflectance from 400 to 1000 nm using four UAV bands and evaluated whether the recovered spectra remained consistent across scales. Multispectral reflectance data acquired at three flight altitudes were used to analyze their consistency with canopy hyperspectral reflectance, and two data simulation methods coupled with PROSAIL-D were employed to compare the constraining effects of prior knowledge data. Cubic spline, piecewise linear–logistic (PLL), partial least squares regression (PLSR), multilayer perceptron (MLP), and SE-ResNet-Att models were compared across different validation sets. The results showed that a flight altitude of 50 m provided the closest agreement with ground canopy spectra (RMSE, 5.085%). Machine learning models showed higher accuracy based on the C-Vine method than the Monte Carlo sampling method, owing to the narrower spectral datasets generated by the joint parameters. With full-prior training, PLSR performed best with ground-resampled inputs (RMSE, 1.352%), whereas SE-ResNet-Att achieved the lowest UAV-field RMSE of 4.298%. However, the proposed model showed limited advantages over simpler models in the leave-one-growth-stage-out validation and model ablation experiment, indicating that the benefits of increasing network complexity were limited. Although reconstructed spectra reproduced broad red-edge and near-infrared patterns, blue relative errors and red-edge absolute errors remained prominent with UAV inputs. The reconstructed red-edge position was correlated with measured values (r = 0.928) but showed a negative bias (ranging from −20 to −9 nm). Its exploratory correlations with canopy water and nitrogen contents (r = 0.589 and 0.727) decreased to 0.110 and 0.203 after adjustment for growth stage and leaf area index relationships. The method proposed in this study supports the extraction and exploratory analysis of additional spectral features from UAV multispectral imagery, but quantitative trait estimation and transfer across independent fields, years, and rice cultivars require further validation.

title: Letting the Crop Speak: A Proof-of-Concept Sensor-Grounded Large Language Model Advisor for Potato Irrigation on a Mediterranean Vertisol
abstract: Low-cost soil sensors are now widespread, but turning a moisture reading into an irrigation decision still requires expertise that many growers lack. This proof-of-concept study describes a conversational advisor in which a general-purpose large language model (GPT-5) receives live readings from a low-cost capacitive probe, together with a short crop and soil profile, and answers the operator in the first person, as the plant. The advisor was used throughout a 14-week greenhouse potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) cycle in a clay-rich Moroccan Vertisol (“Tirs”). Six pots were irrigated only on its recommendation and six by an experienced technician working without sensor data. The advisor-guided block received less water, and its plants grew taller and set more tubers of larger maximum diameter. Because the treatments were neither replicated nor randomised, irrigation was logged per block and tuber mass was not recorded, these observations are descriptive and cannot be attributed to the language model rather than to the sensor, bench position or irrigation schedule. The recorded dialogue showed the advisor reasoning faithfully from its inputs, including a mislabelled moisture unit. The study demonstrates technical feasibility, not the agronomic effectiveness of the recommendations, and defines the controls a replicated trial requires.

title: Solid Matrix Dispensers for Semiochemical-Based Pest Management in Agriculture: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Semiochemicals can provide species-selective pest monitoring and behavioral control, but their volatility, chemical instability, and sensitivity to field conditions make delivery technology decisive for efficacy. This narrative review examines solid matrix dispensers as coupled material–device–environment systems for controlled release of semiochemicals, distinguishing various materials and their characteristics, physicohemical properties, and the assumptions and limitations of commonly used kinetic models. Comparative evidence across applications indicates that performance depends on matching emission rate and spatial distribution to pest phenology, density, crop architecture, and landscape context. Conventional polymers remain technically effective, whereas biodegradable matrices, electrospun fibers, porous solids, smart monitoring, and automated deployment offer promising but unevenly mature alternatives. Future progress requires standardized reporting, mechanistically informed design, multisite validation, and lifecycle and economic assessment that connect material properties to biologically effective plumes and crop-level outcomes.

title: Organic–Inorganic and Microbial Fertilisation Under Continuous Sorghum Cropping: Grain Yield, Soil Properties, and Rhizosphere Microbial Community Responses
abstract: Continuous sorghum cropping causes yield decline in semi-arid regions. In a two-year field experiment conducted on plots previously cropped with sorghum for two years, four fertilisation treatments—no fertiliser (SCK), chemical fertiliser (SCF), organic–inorganic compound fertiliser (SOIF) and compound microbial fertiliser (SCMF; SOIF supplemented with Bacillus subtilis and B. licheniformis)—were compared in terms of grain yield, soil physicochemical properties, potential enzyme activities and rhizosphere bacterial and fungal communities. Year, treatment and year × treatment effects were tested using mixed models that accounted for repeated measurements of the same plots. The complete SCMF formulation was associated with the highest grain yield (10,108.13 kg ha−1, in 2025), exceeding those under SCK, SCF, and SOIF by 42.95%, 11.47%, and 3.59%, respectively. The SCMF-SOIF comparison, in which N, P2O5, K2O and organic-matter inputs were identical, isolates the microbial inoculants; its yield increment was small and not significant in either year (4.27% and 3.59%), so an inoculant-specific yield benefit was not demonstrated. Compared with SOIF, SCMF had higher alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity in both years and higher sucrase (SUS) activity (+36.80%) and available nitrogen (AN; +21.11%) in 2025. In 2025, SOIF and SCMF reduced the topsoil bulk density relative to SCK and SCF, and SCMF shifted the aggregate-size distribution towards the 2–0.25-mm fraction (+47.45–112.62%). Fertilisation altered the composition, but not the alpha diversity, of rhizosphere communities; the treatment effect was larger and more independent of multivariate dispersion for fungi (R2 = 0.167, p = 0.009) than for bacteria (R2 = 0.113, p = 0.049). The fungal response represents an overall treatment-associated compositional difference with weaker statistical evidence in the second year, because treatment differences were significant only in 2024 when each year was tested separately. Nitrosospira, a genus containing members previously associated with ammonia oxidation, was consistently enriched under SCMF, although nitrification was not measured. Overall, the yield benefit was attributable mainly to organic–inorganic fertilisation, whereas inoculant-associated differences were found in potential enzyme activities and fungal community composition rather than in grain yield.

title: Exploring the Impacts of Pre-Stem Elongation Nitrogen Status on Winter Wheat’s Subsequent Growth and Nitrogen Status Using Nitrogen Nutrition Index
abstract: Crop nitrogen (N) status governs winter wheat growth and productivity. This study tested the hypothesis that pre-stem elongation N status determined subsequent N dynamics, with leaf area index (LAI) serving as an associative physiological mediator. Using the nitrogen nutrition index (NNI), we quantified relationships between pre- and post-stem-elongation N status and explored mechanisms underlying post-stem elongation NNI variation. Three field experiments were conducted over multiple seasons using two winter wheat cultivars, with basal and topdressing N rates ranging from 0 to 300 kg N ha−1. We measured shoot biomass, tiller number, LAI, plant N concentration, critical N concentration, and yield. Generalized linear mixed models revealed significant positive relationships between spring-regrowth NNI and NNI at stem elongation and booting across experiments. Simple linear regression analysis yielded corresponding R2 values ranging from 0.50 to 0.61. Under the tested conditions, treatments without basal N showed severe N deficiency, reflected by low NNI values (0.44–0.56). This deficiency constrained growth and persisted despite topdressing. In contrast, basal N application (60–90 kg N ha−1) alleviated these limitations. Structural equation modeling suggested that LAI was an associative mediator linking early- and late-season N status. These results highlight the value of early-season N assessment for winter wheat N management.

title: Next-Day Prediction of 0–20 cm Volumetric Soil Water Content in a Cotton Field Under Mulched Drip Irrigation in Southern Xinjiang, China, Using an ET0-Informed Trend-Constrained Long Short-Term Memory Model
abstract: Surface soil water content is an important indicator for daily irrigation management in cotton fields under mulched drip irrigation in southern Xinjiang, China. This study evaluated a long short-term memory (LSTM) model incorporating reference crop evapotranspiration (ET0) and a trend-consistency (TC) constraint (ET0-TC-LSTM) for next-day prediction of 0–20 cm volumetric soil water content using the preceding 7 d of observations. Four observation periods during 2022–2025 yielded 468 supervised samples, divided chronologically into 169 training, 153 validation, and 146 test samples. ET0 was included as a feature, and a one-sided training penalty restricted predicted increases beyond a tolerance under recent low-water-input and high vapor pressure deficit (VPD) conditions. Persistence, ridge regression, and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network–LSTM (CNN1D-LSTM) model were included as benchmarks. In the original seed-42 experiment, ET0-TC-LSTM achieved a test coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.9574 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.0081 cm3 cm−3, a 29.7% RMSE reduction relative to LSTM. Across ten seeds, the mean RMSE reduction was 2.84%; TC-LSTM had the lowest mean RMSE among the four LSTM variants. Persistence was more accurate, with an RMSE of 0.0046 cm3 cm−3. Sensitivity and conditional analyses showed that the effects of process-informed inputs and penalties depended on parameter settings and evaluation conditions. These results identify improvements within the LSTM framework, but do not establish superiority over persistence for this site and forecast horizon.

title: An Ensemble Learning Approach for Wind Power Prediction Using Hybrid Deep Learning
abstract: Wind power prediction is important for utility grid energy scheduling. However, prediction accuracy suffers from poor data quality and limited feature engineering. Therefore, this paper proposes a data-driven ensemble learning framework to deal with these issues. First, the paper divides raw data into four seasonal groups. A preprocessing pipeline integrating the 3σ rule, Hermite interpolation, and a wind power curve modeling method detects and corrects outliers. Second, we develop a two-stage prediction strategy. In the first stage, a hybrid deep learning model including convolutional neural networks, gated recurrent units, and an attention mechanism jointly learns spatio-temporal features, with hyperparameters optimized using the exponential-trigonometric optimization (ETO) algorithm and the input length determined using the partial autocorrelation function. In the second stage, a temporal convolutional network with ETO-optimized hyperparameters predicts the error sequence, capturing multi-scale nonlinear relationships between input features and error dynamics. Experimental results on real-world wind farm data demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a mean RMSE of 5.89±0.11 MW, MAE of 4.05±0.09 MW, MAPE of 7.24±0.18%, and R2 of 0.928±0.008 over 50 independent runs. A representative single run achieves an RMSE of 5.89 MW, MAE of 4.02 MW, MAPE of 6.9%, and R2 of 0.93.

title: FinTech Access and Climate-Resilient Agricultural Investment: Evidence from Smallholder Farmers in Pakistan
abstract: Access to appropriate finance is central to smallholder agricultural adaptation, but the relationships among digital financial access, financial inclusion, and financial literacy remain insufficiently examined. This study examined the association between FinTech access and climate-resilient agricultural investment, assessing financial inclusion as a mediator and financial literacy as a moderator. A quantitative cross-sectional survey collected data from 384 smallholder farmers in Mardan, Charsadda, and Nowshera districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Respondents were predominantly male (91.4%); therefore, the findings primarily reflect male farmers’ experiences and cannot be generalized to female-headed smallholder operations without dedicated gender-disaggregated sampling. Multiple regression, bootstrapped mediation, and interaction analyses tested hypothesized relationships, controlling for socioeconomic and farming characteristics. FinTech access was positively associated with both investment and financial inclusion. Financial inclusion retained a positive association with investment after adjustment and partially mediated the access–investment relationship, with an indirect effect of 0.222 (95% bootstrap confidence interval: 0.158–0.292), accounting for approximately 57.5% of the total association. Financial literacy positively moderates the association between FinTech access and investment (B = 0.137, p = 0.001), with stronger associations observed at higher literacy levels. These findings support the financial capability perspective, highlighting the distinct roles of financial participation and financial knowledge in climate-resilient agricultural investment. The results provide an empirical basis for evaluating integrated initiatives combining digital financial access, appropriate financial products, financial education, and agricultural extension support.
journal: Journal of Risk and Financial Management

title: MoEMamba: Mixture-of-Scale-And-Attention-Experts Mamba Network for Remote Sensing Change Detection
abstract: The Mamba network has recently emerged as a powerful architecture for remote sensing change detection (RSCD). Notably, the fusion of multi-scale features and heterogeneous attention mechanisms has proven effective in enhancing the performance of Mamba network. However, existing methods fail to quantitatively evaluate the actual contribution weights of different components during feature fusion, thereby limiting the interpretability of their improvements. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel mixture-of-scale-and-attention-experts Mamba Network (MoEMamba) for the RSCD task, which has the following innovations and contributions: (1) a Siamese Mamba architecture is employed to extract features from bi-temporal images; (2) a mixture-of-scale-experts module is designed to enhance the generalization ability across multi-scale objects, which quantitatively evaluates the contribution of multiple scale-specific experts; and (3) a mixture-of-attention-experts module is proposed to improve the accuracy, which adaptively fuses complementary responses of heterogeneous attention mechanisms based on the learned weights. Extensive experiments on the WHU-CD and LEVIR-CD datasets demonstrate that MoEMamba outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, it achieves F1 scores of 94.20% and 92.62%, and IoU values of 89.04% and 86.25%, respectively. Importantly, this study provides valuable insights into the interpretability of multi-scale feature fusion and heterogeneous attention fusion for RSCD research.
