While the One-Shot Baseline is the fastest overall (2 to 6 minutes), RAG and the Agentic AI showed higher recall in discovering compliance omissions on large documents (e.g., the 564-page SUB-002). We also identified a self-evaluation bias, where gpt-4o-mini rates its own faithfulness much higher (4.13/5.0) than the judge (2.21/5.0).

title: A Case Study on Design Strategies and Overcoming Challenges in a 100.8 MW Wind Energy Project in India
abstract: This paper discusses the development of a 100.8 MW captive onshore wind project designed to supply renewable electricity to refinery operations in western and central India. The case study follows the project from early site screening to commissioning readiness, with attention to the engineering decisions that shaped wind measurement, layout planning, foundation design, logistics, grid connection and construction sequencing. Rather than presenting the project only as a feasibility exercise, the paper focuses on how the design was adapted to real site conditions, including land availability, road access, monsoon constraints, utility interfaces, local coordination and execution risk. The project is also examined as part of industrial decarbonization, where large energy consumers need renewable power that is technically reliable, commercially viable and practical to deliver on the ground. The project was developed through an integrated review of wind resource, land suitability, grid access, constructability, regulatory requirements and local sensitivities. Wind conditions were studied using 120 m meteorological masts, long-term correlation and energy-yield modelling. Turbine locations were then refined in WindPRO to manage wake losses while still allowing practical road access, cable routing, crane movement, environmental buffers and safe erection. Foundation designs were prepared using turbine-wise geotechnical findings rather than applying one uniform design across all locations. Logistics planning included route surveys, strengthening checks and movement strategies for long blades and other oversized components. Electrical planning covered pooling substations, transformers, protection systems, SCADA, forecasting, scheduling and coordination with the utility network. The project is expected to deliver a capacity utilization factor of about 32-34%, with annual generation in the range of 280-310 GWh. Layout optimization kept modelled wake losses within about 5-8%, while internal electrical and evacuation losses were treated separately in the energy estimate. The project is expected to avoid about 290,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions each year. The main observation from the case is that a captive wind project of this scale cannot be managed through sequential engineering alone. Wind assessment, layout design, foundation engineering, transport planning, grid-interface work and stakeholder engagement have to progress together. Early route checks, reserve micrositing options, monsoon-aware planning and interim evacuation arrangements helped reduce execution risk and protected the overall project schedule. The paper contributes practical insight into how a captive wind project can be structured for an energy intensive industrial consumer. In this type of project, generation performance, grid access, land control, power quality and commercial deliverability have to be solved as one connected problem. The case shows that moderate-wind sites can still support a bankable development when turbine configuration, hub height, micrositing, wake-loss control, foundation design, transport feasibility, reactive power support and evacuation planning are aligned early. The experience is relevant for developers, industrial consumers, EPC contractors, utilities, lenders, consultants and policy practitioners working in markets where land, access, grid capacity, open-access charges and local coordination can influence project success as much as the wind resource itself.

title: Strategy and Crisis Monitor: An AI-Enabled Autonomous Maritime Monitor for Disruption Intelligence and Operational Resilience
abstract: This paper presents the Strategy and Crisis Monitor, an agentic artificial-intelligence (AI) enabled executive dashboard conceived, built, and deployed end-to-end in days to track regional events, incidents, transport disruption, and energy-market signals during a live crisis. The work pursues three objectives: to demonstrate that autonomous AI agents can convert public maritime, energy, and trade data into always-on disruption intelligence; to replace the analyst-curated executive briefing with a live, evidence-linked signal layer operating under human oversight; and to compress executive decision latency from days to minutes. The architecture comprises three operational layers. An ingestion layer of autonomous agents continuously normalizes heterogeneous public sources, including multilateral chokepoint transit data, vessel-tracking feeds derived from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), international oil and gas statistics, and maritime trade and connectivity indicators, supplemented by market context as evidence layers. A classification layer maps incoming data against a rules-based event taxonomy covering chokepoint disruption, export-route stress, gas exposure, port-connectivity deterioration, and regional trade impact. A prioritization layer scores signals using a weighted composite risk index with exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) and cumulative sum (CUSUM) anomaly detection, and surfaces them through a 60-second executive scan pattern with full drill-down to underlying sources. Deployed live during the March 2026 Strait of Hormuz disruption, when average daily transits collapsed by approximately 95% against the February baseline and the benchmark very large crude carrier (VLCC) rate reached an all-time high, the platform was used to brief senior leadership of a major national maritime and energy logistics operator in near real time. It reduced executive decision latency from a typical 24- to 72-hour analyst cycle to under five minutes per signal, a compression factor of roughly 290 to 860, while integrating more than 40 public indicators. The same detection logic was subsequently applied retrospectively to four historical chokepoint crises, in the Red Sea (2023 to 2024), the Suez Canal (2021), the Strait of Hormuz (2019), and the Panama Canal (2023 to 2024), confirming that the monitored public signals were available weeks to months ahead of official statistics in every case. Those case studies were reconstructed with knowledge of how each episode unfolded and therefore document signal availability and design generality rather than prospective detection performance. The contribution is twofold and is, to the authors’ knowledge, the first implementation of its kind in the maritime-resilience and energy-logistics literature. First, a decision-method contribution: passive public reporting feeds are converted into a structured, always-on resilience instrument fusing maritime, energy, and trade signals in a single operating view. Second, an operating-model contribution: the architecture is public-data-native, lightweight to sustain, and reproducible across operating companies, corridors, and risk domains, and is presented together with the governance, oversight, and control mechanisms required before agentic AI is admitted to a critical operational environment. Both are directly actionable for practicing engineers and planners in operations, strategy, and resilience roles.

title: Real-Time Operator Fatigue Detection Using Physics-Informed AI and Standard Camera Infrastructure
abstract: This paper presents a real-time physiological fatigue monitoring system for energy facility operators using standard camera hardware. The system applies remote photoplethysmography to extract heart rate and heart rate variability from facial video without wearable sensors. It targets control room personnel, drilling supervisors, and offshore operators. A key objective is equitable detection performance across all skin tones present in multinational energy workforces. A seven-stage Physics-Informed Synthetic Dataset generation pipeline (PISD-rPPG) was developed. Photorealistic operator faces were generated using StyleGAN3 and animated using SadTalker. Physiological signals were synthesized with NeuroKit2 and refined using a diffusion model. Forward Plane-Orthogonal-to-Skin (POS) validation confirmed signal integrity before reverse-POS embedding injected signals at melanin-dependent amplitudes derived from Beer-Lambert absorption physics, producing skin-tone-accurate training data across all six Fitzpatrick classifications. A Temporal Shift Convolutional Attention Network (TSCAN) was pre-trained on the synthetic dataset and evaluated on subjects from the MMPD dataset that were unseen during training. The prototype targets a capture rate of 30 Hz and scores operator fatigue using three personalized physiological thresholds calibrated against individual baselines. The study employed a controlled comparison protocol. TSCAN was pre-trained on 793 synthetic videos generated through the PISD-rPPG pipeline and evaluated against the full MMPD real-world dataset as a cross-domain transfer test, achieving a mean absolute error of 15.7 BPM. This result confirms that physics-informed synthetic data produces signal representations that transfer to real camera footage without any exposure to real training subjects. Under the same protocol, an unrefined physics-based baseline of 80 synthetic videos reached 17.2 BPM. The published SCAMPS reference of 2,800 synthetic videos (McDuff et al., 2022) reports 19.05 BPM under a separately published test configuration. Because dataset size and refinement differ together, that gap is reported as a combined effect and not as the contribution of the diffusion stage alone. Demographic fairness across Fitzpatrick Types III-IV and Types V-VI is an objective of the pipeline design rather than a result of this study, and no per-group figures are claimed, since that evaluation is still under replication. The prototype classifies operator fatigue into three graded states: Normal, Mild Fatigue, and Severe Fatigue, each triggering a corresponding supervisor alert. Status descriptions are generated by a rule-based condition engine requiring no language model. Face detection and cropping occur on the operator device, and no full-frame video is transmitted or stored. No hardware beyond existing facility cameras is required. This paper presents the first application of a physics-informed synthetic training strategy for rPPG-based operator fatigue monitoring in energy facilities. The synthetic pre-training stage addresses demographic bias without requiring real subject data, while the diffusion refinement stage demonstrates that effective domain adaptation requires no real subjects at all. This combination is directly relevant to energy industry deployment contexts where diverse workforces and limited data collection opportunities are practical constraints. One boundary should be read carefully. The accuracy reported here is for heart-rate estimation on benchmark data. Fatigue detection itself has not been validated against a fatigue reference in any operator, and a controlled operator pilot is the next stage of this work.

title: Operational Risks and AI Bias in LLM-Based Agentic Systems for a Process Plant: Electric Motor Operations Case Study (Oil & Gas)
abstract: The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has encouraged many industries to explore Agentic AI. Earlier AI tools were used mainly for data analysis and information retrieval. Newer systems can carry out a sequence of related tasks, combine information from several engineering sources and prepare recommendations with relatively limited user input. These capabilities can support document review, procurement quality, maintenance planning, commissioning and operational troubleshooting. However, they also bring risks that are not normally associated with conventional engineering software. Because the output is probabilistic, a recommendation may be influenced by missing technical information, incomplete operating context, biased source material or incorrect interpretation of safety-critical requirements. It may still appear convincing even when its engineering basis is weak. Electric motors are used throughout oil and gas facilities and are essential to the operation of pumps, compressors, fans, cooling systems and other plant equipment. A motor failure can interrupt production and, in some cases, affect the safety or reliability of the wider process. Decisions relating to motor protection, alarms, equipment condition, commissioning, fault diagnosis and maintenance therefore require sound engineering judgement, supported by approved protection settings, operating history, OEM guidance and relevant international standards. This makes electric motors a practical case for examining the use of LLM-based Agentic AI in a safety-critical engineering environment. The paper considers a series of representative motor scenarios covering design review, Factory Acceptance Testing (FAT), commissioning, operational troubleshooting, predictive maintenance, alarm assessment and root cause analysis. The findings show that prediction accuracy and model confidence alone do not establish whether an AI recommendation is safe or technically reliable. That judgement depends on the quality of the available evidence, the completeness of the operating context, compliance with applicable standards and protection philosophy, and verification by a qualified engineer. To manage these risks, the paper introduces the Engineering Trustworthiness Assurance Framework (ETAF). It brings the main checks into one process, starting with the quality of the available engineering information and ending with the approval of the final recommendation. ETAF includes the Engineering AI Assurance Pyramid (EAAP), the Operational AI Risk Propagation Model (OARPM) and the AI Engineering Governance Matrix (AEGM). It also uses three assessment measures: the Engineering Trustworthiness Score (ETS), AI Recommendation Criticality Level (ARCL) and Engineering Confidence Index (ECI). These are proposed as practical, illustrative tools that organisations can adapt when introducing LLM-assisted decision support in safety-critical engineering work. Although the representative scenarios are based on electric motor operations, the proposed framework is applicable to other classes of rotating equipment deployed throughout upstream, midstream, and downstream oil and gas facilities. The paper contributes a practical engineering governance approach that complements existing AI assurance initiatives by emphasizing engineering trustworthiness, protection philosophy, operational accountability, and responsible human oversight during the deployment of Agentic AI systems.

title: Decoding Residual Oil (RZO), Mobile Oil and Solid Bitumen: An Integrated Geochemical Methodology for Characterizing Hydrocarbons Near or Below the Oil Water Contact (OWC) and Free Water Level (FWL)
abstract: Carbonate reservoirs commonly contain hydrocarbon accumulations below the interpreted free water level (FWL) and oil-water contact (OWC), creating significant uncertainty regarding hydrocarbon saturation, fluid mobility, reserves estimation, and development strategy. Conventional petrophysical evaluation often identifies these intervals as hydrocarbon-bearing; however, production performance may be poor if the retained hydrocarbons occur predominantly as immobile residual oil or solid bitumen. This study presents an integrated geochemical and petrographic workflow to characterize hydrocarbon occurrence, mobility, alteration, and charge history within a giant carbonate reservoir in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. The workflow combines mud-log gas evaluation using Total Gas and Wetness-Balance ratios, solvent extraction and extract-yield measurements, Rock-Eval pyrolysis (S1, S2, and pyrogram characterization), Saturate-Aromatic-Resin-Asphaltene (SARA) analysis, gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS), Low-Temperature Hydrous Pyrolysis (LTHP), and petrographic and SEM-EDX investigations. These complementary datasets were integrated with petrophysical observations to understand hydrocarbon presence, distinguish mobile hydrocarbons from residual oil and solid bitumen and to evaluate their distribution relative to the FWL and OWC. The study also assessed the role of biodegradation, charge mixing, and structural evolution in controlling present-day fluid distribution. The results demonstrate that hydrocarbons occurring below the FWL comprise varying proportions of mobile oil, residual extractable oil, and pervasive pore-filling solid bitumen. Extract-yield and pyrolysis data reveal a systematic decline in hydrocarbon mobility from crestal locations toward flank positions and below fluid contacts. Samples associated with productive oil columns exhibit elevated Total Gas, extract yield, S1 yield, and saturate content, whereas intervals dominated by residual hydrocarbons are characterized by lower gas readings, reduced S1 yields, higher S2 yields, and enrichment in resin and asphaltene fractions. GC-MS chromatograms reveal a spectrum of oil alteration, ranging from relatively fresh oils with smooth baselines and complete n-alkane envelopes to heavily altered hydrocarbons characterized by prominent UCM humps and pronounced n-alkane depletion. The coexistence of a substantial UCM hump together with preserved n-alkanes in many samples indicates that biodegradation was followed by a subsequent hydrocarbon charging event, resulting in mixing between an earlier degraded paleo-oil and a later, more mature oil charge. Petrographic observations and SEM-EDX analyses confirm that solid bitumen occupies approximately 21–37% of pore space in selected samples, reducing pore connectivity and contributing to hydrocarbon immobility. LTHP further demonstrates that total hydrocarbon saturation can substantially exceed the fraction that is mobile under primary depletion conditions. Although mobile oil volumes are generally limited, a significant proportion of hydrocarbons remains potentially recoverable through enhanced oil recovery (EOR) processes. Collectively, the integrated dataset indicates that hydrocarbons below the FWL represent a complex mixture of biodegraded paleo-oil, residual extractable oil, and solid bitumen preserved through multiple charging, alteration, and remigration events associated with the tectonic evolution of the field. CSIA results further contextualize these mobility and alteration patterns within the broader framework of reservoir connectivity. The limited carbon-isotope variability observed among MDT oils, produced oils, and crestal-to-flank core extracts indicates a common source and comparable maturity level. This CSIA-based interpretation is important for field-scale reservoir modelling, as it supports a laterally connected petroleum system while acknowledging significant spatial heterogeneity in oil quality and producibility. This study demonstrates that integrating mud-gas interpretation, extract yield, pyrolysis, SARA, GC-MS, LTHP, CSIA, and petrographic techniques provides a robust methodology for differentiating mobile and immobile hydrocarbons in carbonate reservoirs. The workflow improves estimation of recoverable resources, reduces uncertainty in reserves evaluation, and supports the selection of appropriate development and EOR strategies in reservoirs containing significant residual oil and solid bitumen accumulations.

title: Scaling Subsurface Interpretation with Seismic Foundation Models and Agentic Workflows
abstract: Seismic interpretation is rarely a single-task exercise. In practice, an interpreter moves back and forth between data quality, reflector continuity, fault expression, stratigraphic organization, seismic attributes, well control, and geological judgment. A fault cube, a horizon volume, or a conditioned seismic section may each be useful on its own, but none of them is sufficient if the outputs are disconnected from the rest of the interpretation workflow. This paper presents SeismicGen, a framework developed to make seismic AI more reusable and more consistent across interpretation tasks. The workflow is built around a Seismic Foundation Model, or SFM, that provides a shared seismic representation for several specialized interpretation agents. These agents support seismic conditioning, fault characterization, relative geological time estimation, relative acoustic impedance generation, fault and horizon extraction, seismic-to-well tie, and geobody detection. The purpose is not to replace the interpreter with a black-box system, but to provide a common technical layer that helps different AI outputs remain consistent with one another. The workflow starts with seismic preparation, normalization, and quality control. Depending on the interpretation objective, the seismic volume is then passed through selected agents. The outputs are not treated as isolated products. For example, fault probability and displacement indicators can guide fault-surface extraction, while relative geological time can support horizon organization. Results are checked through section-by-section review, geological consistency checks, residual and amplitude analysis, comparison with available well information, and interpreter-led validation. The main practical issue addressed in this paper is the lack of continuity between many existing seismic AI tools. A model may detect faults or pick horizons, but the output often remains separate from the broader interpretation process. SeismicGen is designed to connect these tasks through one shared representation and a coordinated agent workflow. Initial applications indicate that this structure can reduce repetitive interpretation effort, improve consistency between interpretation products, and shorten the path from seismic volume to review-ready subsurface outputs. The contribution of the paper is a practical architecture for applying foundation-model and agentic-AI concepts to seismic interpretation. The paper focuses on workflow design, technical integration, quality control, and interpreter validation, without requiring disclosure of proprietary model architecture.

title: Proppant Pack Conductivity Under Closure Stress: Physically Bounded Permeability Model
abstract: Reservoir stimulation enables production from low permeability reservoirs by creating hydraulic fractures that serve as flow pathways between the formation and the wellbore. Proppants keep these fractures open against the closure stress of the formation, and the conductivity of the proppant pack is critical for well deliverability throughout the life of the field. In the industry, engineers estimate the decay of proppant permeability using exponential decay functions, but these functions carry a fundamental defect: they predict both zero porosity and zero permeability as the effective closure stress increases, with no physically bounded lower limit. This study proposes new asymptotically correct relations between proppant permeability and applied stress that serve as potential substitutes for the conventional exponential decay models. The work reformulates three established compressibility models (hyperbolic, exponential, and power) in terms of the yield stress, computed at the point of maximum curvature of the compression curve consistent with the Casagrande method, and derives permeability models with bounded asymptotes through the power relation between permeability and void ratio. We compare the predictions of the proposed models with proppant and sand data compiled from published studies, and evaluate performance against the conventional exponential model. The hyperbolic model fits the compression data best, including the sharp decrease in void ratio after yield in brittle sands. The proposed permeability models predict the hydraulic conductivity from the fitted compressibility parameters with a single free λ-exponent, while the conventional model underpredicts or overpredicts the conductivity around the yield stress and the difference grows at high stress where the pack retains a finite residual conductivity. The framework implements in three stages: characterize the proppant once through standard laboratory tests, predict the permeability at any effective closure stress, and integrate the revised equations into fracture models for production forecasting in unconventional and geothermal operations.

title: Generation of a New Empirical IPR Correlation for Vertical Wells Producing from Multi-Layered Oil Reservoirs with Crossflow Between the Layers
abstract: The Inflow Performance Relationship (IPR) is a foundational tool in petroleum production engineering, quantifying the relationship between reservoir pressure drawdown and wellbore oil production rate. Classical empirical IPR correlations, most notably Vogel (1968), Klins and Majcher (1992), and Wiggins (1994)—were derived for single-layer, solution-gas-drive reservoirs through numerical simulation and regression analysis. Despite their widespread adoption over more than five decades, these correlations share a critical and well-documented limitation: none accounts for the inter-layer crossflow that occurs in multilayer reservoirs where adjacent layers communicate under contrasting pressure conditions. In multilayer systems with active crossflow, a low-pressure layer can act as a net fluid receiver rather than a producer, exhibiting negative production rates at high bottomhole pressures—a physical regime entirely outside the predictive scope of all existing empirical correlations. This study fills that gap by developing and validating the first closed-form, dimensionless empirical IPR correlation for vertical wells completed across two communicating oil-bearing layers under active crossflow. A two-layer black-oil simulation model was constructed using commercial black-oil simulation software, with Layer 1 initialized at 1,000 psia and Layer 2 at 3,500 psia to create a controlled and physically representative pressure imbalance that induces inter-layer fluid communication. A systematic one-factor-at-a-time sensitivity analysis across five key reservoir and fluid parameters—porosity (ϕ), horizontal permeability in x- and y- directions (Kx, KY), API gravity, and oil viscosity (µo)—generated 574 dimensionless simulation data points. Nonlinear regression in commercial statistical software yielded a six-parameter power-law additive correlation validated by a coefficient of determination R2 = 0.904, Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 0.596%, and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.772. The physical significance of each regression coefficient is interpreted with direct engineering relevance: viscosity dominates the model with an exponent of -7.623; vertical permeability carries the only positive exponent (+0.456), representing its role as the inter-layer communication conduit; and API gravity exhibits a reversed trend under crossflow conditions—lighter oil enhancing the crossflow drive and paradoxically reducing individual- layer deliverability. An explicit applicability domain is defined for all nine model parameters. A step-by-step practical application workflow is provided to enable direct field use. The correlation provides a practical screening and forecasting tool for multilayer well deliverability assessment where crossflow complicates conventional IPR analysis, and its performance is benchmarked against the Vogel IPR baseline.

title: Benchmarking Time Series Foundation Models for Oil and Gas Data Forecasting and Well Event Detection
abstract: Forecasting and event detection in oil and gas operations are critical for maintaining flow assurance and equipment health, yet traditional analytical models often struggle with complex, non-linear time-series data. This study evaluates the efficacy of a newly developed time series foundation model against existing state-of-the-art foundation models for forecasting operational sensor dynamics across diverse well event regimes. Performance is benchmarked using open-source operational datasets, specifically a flowloop laboratory dataset representing multiphase flow slugging, and a comprehensive offshore dataset covering regular flow, unstable flow, severe slugging, and rapid productivity loss scenarios. Results indicate that the proposed model generally outperforms the baseline models, demonstrating superior accuracy in forecasting typical periodic or semi-periodic patterns associated with severe slugging flow, as well as tracking the slow progression of degrading equipment conditions. However, the evaluation also highlights specific limitations; the proposed model is less effective under conditions where operational changes are sudden and abrupt, scenarios in which alternative models exhibit lower error rates. Ultimately, this benchmarking highlights the strengths of specialized foundation models for predictive maintenance and flow assurance, while outlining areas for future algorithmic refinement in handling abrupt transient events.

title: A Framework for Efficient Well Control Modeling in Machine Learning Surrogates
abstract: Numerical reservoir simulators are computationally prohibitive for many-query tasks such as field development planning; which motivates a new generation of machine learning surrogates that promise significant speed ups over traditional solvers. A persistent challenge in that work is the treatment of dynamic well controls and sparse, time-dependent well data. Surrogates that reproduce cell-centered fields accurately often leave the quantities an engineer actually depend on, namely bottomhole pressure, phase rates, water cut, and gas-oil ratio, either outside the model or regressed by unconstrained output heads that need not respect rate control or the underlying inflow physics. We address this by coupling a three-dimensional Temporal Neural Operator (TNO), whose branch and trunk factorization decouples spatial geological heterogeneity from temporal well control inputs, to an analytic and fully differentiable black-oil well module placed inside both the training graph and the forecast loop. TNO predicts pressure, water saturation, and gas saturation on the Norne benchmark model. The well module samples those fields at the 504 completion cells belonging to 36 wells, evaluates black-oil properties and three-phase mobilities, corrects each completion pressure to a common bottomhole datum, and recovers the rate-controlled bottomhole pressure in closed form. Phase rates are aggregated per well and the computed pressure returns to the operator input, closing the loop. We trained the TNO on 400 Norne cases and evaluated on 50 held-out cases over a 61-step sequential forecast, the model reaches a pressure MAE of 0.559 bar, a bottomhole pressure MAE of 2.99 bar, and a water cut MAE of 0.034. Scheduled rate closure holds by construction rather than by fit, so the well responses stay physically consistent at the cost of a forward pass rather than a simulation run. This framework presents a step toward fast, physically consistent proxies that closed-loop reservoir management requires.

title: From Tender to Total Depth: Artificial Intelligence and Generative AI Agents Deployed Across Well Construction Planning and Execution
abstract: Well construction projects face data and decision challenges across two distinct phases: pre-well planning and tender preparation, where manual offset analysis limits coverage and introduces bias; and active drilling execution, where non-productive time (NPT) events demand rapid, data-backed decisions. This paper describes an AI-driven platform that serves the full well lifecycle — automating time and risk estimation during tender preparation, and providing real-time generative AI agent support during drilling execution. The platform integrates 13+ AI and machine learning engines applied to Daily Drilling Reports (DDRs) across two workflow phases. For tender and planning: a transformer-based model classifying drilling activities from operational text in English and Spanish; Monte Carlo simulation for probabilistic time forecasting; a genetic algorithm adapted from multiple sequence alignment techniques to predict operational sequences from historical patterns; a Well Risk Index (WRI) for quantitative, data-driven risk scoring; and hierarchical aggregation from section to campaign level, enabling AFE and P&L scenario construction at tender scale. For drilling execution: a suite of generative AI agents that mine offset cases, rank hypotheses, and deliver remediation recommendations for NPT events including stuck pipe and loss circulation; a location-specific Optimum Fishing Time (OFT) model that replaces global cost rules of thumb with field-calibrated economic thresholds; and a generative AI agent that automates end-of-well report generation from DDR data. The platform is actively used by more than 250 engineers with 38% annual growth, supporting assessment of well construction tenders valued at $10-17 billion annually. Well classification time has been reduced from 8 hours to 20 minutes per well; offset coverage has expanded from the 10-20 wells an engineer can manually review to the full available dataset; data preparation effort has been reduced by 56%; risk assessment is 26 times faster than manual evaluation; and a MENA region tender involving 56 well architectures and 158 sections was completed in at least half the previously required time while evaluating all available offset wells. End-of-well report generation has been reduced from four days to two days. Automated technology identification has been estimated to recover approximately $34.7 million in value per year. P10 well time targets — previously aspirational — are now consistently achievable with actionable steps across the Integrated Well Construction (IWC) portfolio. This paper presents a field-validated, multi-component AI architecture structured around three operational phases — winning work, planning wells, and executing well construction programs — that links time estimation, AFE optimization by constructing scenarios, risk quantification, NPT classification, technology identification, local fishing economics, and real-time drilling event support within a single, data-driven ecosystem. Finally, this solution enables engineers to spend their time in high value activities than in manual excel intensive tasks.

title: Predict, Prevent, Protect: Transforming Onshore Road Safety by Leveraging Data and Technologies
abstract: ADNOC Onshore operates across a large and dispersed onshore environment where road transport is a daily operational exposure for employees, contractors, logistics teams, project personnel and heavy-vehicle movements. This paper presents ADNOC Onshore's development and early implementation of an AI-enabled road safety transformation aimed at progressing toward zero motor-vehicle incidents. The program is organized around a six-pillar strategy—driver compliance and capability; people, compliance and engagement; infrastructure and vehicle movement control; technology and AI enablement; awareness, enforcement and culture; and joint partnerships and alignment—delivered through a dedicated Road Safety Taskforce and a structured Motor Vehicle Crash (MVC) reduction framework. Within that strategy, the paper examines the technology and AI enablement pillar, delivered through an initiative under the iASPIRE program that combines In-Vehicle Monitoring System (IVMS) data, Anti-Fatigue Driver Detection (AFDD), AI-camera pilots, drone-surveillance pilots and AI agents. The Road Safety Command Center (RSCC) follows a prevention loop of monitor, detect, intervene and learn, supported by a workflow of detect, assess, act, verify and close. Early results show improvement despite rising exposure: driving exposure increased by around 22%, while incidents decreased from two to one and the incident ratio improved from 0.013 to 0.0053 per million km. Because the incident count is small, greater emphasis is placed on leading indicators, including a 33% reduction in IVMS violations and a 77% reduction in unknown drivers. The paper concludes that the early improvements reflect the combined contribution of all six pillars, with technology and AI enablement making road safety risks more visible and actionable, and human coaching and field intervention converting digital insights into safer driving practices.

title: Geology-Consistent Seismic Conditioning Using Foundation Models for Improved Interpretation Readiness
abstract: Seismic conditioning is a high-impact but high-risk step in the interpretation workflow because it modifies the data used for fault mapping, horizon tracking, stratigraphic interpretation, amplitude review, and reservoir characterization. Conventional filters can improve visual continuity, but they may also attenuate subtle geological signal when faults, terminations, or low-amplitude events occupy the same frequency, dip, or continuity range as noise. This paper presents a geology-consistent AI-assisted conditioning workflow designed to improve interpretation readiness while preserving reflector geometry, amplitude character, structural discontinuities, and stratigraphic terminations. The workflow uses a pretrained conditioning agent derived from a reusable seismic foundation model. The broader SeismicGen foundation-model and agentic interpretation framework is described in the companion paper [1]; the present manuscript focuses on the conditioning task, residual output, technical quality control, and interpreter-led validation. Unlike survey-specific denoising models, the conditioning agent is designed for direct inference and does not require retraining for each new survey. Adaptation, when used, is optional and limited to calibration or parameter tuning rather than full model retraining. Because the agent is foundation-model enabled, it does not operate as a generic random-noise removal tool. It uses learned seismic context to distinguish geological coherency from incoherent noise, helping preserve faults, stratigraphic terminations, and amplitude features that may be weakened by conventional filtering. The workflow is evaluated using side-by-side comparison of input and conditioned seismic, residual inspection, amplitude-distribution review, spectral checks, continuity measures, and geological plausibility assessment. Representative examples show improved reflector continuity, reduced incoherent background noise, clearer fault expression, and better visibility of subtle discontinuities. The residual panels provide an essential transparency check: a technically acceptable residual should be dominated by incoherent or unwanted energy and should not contain coherent reflectors, fault planes, stratigraphic terminations, or reservoir-related amplitude events. The contribution of the paper is a practical technical framework for AI-assisted seismic conditioning that combines residual-based transparency, interpretable quality-control metrics, and expert validation. The workflow is positioned as an interpretation-readiness step that supports downstream fault interpretation, horizon tracking, stratigraphic framework building, and reservoir characterization while retaining geoscientist oversight as a non-negotiable acceptance criterion.

title: Classical finite-element solvers as differentiable graph programs on GPUs
abstract: Conjugate heat transfer in turbomachinery, heat exchangers, and energy systems couples buoyant flow to the surrounding solid on complex geometries. The cost of simulating it is dominated by large sparse linear solves on CPUs. We recast a mixed finite element discretization on unstructured meshes, and its multigrid pressure solve, as sparse graph layers within an automatic differentiation framework. Nothing is trained: weights are entries of the assembled operator, and manufactured solutions recover theoretical convergence orders. Reverse-mode sensitivities match central finite differences; one gradient costs 5.6 forward solves with unrolling and 4.9 with implicit differentiation, nearly constant from one to 32 parameters. Implicit differentiation through every linear solve substantially reduces truncation-induced sensitivity error and makes memory independent of forward iteration count. Against three established solvers, no single code is fastest; the ranking depends on the regime, the size of the problem, and the accuracy demanded. With the discretization, mesh, time step, and tolerances held fixed, the same problem runs up to 181 times faster per step on one GPU than on 32 CPU cores, and the pressure solve alone runs 18.7 times faster. The graph representation depends on operator sparsity rather than the governing equations, providing a route to other assembled discretizations.

title: The leakage premium in decomposition-based cryptocurrency forecasting
abstract: Decomposition-ensemble models, which split a price series into components with methods such as CEEMDAN and VMD and forecast each component with a neural network, report remarkable accuracy for cryptocurrency returns. This paper shows that most of that accuracy is look-ahead. The decompositions are two-sided, so components computed on the full sample carry future prices into every input. A typical pipeline that stacks VMD on top of CEEMDAN is run on daily prices of five major crypto-assets from 2018 to 2026 under three protocols that differ only in the information each decomposition uses, with data, networks and random seeds held fixed. With the full-sample decomposition the model calls the direction of next-day returns correctly on 93 per cent of days and explains 96 per cent of their variance. Computed causally, the same model is right on 52 per cent of days and has an out-of-sample R 2 of -23 per cent, worse than a forecast of zero. Look-ahead accounts for essentially the entire premium in directional accuracy, a premium that grows with each added decomposition layer and hardly moves across market regimes. A second mechanism explains why causal decomposition forecasts are harmful rather than merely uninformative. The revisions of end-point components cancel across components in the target but not in the forecasts. A long-flat rule driven by the leaky forecasts would show phantom profits of about 146 basis points a day net of costs. A simple falsification test, proposed here, detects look-ahead in any such pipeline. JEL classification: C45; C53; C58; G14; G17

title: ddmtorch: A Differentiable, MPS-Accelerated Toolbox for Drift-Diffusion Model Estimation on Apple Silicon
abstract: The drift-diffusion model (DDM) explains choice probabilities and response-time (RT) dis- tributions through a small set of interpretable parameters, but fitting it requires repeated eval- uation of the Wiener first-passage time (WFPT) density. Existing tools are predominantly CPU-bound, rely on compiled code, or are embedded in Bayesian sampling frameworks. We present ddmtorch, an open-source PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019) implementation that vectorizes the WFPT likelihood across trials and subjects, supports automatic differentiation, and runs on CPU and Apple Silicon Metal Performance Shaders (MPS). It provides batched maximum- likelihood estimation, a hybrid large-time/small-time density following Navarro and Fuss (2009), synthetic data generators, and a fixed-proportion contaminant mixture. On an Apple M5 Mac- Book Air, MPS evaluates a forward–backward pass over one million trials in 0.62 s, versus 1.22 s for CPU float32 and 3.21 s for CPU float64; a 50,000-trial, 20-subject MLE fit takes 2.32 s ver- sus 4.10 s and 7.30 s. In 100 synthetic datasets with 500 trials each, parameter correlations ranged from 0.981 to 0.998. On a public motion-discrimination dataset, ddmtorch and PyDDM recovered nearly identical parameters; on a 14-subject dataset, ddmtorch MLE and a PyMC 5 HDDM-style hierarchical fit correlated at r = 0.996–0.9995, with the expected shrinkage. The WFPT math is inherited from the literature; the contribution is a differentiable, MPS- ready implementation and a transparent evaluation. We document limitations, including the absence of inter-trial variability and hierarchical priors. Because MPS does not support float64, precision-sensitive workflows should use the CPU float64 path.
